Uniform title: Parātriṃśikāvivṛti Main title: Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa Secondary title: Parātriṃśikāvivṛti
Author: Abhinavagupta Editor: Śāstrī M. R.

Publisher: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State Publication Year: 1918 Publication City: Srinagar

Oṃ tatsat. Salutations to Śiva, whose body is self-luminous bliss.
Now.
The Śrī Parātriṃśikā Text,
accompanied by the commentary titled Tattvaviveka composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
[Salutation to] the Great Mother, the source of fresh creation, who rests upon the stainless arts (kalās).

May my heart— filled with the body of the Father (Janaka), who is beautiful and concealed within five faces, and consisting of the emission (*visarga*) of the state that flashes forth from the union of those two— throb as the lineage of the nectar of the Absolute (*anuttara*). [Abhinavashṛṣṭi]

The Mother Śakti is the locus of the pure sacrificial form (*śuddhādhvarūpā*), whose splendor (*mahaḥ*) is characterized by absolute fullness; she is the refuge of the stainless digit (*vimalakalā*), whose essence is supreme awareness (*paravimarśa*). Likewise, she is "five-faced" (*pañcamukha*), meaning her desire is fulfilled by the five powers; because she is devoid of anything further to be desired, her body is completely full (*bharitatanuḥ*).

Śiva is the progenitor whose nature is fullness; "from the union of those two" means from the friction consisting of their aesthetic harmony (*sāmarasya*), there arises a state of vibration—a creative emission (*visarga*) whose nature is the desire to overflow outwardly, which is the primordial matter (*prakṛti*).
May such a family of the nectar of the Absolute (*anuttarāmṛtakula*), whose form is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), throb within my heart.
"For here, everywhere, the word 'I' has as its sole object pure consciousness alone"—
by this statement of the Mīmāṃsā, may the heart of the consciousness of "mine," characterized by sovereignty and bestowing existence,
that ultimate reality denoted by words such as "world-bliss" (jagadānanda) and so forth, shine forth perfectly.
The meaning is: "May consciousness, which is devoid of freedom, blossom; for consciousness that lacks freedom is indeed non-consciousness.
Therefore, having cast aside that lack of freedom which is the characteristic of non-consciousness in consciousness, may it manifest as consciousness.
Furthermore, it is well known that Abhinavagupta’s mother was named Vimalā and his father was Narasiṃhagupta.
The detailed explanation of this pentad, however, is found in the *Tantrālokaviveka*; that alone should be consulted. || 1 ||
Within which this entire universe shines forth as an external appearance during the process of emanation;

I bow to that Goddess, the singular self-awareness, who abides in the state of the unsurpassed when agitation has ceased; within whom—the meaning being that although the universe, which is the appearance of "this-ness," possesses the characteristic of being a reflection, it is not separate from her despite appearing distinct.
*Note: The phrase "within whom" (*yasyām antaḥ*) implies that because the universe is endowed with the nature of a reflection, it exists as non-separate even while appearing as something additional.*
It shines forth. When "agitation"—characterized by the manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā*)—has subsided, there is self-awareness:
that whose luminosity is consciousness within itself, by itself alone. This is the description of the nature of the Absolute (*anuttara*). I salute it;
I enter into it. || 2 ||

I bow to the Supreme Anuttarā, who, having established within her heart the Trika consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, causes it to shine forth— meaning she manifests that which resides within externally.
The wonder of intuition regarding one's own speech [that is, one's own powers]. || 3 ||
Victorious is the illustrious primordial Guru, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, whose greatness is priceless and who has liberated the multitude of bound souls. 4.
(p. 3) Accompanied by the commentary composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta;
for the awakening of his own disciples [so that their awakening may occur without dependence on other treatises].
And for the sake of reminding those who have been awakened by other scriptures,
this slight effort— characterized as a systematic treatise— is being made by me, Abhinavagupta.
The venerable Goddess said:
O Lord, tell me the unsurpassed teaching that immediately bestows the *kaulika* accomplishment,
by the mere knowledge of which—
One attains equality with Khecarī. || 1 ||

The Supreme Lord, whose nature consists of the fivefold acts, is eternally—[even while the manifestation of creation and so forth continues]—pervaded by His supreme form of power (*śakti*) which consists of grace; in reality, He is essentially one with grace alone, for power cannot be perceived as distinct from Śiva. And that power consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of grace toward the worlds.
First of all, [the power] consisting of reflective awareness (parāmarśamayi), which is the Visionary (paśyantī)—
[meaning that the infinite powers are not yet externally manifested]— is initially differentiated by hundreds of infinite powers.

Established within consciousness—which consists of the supreme great mantra and is not limited by space or time—the Paśyantī level exists precisely as an undifferentiated state of both speech and response that is yet to arise. And that very [consciousness], being non-dual with the consciousness of all subjects, is indeed eternal. [It is indeed eternal.]
Even upon the manifestation of Paśyantī and the other levels, Paśyantī, existing in its present form, [whatever— that is,
whatever collection of objects such as that which is desired— is] intended, that very thing,
awakened by the restriction of appropriate causes [the cause being desire and so forth], [is manifested] by the mere thread of consciousness.
He reflects as follows: "Since [the intuition] perceives everything as being common [to all], how can there be a sequence such as desire (*icchā*) and so forth therein?
To clarify this point, he provides an example, saying "just as" (*yathā*).

This refers to a variegated cognition (*mecakadhiyaḥ*), that is, a cognition of blue, which is conditioned by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the cognitions of many existents and non-existents.
Because of the suitability for awakening the seed of memory— since one or another of the factors that awaken memory, such as a similar object, perception, or reflection, is present—

a particular thing alone is recalled by memory; for there is no differentiation here at the time of the initial cognition, because in the state of *paśyantī*, differentiation is not manifested through the perceived object and so forth.

In that state where there is non-difference between the specific signified and the signifier, speech vibrates; however, in the intermediate stage (*madhyamā*), having manifested the difference between those very same signified and signifier, it proceeds through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [that is, identity].
But *vaikharī*, characterized by the function of deliberation (*vimarśa*), consists precisely in the manifestation of the distinction between those two;

this being the established state proven by one's own self-awareness—[the sense being that since the clear distinction therein is established by one's own experience, it is not something to be reached through external means of knowledge]. That very ground which is *parā-vāc* is itself...

Consisting of the essence of the ultimate nature of the power of the illusory word, which is non-conventional, uncreated, and absolute, it is impelled by the portion that constitutes the vitality (*vīrya*) of mantra according to the method to be described; subsequently,
it remains established in reality even within the states of *paśyantī* and the others, for without it, [those states] would not exist.
Because it would follow that it is insentient due to the consequence of lacking luminosity. In that regard—[the word "therein" refers to the primary ground;

the sequence beginning with "this" is the specification of the essential nature of space, time, and so forth, both free from conceptual construction and involving conceptual construction]—there is no such thing as the mental construction of distinctions such as "this," "thus," "here," or "now," and for that very reason...
Beginning from the form emitted by the supreme power of the Great Mantra— [meaning *paśyantī*]—
and extending as far as the manifestation of the distinctions of states issued forth as *vaikharī*,
this [this ground of supreme speech] consists of its own self-revelation (*svacamatkṛti*).
(p. 6) Having come to rest within its own self, which consists of light, it vibrates as that very "I," whose ultimate reality is uninterrupted manifestation. This will become clear further on.

Right in the midst of that, however, where there is the non-manifestation of the aspect of differentiation in Paśyantī, and where there is the manifestation of differentiation in Madhyamā— in both those cases, in the form consisting of the powers of knowledge and action,
which is the essence of Sadāśiva and Īśvara [the term "possessor of the power of knowledge" is used by way of metaphorical identification of the power and the possessor of the power].

Sadāśiva is Īśvara when his power of action (kriyā-śakti) is predominant. The wonder "I am that very [power]" is a state of consciousness filled with the wonder of the infinite universe contained within it; this consists of the Paśyantī and Madhyamā stages, wherein one's own self alone—meaning one's own nature characterized by both undifferentiated and differentiated subject-object duality—is realized.
In reality, it is Supreme Consciousness itself that contemplates that which consists of the consciousness of another, and this Supreme Consciousness is called the Goddess. To this extent,
by means of the play consisting of the bliss of self-reflection— ranging from the sequence of emanation beginning with Paśyantī down to external objects such as blue and so forth,
and proceeding according to Her own will— the term "play" (krīḍā) here refers primarily to a vibration (spanda) that follows joy.

The intended meaning is precisely the description of the essential nature of Bhairava, the Blessed One, who, by transcending all things, abides in a state of supreme excellence; thus— [p. 7] —of Bhagavān Bhairava. Thus...
With the desire to abide in supreme excellence— that is, with the nature of a victor—
by means of performing such worldly transactions as infinite knowledge, memory, doubt, and certainty,
and by means of the manifestation consisting in the appearance of that very blue and so forth within everything appearing everywhere, [it is perceived] by all indeed.
Because it is praised by those who are inclined toward Him through the penetration of His light, it has been said:
"There is no other entity called 'praise' apart from the all-pervading Supreme Lord;
for praise consists in the realization: 'I am Śiva,' in a form that transcends all."

Thus: "And according to one's desire, by attaining the state of being the Self of all through the limitation of space and time"—here, one should not suspect a contradiction in the phrase "by attaining the state of being the Self of all through the limitation of space and time," because that which is all-pervasive necessarily exists in all directions and at all times; it is not, however, [limited].
The state of being the self of all, without limitation by space, time, and so forth, has been stated by the venerable Somānandapāda:
"Pervasiveness is obstructed by the characteristics of space, time, and the like;
for that which is necessarily pervasive exists in all directions."
Thus:
"Salutation to the peaceful radiance, whose form is infinite pure consciousness unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and for whom self-experience alone is the sole means of knowledge."
Thus, that definition of "being the self of all" (sarvātmatā) which was formulated by the venerable feet of Bhartṛhari has been refuted by this [work]. For this very reason, primarily... [p.
The divinity of Bhairavanātha alone is intended, while that of his Śakti, the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī), is her very nature as a Goddess (Devī).

As it has been said: "The root *div* is used in the senses of playing, desiring victory, worldly transaction, splendor, praise, and motion. And likewise, [this occurs] through the grace of the portions and sub-portions of divinity consisting of such supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya*).
Regarding Viṣṇu, Viriñci, and the others— as has been determined elsewhere by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:
"Thus, when the group of Lords of the Tattvas has dissolved, at the time of creation again,
those who seek that state, or those beloved by Śiva, preside over that station."

That which is called *brāhmī* is indeed the power (*śakti*) of another; by causing that [power] to descend therein, he becomes Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth, according to the sequence of the Vaiṣṇavī and other powers.

Thus ends the discourse on the deities. In this way, when the Blessed Goddesses Paśyantī and Madhyamā reflect upon their own very self, thinking, "I alone am the supreme goddess Parāvāk; thus have I spoken," then, by virtue of that form in which the commencement of Māyā shines forth, this pair—characterized by the manifestation of the objectivity of "this-ness" (idantā)—arises. Therefore...

The meaning is "the undertaking of *māyā*. By virtue of its dependence upon one's own self (*svātman*), in accordance with the differentiation belonging to that *māyā*, one [perceives] that very supreme state (*parābhūmi*) as consisting of one's own self (p.
Regarding it as a reality [in its general state, or as having been in a past time],
they conceive of it as being beyond the reach of the internal and external senses— which are the life-force of the manifestation of difference— and thus perceive it as indirect (*parokṣa*);
for the definition of the indirect is that which is "beyond the senses" (*akṣebhyaḥ yat param*).

Because there is no delimitation by "today" based on the division of days dependent upon the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies—[the meaning is: since the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) is situated above Mount Meru while the sun is situated below it, how can the conventional usage of "today" be determined there by the movement of the sun and so forth?]. A day of Brahmā is measured by many kalpas.

Furthermore, because Viṣṇu and the others exist above that, and because the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth occurs within [the body], one should infer for oneself that the emergence of sixty years occurs right there—wherein, during an external day, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred movements of the prāṇa. Thus, even within a hundred-thousandth part of the vital breath, there is the conventional usage of "day"; this is established as being conceptual (kālpānika).

According to the principle that "how could there be 'presentness' (adyatanatva) in the non-conceptualized body of consciousness?", one should reflect by means of the sequence of the third person singular (uttama-puruṣa) in the remote past tense, completing the sense of a past, non-present, and remote object: "I myself, being none other than that Supreme Goddess of Speech (parāvāk), spoke thus, since there is no differentiation between the signified and the signifier."
The intended meaning (tātparya) is as follows:
"I indeed lamented while dreaming"—this is precisely how it is logically established. For instance, that past state...

One does not remember [the previous state] because it was not previously experienced; now, however, through the greatness recounted by another person, or through the onset of bodily transformations such as stammering produced by acts like excessive lamentation and singing, one attains that state through wonder. For this is not merely a lack of cognition, as in the case of one who says, "I was indeed intoxicated" or "I was asleep."
"He lamented"—for in states such as intoxication, sleep, and fainting, there is a state of "remoteness" (*parokṣatva*) due to the non-apprehension of specific objects of knowledge;
however, in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*), there is simply the absence of any specific object of knowledge at all.

Here, because it consists of the nature of the Fourth (*turya*) through the realization of identity with the knower alone, whereas in intoxication and the like, there is a predominance of delusion and possession.

Thus, this is the distinction; however, the state of being beyond direct perception (*parokṣatā*) is exactly the same. In this way, every cognizer (*pramātṛ*), whether situated in the roles of teacher and disciple or in any other worldly transaction, at all times, while performing whatever action, becomes the vessel for all transactions only by entering into this very consciousness (*saṃvit*). Therefore—
The Goddess speaks, reflecting upon that very reality as it has been stated: "I alone am eternally everything, through non-duality.

I reflect upon this on the supreme level (*parābhūmi*); otherwise, for one who perceives it differently, this clear manifestation belonging to the intermediate level (*madhyamābhūmi*) would not exist at all. Thus it is said: "The Goddess said. In the same way, it should be understood that later on it will say, "Bhairava said. For even there, it consists of the non-differentiation of one's own power and the power of the other.

"I am indeed the very self of Bhairava"—this is the meaning. When there is the reflective awareness (*amarśa*) of the nature of emanation, characterized by the predominance of Śakti, the appropriate reflective awareness of the Goddess is "I" (*aham*);
when there is the reflective awareness of absorption in withdrawal, characterized by the predominance of the possessor of Śakti, it is "Maha-A" (*maha-a*).

It is the wonder of the form of Bhairava. This will be made clear later. And having summarized all that was previously stated, he says "this" (*etad*): the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the supreme consciousness—which consists of the power of will—precisely within the ground of the *paśyantī* and *madhyamā* stages, which consist of the power of knowledge; and that alone is...

Therefore, the purpose of this entire treatise, from beginning to end, is precisely the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the true power of the supreme mantra, which arises through the unfolding of the sequence of preceding and succeeding words and sentences within the power of knowledge that consists of Sadāśiva— namely, the letters *da*, *e*, *va*, *ya*, and *u*.
The arrangement of words and sentences beginning with the letters *va*, *ā*, *a*, *bha*, *ai*, *r*, *a*, *v*, and *a* is as follows. And it is said in the *Svacchandatantra*:

Abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple, the Lord Sadāśiva himself brought down the Tantra through sentences consisting of preceding and following words. [The phrase "in the roles of teacher and disciple" refers to the characteristics of Śiva and Śakti; "Tantra" refers to the scripture characterized by reflective awareness (vimarśa).]

Thus, the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*) is eternally unsetting within all subjects; for it has been said that [having entered into consciousness itself, it becomes the vessel of worldly transaction].
This very supreme relation is the sole life-force of the *Ṣaḍardha-sāra* scripture, as it has been stated:
Of Śiva, who is perfect, supreme, and of immeasurable splendor,
there is his power called Sādākhya, which is the sphere of his own volitional agency.
The wise know that through that [power], Sattva first attains a connection;
and then, by means of intermediate yoga, it gradually [attains a connection] with the one called Sāda.
The second was proclaimed by him as attained by the god Ananteśa;
and the third, O Goddess, was [attained] by Śrīkaṇṭha together with Nandin.
Because it was received from the gods by two [means], it is proclaimed as "divine" (divya);
and it was briefly expounded by Nandin to the sages.
That fourth [empowerment] was proclaimed by the Blessed One as both divine and non-divine,
through the application of the sequence of exposition, for the worship of the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).
The fifth [type] consists of the mutual relationship between disciple and teacher;
thus, this fivefold connection has been fully described.
Thus, because even a scent of duality has dissolved within this very oneness,

and because it is characterized by fullness— the state of being the self of all— all other types of relationship are, in this context of the Absolute (anuttara), [subsumed within] the Supreme Relationship alone.

13) Because of the teaching already mentioned, there is a great interval [between] the divine, the non-divine, and so forth, due to their being essentially one with the Supreme (para). This has been stated in the *Trikahṛdaya*:

The Supreme Lord is eternally intent on emission within His own power; He is the soul of grace, the creator, and the destroyer, and He is unrestrained. [“Intent on emission” means being solely absorbed in that; in the form of the creator He is “I,” and in the form of the destroyer, by way of its opposite. He is unconditioned.

Thus, in this manner, because the Supreme Lord— the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*)— is eternally emergent and consists of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that very internal object which flashes forth in its undivided state is, upon reaching the level of *paśyantī*, grasped with the desire to differentiate it into phonemes, words, and sentences; and on the level of *madhyamā*, it remains established in a state of differentiation.
Beginning with the *vastu* (the objective ground) and extending up to the end of *vaikharī* speech, it is unsurpassed; how so?

It consists of the arrangement of phonemes, words, and sentences belonging to the differentiated realm of *māyā*. This very [reality], which is not perceived as such, is the mouth of Bhairava, whose essence is the reflective awareness of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*).

The seed-syllable of the expansion of the Trika scriptures, the stable state (*dhruvapada*) consisting of the agitation arising from the meditative union (*samāpatti*) and the friction (*saṃghaṭṭa*) of the powers of Śiva and Śakti, whose forms are the essence of the unsurpassed sense of "I" (*anuttarāhaṃbhāva*).

The primordial [reality] is the singular form of life for all living beings; therefore, because there is no exclusion and because designations such as "place" are inapplicable, [one might object]: "Indeed, this is the rule of the dependent (paratantra) system—namely, that at the outset, a certain devotee, preceded by an announcement to those who are to be graced, performs the designation of the place of the Goddess and Bhairava."

Just as in the *Svacchanda* and other texts it is said, "seated upon the peak of Kailāsa," and so forth, why has that same [description] not been applied here as well? For this very reason, he says, "because there is no exclusion," and so on. Furthermore, one should not think that this mention of the location and so forth is appropriate only in the gross sense and not in its internal nature; for even in the case of "Kailāsa" and the rest, [the same applies].
Because it is precisely the subtle reality that must be explained, it is as follows: what is the *elā*—the throbbing power (*śakti*)—in the aperture of Brahmā at the crown of the head?

Seated upon that is the seat (*āsana*), the upper station, of the Peak (*śikhara*) which consists of the pervasive (*vyāpinī*) and the equalized (*samanā*) levels, a state situated above all paths; that is the peak of Kailāsa, and there he is seated.
[Thus,] the principle of luminosity (*prakāśatattva*) transcends that [duality]. Therefore, the sequence beginning with "place" (*sthāna*) and so forth is not tenable.
Furthermore, the reality (*vastu*), consisting of the question and its answer, is eternally manifest from the very beginning as undivided.
Consequently, this alone is the intended meaning here: one's own self (*svātman*), which is the intrinsic nature of all things, is itself self-luminous.

One's own self alone, through the distinction of questioner, respondent, and answer—consisting of one's own self as the "I"-ness—[is established] by means of questioning, answering, and speaking. (p. 15)

Marveling, he reflects: "I myself, desiring such diverse wonders, while knowing it to be so, become exactly thus"—this is the extent of his thought. At that very moment, the Goddess said, beginning with "How is the Absolute?
and Bhairava replied, "Listen, O Goddess," continuing from the middle until the words "this is the Rudrayāmala. Or else:

All the treatises, beginning with the *Pañcasrotas* and extending to this worldly convention— that is what is called the "supreme connection. It is the secret essence of instruction, which immediately brings one to the state of Bhairava and is ever-present.
The *Praśnasarvasva* has been explained by me, Abhinavagupta.
Out of a desire for the welfare of our disciples, however, we shall state this very point in summary:
whatever is to be known or to be done in all worldly transactions,
that unfolds, free from duality, in the supreme fourth stage (turyabhūmi).

In Paśyantī, which consists of the outlining of distinctions and possesses sequentiality, there exists a connection with a clearly manifest sequence within; in Madhyamā, one partakes in that differentiation.

The intermediate [state] is the Visionary (paśyantī), and then the Supreme (parā); by means of the non-differentiation of these, one should intensely contemplate that state at that moment as if it were beyond perception, like one who is intoxicated or asleep.
In the midst of those who are like the primordial syllable *u*, who are free from all duality,
who are like the mother (*ambā*),
and who shine with the non-dual radiance of the center; there, within the fire-pit of the yogis, the first fruit of the practice of the *jāhnaṇa* (yogic heat) is manifested.

By means of desire, through the non-attachment to similarity and dissimilarity, and by the continuous application of the practice of the supreme jewel of the mind, one should remain established in the state of non-distraction.
In this very way, he will explain this state of unsurpassedness— thus it was said by the venerable Somānanda:
"Immediately following the first pulse of Śakti belonging to the Lord Bhairava-Bhaṭṭāraka, who is intent upon the fivefold act..."
And so forth, as stated in his own commentary (*nijavivṛtti*). "For the purpose of shattering that knot" means: the "knot" (*granthi*) is the non-clear expression of the meaning;

its "shattering" (*nirdalana*) is the discernment (*viveka*). This is our effort, we who have been sanctified by that teaching. The connection (*saṃbandha*) has been stated. The subject matter (*abhidheya*) is the *Triśikā*, which refers to the three powers—will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and...
Of actions— such as creation and so forth, which are otherwise designated by names like "exertion" and the like.
[Creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace—these are "creation" and so forth; likewise, exertion and so forth;

and arising, manifestation, relishing, the swallowing of time, and resting in one's own nature—these are what are designated by such various names. She is the Sovereign (Īśikā), the Mistress (Īśvarī), and the Power of Sovereignty (Īśanā).
Because it is impossible for the aspects of action (*karman*) to enter [into consciousness] without being inseparable from that which is to be ruled (*īśitavya*), there is non-difference from that.
"The future one" (*bhāvinī*) refers to the Blessed Lady Bhaṭṭārikā Parā, the Consciousness who transcends these three divisions of power and consists of the non-differentiation of those powers;
she alone is the denoted meaning (*abhidheya*). And precisely because of the connection with her, this designation called the *Trīśikā* (The Triad) exists.

The venerable teachers also read it as *triṃśakā*; and because of the similarity of the syllables, they provide this etymological explanation (*nirukta*): it is called *triṃśakā* because it "declares" (*kāyati*) the three powers (*tisraḥ śaktīḥ*), and not *triṃśikā* because of its connection with thirty verses, since even this much [meaning—that is, the meaning of the two hundred thousand verses—] is contained within the meaning of the *triṃśakā*.
For it is said in the *Śrītantrasāra*:
"The meaning of the thirty [verses] has been proclaimed by you in an expansion of one and a half crores.
Furthermore, the relationship between the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheya*) is precisely one of identity (*tādātmya*), as has already been largely explained.
And the purpose for all cognizers is [to become] a vessel for this much unsurpassed knowledge, produced by virtue of the grace of the pervasive Lord’s supreme descent of power (*paraśaktipāta*).

Thus, through the state of the heart becoming one with the innate nature of all entities, there occurs an identity with the *ahantā* (I-consciousness) filled with the wonder of one's own self— the *ahantā* in which the entire multitude of principles esteemed as "bondage" appears as differentiated only through the play of the abundance of its own fragrance.

Liberation while still living consists of an immersion (*samāveśa*) into the non-difference from the very nature of Bhairava. For it is proclaimed that liberation from what is considered bondage belongs to one who is firmly rooted— even within the sphere of the vital breath, the body, and so forth, which constitute the objects of the internal and external senses— in that state known as "impulsion" (*preraṇā*), which takes the form of exertion, power, life-force, and the like.
For even when the mere conditioned constructs (*saṃskāra*) of illusion have been shattered, what is this talk of "liberation," and with respect to what?
Thus it is said in the *Śrī Spandakārikā*:
"Or rather, for whom the entire world is consciousness as play..."
Seeing thus, he is constantly disciplined; he is liberated while living, without a doubt.
Thus [it is said]. And this will become clear very soon:
"Kill, kill! Run, O Jaṅkuṇa! Here and there are those who have no fear of death; they remain with their feet raised upward, seeking the forest of the fruits of this world."
p.

19) Therefore, by means of this self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the very purpose (*prayojana*) here is the final culmination of all human goals; thus, there is no room for a further purpose of the purpose. As it was said in the *Stotra*:
O Lord, the ultimate fruit of actions or ritual injunctions is indeed nothing other than absorption into You;
however, as for those who desire fruits here [in this world], [their attainment is otherwise].
The state of being deluded would result in an infinite regress.

The relationship, the subject matter, and the purpose have already been stated. Now, the meaning of the text is explained. Regarding the term *anuttara* (the unsurpassed): it is so called because there exists nothing higher (*uttara*) than it. Just as...
For the thirty-six other principles, culminating in Anāśrita-Śiva,
possess the capacity to augment consciousness only after they have attained their respective states of perfection through entry into the awareness of Supreme Bhairava;
however, the supreme, perfectly full consciousness of Supreme Bhairava does not [augment itself] by anything else whatsoever distinct from itself.
It transcends [all else], because its essence consists in the wonder of a perpetually self-manifesting flow that is unrestrained and independent.

Thus, there exists no "answer" (uttara) in the form of a response to a question therein, precisely because it is the great ocean of consciousness, the ultimate abode of the infinite flashes of intuition (*pratibhā*) that surge forth.

When the disciple becomes a vessel for inspired inquiry, eloquence, and so forth, that very state is in reality the eternally manifest Reality— what else, then, could be the Teacher’s answer? For "uttara" means both "answering" and "the higher."
For that liberation (apavarga) favored by the proponents of dualism does not, in reality, transcend being animated by necessity (niyati). To explain:

first, having entered from the body into the state of vital breath (prāṇa), then having ascended from there to the plane of intellect (buddhi), and then having further assumed the nature of life known as vibration (spandana), and even from there...

Having established oneself in the state of the void (*śūnyapada*), which consists in the exhaustion of all that is knowable, and then, upon attaining the peak of the progressive attenuation of all impurities, the individual soul (*aṇu*) is liberated through the manifestation of Śiva-nature,
because superimposition has become purposeless— thus [it is said]. Such indeed is the [state] at the navel, heart, throat, palate, and the [planes of] Brahmā and Bhairava.

21) The sequence of ascending [through the stages] attained through the sequence of presiding over the letters beginning with *la* is as follows; likewise, in the *Tantrāloka*, according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*):
"That which is pure consciousness alone, whose ultimate reality is light..."
Having cast off that object of cognition from itself, the sky shines forth in its isolation.
That very Self of mine, when this object of cognition is differentiated, becomes intent upon appropriating it;
falling [into manifestation] as a surging upward force, it is designated by such terms as "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) and "vibration" (*spanda*).
Therefore, they say that consciousness first transforms into the vital breath (prāṇa),
and thus the wind becomes the substratum for the principle of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
This is that power of vital breath (*prāṇa-śakti*) which grants the longing for internal exertion;
it is considered to be vibration (*spanda*), throbbing (*sphuratā*), repose (*viśrānti*), the living soul (*jīva*), the heart, and intuitive insight (*pratibhā*).
That activity of the vital breath (prāṇa-vṛtti), by means of its fivefold forms beginning with prāṇa, makes the body its own;
through that very [activity], consciousness becomes full.
Thus: in this way, by means of the contemplation of dissolution (*layabhāvanā*) according to the natural flow of emanation, there is an upward ascent (*ūrdhvakramaṇa*).
Because they ascend in such a manner, it is "the higher" (*uttara*); the "higher" is bondage, the "higher" is crossing over, and the "higher" is liberation.
Where there are no such "higher" states, and where even the word "higher" does not exist in any respect—that is what is meant by "such" (*īdṛśam*).
Exclusion by way of direct perception is "such-like" (*tādṛśam*), while exclusion by way of indirect perception is [the other].
One should effect the exclusion as "such-like"; that wherein this does not occur is the unexcluded, which is the "incomparable" (*anuttara*).
For even the term "this" (*idam*) has its very life in the exclusion of an excluded answer—thus, because it functions as an excluder.
It is of the very nature of conceptual construction;
for this very reason, the subject belonging to the realm of Māyā who wishes to enter the unsurpassed form is, for the time being, merely imagined.

But in that case, regarding the specific nature (*viśeṣātman*), that which is non-conceptual and inseparable [from it] is, in reality, the unsurpassed; for, without the manifestation of that conceptualized form, the existence of [entities such as] *bhāvanā* and so forth is simply untenable in reality. Thus, it is said to be "freed from the instrument of *bhāvanā*" (as stated by the venerable Śrī Somānanda): [The verse follows: "Just as the moon does not exist apart from its rays... etc.
What is the use of meditation and practice for Śiva, who is eternally manifest?
Once gold is known, what further need is there for meditation, practice, and the like?
Truthfulness consists in maintaining a firm resolve, always as steadfast as that toward one's mother, father, and so forth;
it is established once through valid means, whether from scripture or the word of a guru.
Once Śiva-nature, which resides in all things, has been known through firm realization,
there is no further need for any instrument or even for meditative cultivation anywhere.

Thus [it is said]. But it is not merely due to a lack of utility that such a supreme state exists even within the functions of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) in this very same way. As I have stated myself in a hymn:
"Like the sky, it is spread out without any interruption..."
The mass of water falling as a thin stream is not clearly perceived;
[it flows] over the branches of the trees in the grove and the thick parts of the houses.
However, by the power of its limiting adjuncts, it is clearly perceived.
It never at all comes within the range of experience.
Then, through their conjunction with place, form, time, arrangement, stability, vibration, and agency,
they produce a consciousness that is capable of experience.
Those whose awakening instantly surpassed that of Bharavi;
And so forth. Furthermore, it will be stated later that "the answer to the answer is also no answer," and this is explained as follows:
in this very way, for the individual soul (*narātman*), the Śākta is the answer; beyond that, the Śāmbhava;

and likewise, even within those, through the distinctions of the elements (*bhūta*), the principles (*tattva*), the self (*ātman*), the Mantras, the Īśvaras, the Śaktis, and so on, there is a state of successive higher levels (*uttarottaratva*) within one's own self alone.

Even within the elements such as earth and the rest, for one who is awake, the dream state follows; from that, the deep sleep; from that, the fourth state (*turya*); and beyond that, the state transcending even that. Thus, even within the states of waking and so forth, and within one's own self, there is a successive progression through the distinctions of the fourth and the rest. This very point [is stated by] Śrī—

24) This has been determined by me in detail in the *Pūrvapañcikā*; it is not explained here at length because it is of no use [in this context] and would result in excessive bulkiness of the text. Such is that state of being "subsequent" (*uttaratva*), which produces the delusion of non-duality regarding the sequence of what comes before and after.

Where there is no division based on the castes of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, or outcastes, nor any inequality; where the emphasis lies on the state of being (*bhāva*) rather than the subsequent term. The "subsequent" (*uttara*) refers to the powers such as Paśyantī and the others, Aghorā and the others, and Parā and the others—[namely] Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, in their subtle and gross forms.
These are established as the single *hari* (the one who takes away), and they are not sequentially the powers (*śakti*) consisting of will, knowledge, and action;
rather, they are the powers characterized as the presiding deities: Aghora, Ghora, and Ghoraghorā.
Their nature as *Parā* and the others is as described elsewhere: "That by which He sustains this universe, from Śiva down to the earth, as nothing but non-conceptual pure consciousness."

The Supreme Lord perceives, illuminates, and [manifests] that which is His supreme power (*parā-śakti*). That [power] is "supreme-cum-non-supreme" (*parāparā*) by virtue of both difference and non-difference, like a mirror or an elephant [reflected therein]. That [power] is "non-supreme" (*aparā*) by virtue of difference, through which [entities] appear as mutually distinct. This triad is embraced within Himself by her, through the nature of synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*).
She too, designated by another term as *Kālakarṣiṇī*, is indeed the Supreme (*parā*) who seizes. Elsewhere [it is said]:

"By whom this [universe] is not [perceived], where these [states] would not exist... Regarding the root *nud* (in the sense of "impelling"), there is *nuta* (impulsion); by that, there is crossing (*taraṇa*) through the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*).
The "crossing" (*taraḥ*) is the consciousness of the disciple; the Guru is the consciousness—
p.

25) "The Guru should, by means of his intellect, impel [the disciple's consciousness] to grasp the Self at the time of initiation"—according to this principle, one's own awakened consciousness is impelled into the unawakened consciousness of the disciple. By that...

Through the sequential arrangement of the various locations—beginning with the *haṃsa*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the void (*śūnya*) at the equinox (*viṣuvat*), and so forth—and by means of the application of the *pūrṇāhuti* (the final oblation) in both the *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts) rites, he ordains here the initiation that bestows liberation; for it is said in the *Tantrasāra* regarding the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*): "Initiation is of the nature of union with Śiva. And therein lies the [union] of consciousness.

How can there be a connection—whether gradual, preceded by a cause, or an effect—for that which is self-luminous, all-pervasive, and undifferentiated by specific space, time, or form? For instance: since it is undifferentiated by form, how could it be in the "entire" or the "partless"?
Since it is all-pervasive, how could there be a conjunction? Since it is undifferentiated by space and time, how [could there be a sequence]?

Since it is said that [the scriptures] prescribe initiation (*dīkṣā*) which bestows liberation, how could there be any injunction (*vidhāna*) regarding that which is self-luminous and autonomous? In this regard, the sequence of initiation consists of the yoga of both the *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts) for the sake of attaining enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), whereas the *niṣkala* alone is for the sake of attaining liberation exclusively. Are these not mere mockeries?
Thus, that in which there is no crossing (*taraḥ*)—that is, no traversing—by means of such a pushing or impelling (*nudā-preraṇena*), is the "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
As it will be said: "For one who knows this in its true essence, there is the path leading to *nirvāṇa*."
Initiation occurs... [text missing] ...initiation.
Thus: from the root *an* (to breathe), with the suffix *kvip*, *an* refers to the non-subtle (*aṇu*) Self, such as the body, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth. Likewise, *anana* is life;

that which is called "life" is essentially nothing but the state of being devoid of the various individualized powers and the sense of ego (*ahaṃtā*) residing within the body and other such structures. (p. 26)
The commentary: That which is the empty subject—
that very reality of Light (prakāśatattva), which indeed appears as the universe consisting of the triad of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge through non-difference from itself,
and which is not yet differentiated by the powers such as will— is, by its own sovereignty, within itself...

In order to manifest the object of knowledge—which is the self of the universe existing in non-differentiation from Himself—the Self separates [the object] from Himself through the reflective awareness, "I am transcendent to everything. Because He is devoid of all objective states (*bhāva*), He is traditionally taught in the *Āgamas* as the "unobscured subject" (*nirāvaraṇa-pramātṛ*). And here, emptiness (*śūnyatva*) refers to...

This is due to the destruction of all objective states (*bhāva*), but not because consciousness itself is likewise [destroyed]; for if that were the case, everything would become blind and mute. And it has been said elsewhere:
"By means of all objects of cognition and all dharmas, and by all principles (*tattva*) without exception..."
It is empty of all latent tendencies toward affliction, yet it is not empty from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Thus it is said: the state of being his very response is the supreme transcendence in every respect due to its ultimate reality.
Since the world is filled with both the insentient and the sentient because of its singular nature as Bhairava, the insentient remain submerged within the single life-force (*jīva*).
Herein lies the intended meaning: what is the sense of the statement "the jar manifests to me"? It is my own manifestation.
Being permeated by vibration, it has indeed attained my own nature because it consists of consciousness. And it has been said by the venerable master Utpaladeva:
"In this way, although these [phenomena] appear as if unreal within the Self, they exist only as the manifestation of Light itself."
The dull-witted ones... [text missing] ...the dull-witted ones.

Thus, even those others who are known as "living" among the insentient (*jaḍa*)—their bodies, vital breaths, subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and forms of emptiness are likewise indeed insentient; what then can be said of them?
This being so, that which is attached to the jar, the body, the vital breaths, the subtle body, pleasure, and its absence—being real—is [the Self].
That very [consciousness], having become the form of the individual soul (jīva), shines as reality. Likewise, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"For thus, the foundation of insentient things rests upon the living being."

And for those who live, what is called "living" is that single supreme sovereignty of the Lord, consisting of knowledge and action, as previously described. For even in other [systems], it is only the body and so forth [that are considered living or non-living]. Thus, they are "non-living" or "living."
The meaning is that [the object] appears only at the initial moment of perception (*āpāta*), but not within the nature of consciousness itself. It appears as something separate;
however, that which is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is self-luminous precisely through non-duality, and this alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
As it was stated by the venerable Utpaladeva:
"Knowledge and action are considered the life-force of living beings.

Thus, life itself consists of knowledge and action alone. And as for this "A," it is that which is the waveless ocean of consciousness, resting in the great natural light that is free from *māyā* and beyond the reach of the scriptures.

The first stage consists of the wonder of one's own self (*svātmacamatkāra*), which culminates in the perfect state of "I-consciousness" (*paripūrṇāhaṃbhāva*) characterized by the reflective awareness of the universe as consisting of the unfolding of power (*śāktollāsa*); it pertains to both stages [the first and the second]. [The first stage, consisting of the unfolding of power: "I" as the reflective awareness of the universe.]

The stage of the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*) means the final stage. "Kalā" refers to that very [stage], which, according to the method to be explained, is this state ending in emission (*visarga*); its "crossing over" (*taraḥ*) is the surging upward above all things.
p.

29) Where there is the state of functioning (*vṛttitva*); where there is no *nut*—that is, no impulsion consisting of action characterized by sequence and dependent on duality such as going to and coming from space and time—that is *anut*. [It is so called] because it is more [subtle] than even space and so forth, according to worldly convention.
That which is with excellence is unsurpassed; [the author speaks of the excellence even of that unsurpassed state with the words "tasyāpi" and so forth].

For in the case of space and the like, such a sequential action might indeed occur due to the influence of various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as pots that possess conjunction, and due to the connection with inherent properties (samavāyin) such as sound; however, in the principle of consciousness (saṃvittattva), this is not so.

In that which is the essence of sovereign freedom— complete and uninterrupted in every respect— the multitude of states constituting the locus of all thisness (*idantā*), comprising the various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that are suspected [of being other], is filled by resting in a state consisting of the wonder of differentiation; thus, the Self is fulfilled.

In the Self, which is without appearance yet eternally manifest, and in which non-appearance has been made into an appearance through self-acceptance, there is no succession dependent on space and time— whether as the appearance of "this-ness" or its non-appearance; therefore, it is indeed without succession,
consisting of the intensity of the self-reflection of one's own nature, known in traditions such as the *Matsyodarīmata* by the name "Reflection" (*vimarśa*).

Regarding the term *kriyā*: that very same [word] is *anuttara* (unexcelled). The suffix *tamap* is prescribed for the mere sense of excellence (*atiśaya*). In this case, where there is a dual number or a word expressing distinction (*vibhakti-upapada*), the suffix *tarap* is used. For example: "This one is white, this one is white; of these two, this one is the whitest."
The meaning in this sentence is as follows: between these two white things, this one is more white—*śuklatara*;
or among these many white things, this one is most white. But what is this additional meaning?
For instance: "This palace is white," "This cloth is white," and "This swan is white."

Regarding these, [one might say] "this is the most white, being superior"; in that case, since both the palace is white and the cloth is white, what would be said more significantly? To apply such a statement even with respect to that cognition (pratyaya) is indeed improper. Furthermore, the suffix *tamap* could not denote a greater degree of excellence than the suffix *tarap*. This might be so, however, when [the distinction] is not intended to be expressed.

The suffix *tamap* is used when there is a specific counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*); however, when there is a requirement for a specific counter-correlative, the suffix *tarap* is used—this is precisely what depends upon a counter-correlative.

The meaning of the dual number and the sense of "distributive" (vibhajya) would require that there be only one counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), such as "of these two, this one is whiter by excess"; thus, a third [term] is not perceived, because through the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), it is understood that only the first [of the two] is the counter-correlative. Furthermore, there is no dependence on two or more [terms], since a single [entity] depends simultaneously on each one individually.

The term *mata*—in its sequence—carries no further meaning whatsoever. As for the usage *tāratamya*, it is simply a conventional term (*rūḍha*) established for an excess of sequence; it does not arise from following the sense of the suffixes *-tarap* and *-tamap*, for otherwise one might also have forms such as *tāryam* or *tāmyam*. Therefore, enough of this display of skill with fragments of grammar at an inappropriate time.
But here, when there is a requirement for a correlative term following the sequence [of comparison], even in the usage "anuttamam" (unsurpassed), this is precisely the meaning.
For instance, in another scripture:
"That which even today is not known to the perfected ones (siddhas) who possess awakened consciousness..."

Nor is there anything unsurpassed that remains unknown to anyone— even today— regarding the attainment of perfect illumination, for this concerns the perfected ones (*siddhas*) whose lineage of teachers, scriptures, and traditions has blossomed through the power of the supreme descent of grace (*para-śaktipāta*), and who are therefore endowed with true awakening.

That which is not known by itself—by those who possess the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) rooted in the consciousness called autonomy (*svātantrya*), because it is the very nature of both the support and the supported—is not known as an object of cognition; yet it is not unknown to anyone, for without it, the accomplishment of anything would be impossible. Thus, it is indeed known.
For this very reason, it is worthy of being known; because it appears as something contradictory at first glance, the phrase "something" (kimapi) means that it is the most excellent of all.
p.
31) Thus, Anuttara is the body of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), which is permeated by the essence of absolute freedom (svātantrya).
As it was said by the venerable Utpaladeva:

And as for the sequential nature of worldly activity—[“worldly” meaning that which consists of the raising and lowering of the hands, and so forth]—it arises from the power of Time, that is, from a specific power of the Supreme Lord characterized by the capacity to manifest the differentiation of appearances. It is “eternal,” meaning it has not abandoned its primordial nature; it is “of the Lord” (prābhavyā).
[This refers to] that which is non-different from the Lord. Herein is the intended meaning:

the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) of the Divine is the capacity for the manifestation of the knower and the known, which is the root of worldly cognitive activity; and within that very [capacity], the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), whose nature is the sovereignty of conjunction and so forth, is indeed the power of action (*kriyā*).
However, although it is in fact devoid of succession, it appears as if successive because it accepts a limiting factor that is colored by the reflection of the object of knowledge;

thus, since it is not delimited by time, its state of being non-successive remains established—so what more need be said here? Even when the multitude of objects of knowledge has unfolded, one who occupies the station of the subject under the influence of *māyā* [perceives it thus].
The Blessed One [has taught that] the entire aggregate of external and internal forms to be experienced rests within one's own self— the repose of the Self within the Light.
Thus.
By the principle beginning with "this," [the Lord] brings [the object] to rest and devours it; thus, even the sequence of manifestation established therein is itself swallowed.
This is the state that culminates in the withdrawal of the illumination of all phenomena—variegated by the processes of conjunction and so forth—which is expressed as "I."
That action, characterized by specific deliberation, is indeed an emergence;
however, it does not apply to the eternal power of *prābhava*, which belongs to the Lord, just as [the power of] sovereignty belongs to the Lord himself.
Thus it is said. This unsurpassed [reality] has been explained as being sixteenfold. As stated in the *Sāraśāstra*:
"The Unsurpassed is that Heart; in the Heart, there is the nature of a knot.
Having known the knot to be sixteenfold, one may perform ritual action according to one's pleasure."
Thus [it is said]:
"The knot that resides in the heart... [and so forth].

And so forth. In what manner is this such an *anuttara* (the unsurpassed)? Is it by way of abandoning the form of an answer (*uttara-rūpa*), or rather otherwise?—[here, "manner" (*prakāra*) is a specific distinction that excludes generalities; "in the form of an answer" means by way of a nature transcending the universe (*viśvottīrṇa-svarūpa*), while "otherwise" means by way of accepting a nature consisting of the universe (*viśvamaya-svarūpa*)]. And who is this?

The manner is as follows: since this entire world—consisting of the totality of knowledge and the objects of knowledge—is indeed twofold, and because all things within that collection of knowledge and objects of knowledge perceive mutual differentiation and contradiction from every side, there must necessarily be a hierarchy of superiority and inferiority among them. Thus, in what manner could liberation alone...?

Regarding the phrase "even in that which is considered bondage": the sense of the word *api* (even/also) is this: does such an unsurpassed nature (*anuttara-svarūpa*) exist only in liberation, or is it found even in *saṃsāra*, that which is considered bondage?
According to the principle previously stated—that *saṃsāra* does not exist in reality—*saṃsāra* is in fact impossible.

"Even that which is considered bondage by the power of delusion (*mohanī-śakti*)."—Thus, because the suffix *-tham* (forming *katham*) is prescribed merely in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*) without restriction to a specific case ending (*vibhakti-viśeṣa*), this question pertains solely to the manner [of bondage]. The word "Deva" has been explained. As for "Kula":

This is because [the self] consists of a collection of gross, subtle, and supreme vital breaths, senses, elements, and so forth, and exists in a relationship of cause and effect; as it has been said (p.

Because it acts through combination (*saṃhatyakāritvāt*). Thus, the family (*kula*) of consciousness itself, by way of its solidified form, becomes congealed (*styānībhavati*)— for Śiva, who is indeed Light, extends according to the sequence beginning with Śakti and Sadāśiva, down to the five elements (*bhūtapañcaka*).

Because the nature of the knower has receded into the background, solidity (*kāṭhinya*)— which consists of the excellence of the object-to-be-known— and likewise the process of congealing (*styānībhavana*),
comes to be regarded as bondage within one's own self by the bound soul (*paśu*).
Even in this state of solidification, he says that it never abandons its own essential nature, just as ice does not abandon its nature as water.
"Not so," and so forth. And it has been said in the *Mahārthamañjarī*:
"Due to the activity of that which is congealed, just as in the case of sugarcane juice, the five elements—like lumps of molasses—do not abandon their sweetness, even within the light of Śiva."
Thus, because of its very state of being, and due to the sovereignty of consciousness itself, there arises the conceit of bondage. For it is said:
"The root *bandh* means 'to gather' (*saṃstyāna*) and 'among kinsmen' (*bandhuṣu*).
Indeed, this is not so, because [consciousness] is of the singular nature of pure light and the singular form of awareness. [The phrase "because of the singular form of awareness" is used.]
The manifestation of objects is possible only for those that do not abandon their identity with the pure, conscious subject;
therefore, since memory, conceptualization, and so forth are rooted in the power of cognition, they too must be understood in this very same way. And it has been stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
The manifestation of entities appearing as present is possible only for those that exist internally, [manifesting] in an external form.
Thus: "Apart from"—that is, without—anything of these [objects] being unmanifest; [the term] "unmanifest" refers to the class of objects such as blue and so forth.

If being blue and so forth is itself the state of manifestation, and not a state of manifestation that transcends the body of the object, then— just as when a cognition does not arise, that [object] is called "blue" for everyone—
or rather, in reality, it is blue only within its own self and not for another.

Since the state of being established in another is untenable, it is neither blue nor non-blue even within its own self, because without the favor of manifestation, no determination is possible; likewise, there is also the state of non-manifestation.
Thus, the consequence of non-manifestation comes to an end, and therein the Kaulikī, which belongs to that family (*kula*), is established as her true form.

*Siddhi*—the firmness of suchness achieved through transformation—is the identity with the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Śiva, whose nature is the supreme consciousness of the heart and whose form is bliss. [The phrase "nature of the heart" refers to the nature of *spanda*. That *siddhi* bestows [this state], for it is in the identity with the unsurpassed essential nature that the *kula* resides.
It is so; as it has been said:

"The certainty regarding the other and one's own nature arises through exclusion and inclusion [namely, that in the existence of one's own being there is the absence of the other, and in the absence of the other there is the existence of oneself]."
Establishment, foundation, accomplishment, and completion are thus described.

Thus, the word *sadyas* functions in the sense of "on the same day," according to the aforementioned method [and the method has been stated as to how "presentness," which is conceptual, could exist in the non-conceptual body of consciousness]. Because the day is not fixed, [the term applies] to the same moment.

In this context, [the word] functions in this sense: the identity of the moment (*kṣaṇa*) does not consist in similarity, but rather culminates in its very essence; such indeed is the cognition derived from the word *sadyas*. Therefore, [it means] "in that very same moment."

Because the present moment is defined by its exclusivity, it excludes other past and future moments; consequently, the very temporality of the present—which is sustained by its relation to those two—would also be negated.
This is because this [present] is, in fact, the wheel of rays belonging to the Supreme Lord, Bhairava-Bhānu.

The Kula is said to consist of the expansion of one's own speech; and when that very [Kula] attains cessation— characterized by identity with the inward-turned supreme consciousness of Bhairava— then it alone becomes the unsurpassed, eternal state, consisting of the savor of the nectar of supreme bliss, and undivided by space or time.
It is of the nature of the *visarga* (the emission) and is perpetually arisen. This has been stated in the venerable *Vādyatantra*:

"Having restrained [it]—here, this very 'restraint' consists in the submergence of the objective world (*arthajāta*), such as blue and so forth, which had previously become solidified through the conceit of subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) regarding the body, vital breath, and so on, due to the intensity of its manifestation; [submergence occurs] because of that [conceit]."

By the aforementioned method, having drunk the unsurpassed nectar of one's own circle of rays— which is absorbed solely into the Light and is undivided by the two times— one becomes happy in the present.
Thus [it is said].

And the non-delimitation of both time and space has been explained at length by me elsewhere. Likewise, the accomplishment (siddhi) that arises from the body, the vital breath, and so forth, consists of the ascertainment of blue, pleasure, and other such objects which are animated by duality.

"He gives that" — explaining in detail that which was stated briefly as "the body and so forth," he says, "for the body and so forth," etc. The meaning here is this: as others have said, all worldly activity arises solely from the connection with merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); by that very quality of desire (*icchā*), the instruments [of action] are produced.
The doubt [raised here] is that even insentient things proceed toward their respective effects, yet not by means of being presided over by that [consciousness].

The word "jhagiti" (instantly) implies that this occurs without the intervention of will (*icchā*) and so forth; for it is "instantly," through the penetration of the power of the unsurpassed, eternal emission (*anuttara-dhruva-visarga-vīrya-āveśa*), which is untouched by time.
By ascending the middle ladder beginning with *prāṇa*, they effect the accomplishment (*siddhi*) consisting of the ascertainment of the true nature of entities. As it has been said:
"But rather, through contact with the power of the Self, a person may become equal to That."
"One becomes equal to Īśvara because of the characteristic of sovereignty that does not depend on another subject" (Svacchandatantra 1.8).
Likewise—

Thus, although the Kula— which consists of Śiva and Śakti— is ever-present, accomplishment (siddhi), consisting of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā), is attained according to the method described above.

The state that gives birth to the desired powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth— [namely]: "Atomicity (*aṇimā*), magnificence (*mahimā*), lightness (*laghimā*), heaviness (*garimā*), reach (*prāpti*), irresistible will (*prākāmya*), lordship (*īśitva*), and control (*vaśitva*)— these are the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*)."

Thus, it should be understood that the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) herein have non-duality as their very essence. For instance: because the nature of consciousness alone is capable of encompassing everything, it is *aṇimā* (minuteness); because it is all-pervasive, it is *mahimā* (greatness);
because it lacks the weightiness inherent in duality, it is *laghimā* (lightness); and because it is the locus of ultimate rest, it is *prāpti* (attainment).
Because of the grasping of the manifold variety of the universe, there is *prākāmya* (the power of irresistible will); because of being unimpeded, *īśitva* (lordship);

because of sustaining everything, *vaśitva* (mastery); and *yatrakāmāvasāyitva* (the power of determining things according to one's desire)—these are the *siddhis* that exist truly and in their full perfection. [One should realize] that very [state] immediately, even before it has been fully conceptualized.
He bestows [the fruit] precisely by being devoid of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), ritual action (*karaṇa*), and so forth. As it was said by the venerable Śrī Somānanda:
"What need is there for cultivation or ritual action for Śiva, who is eternally manifest? [The absence of cultivation and ritual action is itself the reason;
even in the manifestation of various forms, that very same [eternal manifestation] is the cause]."
Thus it is said. Likewise:
"Once" (meaning, as in the *Tantrāloka*, by virtue of the purification resulting from the composition of a collection of arguments based on the words of the Guru).

When the cloud of doubt has dissolved— whether through consolation regarding the scriptures or from what has been declared by those who have attained realization— touch the feet of the Lord, whose splendor shines in the sky of the heart like the sun, as you lie within the darkness.

Thus [it is said]. "By means of a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇena*) means by what one has inferred for oneself; or by a valid means of knowledge derived from scripture or from the words of a teacher.
When Śiva-nature, which resides in all things, is known through a firm-minded realization, [one attains liberation]. (p. 38)
"There is no purpose whatsoever served by ritual action (*karaṇa*) or even by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Thus, within the *Kula*—which consists of the union of Śiva and Śakti—that very power (*śakti*), which is emitted, abiding internally yet manifesting externally as the nature of extroversion, characterized as emission (*visarga*), has arisen; this is the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of Śakti.
From the initial expansion of the form of the "Ha" (hādi-rūpa-prasaraṇāt) up to the blossoming of the external mass of existence (bahirbhāva-paṭala-vikāsa-paryantam),
it bestows the manifestation of duality; for that very [reality] is the unsurpassed (anuttara) essence of the Great Light, which,
precisely because it is unsurpassed, contains within itself the expansion of all objective existences consisting of consciousness.
Due to the weight of the wonder of His unsurpassed sovereignty and absolute freedom, He unfolds duality.

For that which is not of the nature of light could never be the cause for the manifestation of the light of phenomenal existence; and if it is indeed of the nature of light, it must certainly be the very form of the Supreme Lord, Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka—so what need is there for anything else? [In this regard...]

If [principles such as] Māyā, Prakṛti, or atoms were of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), then what would be the use of stating them? And if they are not so, then being devoid of established existence (*alabdhasattāka*) within themselves, how could they attain causality toward another? Thus, by means of this web of words, the measure (*mātrā*) is known through that unsurpassed distinction (*viśeṣa*) by the means of knowledge (*māna*).

That by which the *mātrās*— those whose nature as subjects consists in protection and guardianship (*patitva*) through the form of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the act of knowing (*pramiti*)— are known, is "that which has been cognized" (*vijñātamātra*).
p.

39) Likewise, that which is known through the firm binding of specific realization is indeed already manifest; it is not something to be cultivated further, because its nature is once-and-for-all manifest (*sakṛdvibhāta*). Thus, that which is merely known is simply known.

Because it possesses the single form of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the jar and so forth never possess the form of the knower (*jñātṛ*); likewise, the knower does not possess the form of the object of knowledge. This *māyā* consists of duality; that state where both of these have vanished is "pure consciousness alone" (*vijñātamātra*). In that state, the jar and so forth, by virtue of having the single form of the knower, are self-luminous in nature. In that [state],...
And because illusion has no power over that which is merely cognized, [the yogin], abiding in the sky—that is, in Brahman whose nature is non-differentiation—moves;
he perceives the object, likewise performs activities such as rejection and acquisition, and remains in his own true nature.
Thus, *khecarī* consists of the internal and external senses, their objects, pleasure, and forms such as blue, and so forth. For it is thus:
In the void where the state of the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower does not manifest, in the manifestation of the vision of pure consciousness alone,
in the manifestation of duality indicated by the form of internal unity residing within the objects of knowledge, and finally in the emergence of clearly manifest duality—
therein arise, respectively, the powers known as Vyomacarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī.
40) Those [powers] are, in reality, according to the method stated, indeed inseparable from the power whose form consists of the *svabhāva-cara* and *khecarī*;
thus, she is one alone—[for she is the single, ultimate power of the Supreme Lord, non-different from his own nature, who is this "this-ness" (*idam*)].

Manifesting through a differentiation of various forms produced solely by a distinction in conceptual grasping (*parāmarśa*), it is worthy of being designated as "many" even while existing as a single entity. Furthermore, the designation of individual manifestations (*vyakti*) by the term "power" (*śakti*) is according to the view that power is not distinct from the Supreme Lord; indeed, this is precisely for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of difference.

The purpose [is as follows]: it is the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord. As it has been said: "His powers are this entire universe, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power. Therefore, there is a designation in the feminine gender; for [it is not the case that it refers to] the self, the mind, or the external senses.

Furthermore, the establishment and regulation of the object of differentiation is logical—because [otherwise] there would be no application of intentionality and so forth, and because [the object] would not be manifest. That very *khecarī* is perceived as being uneven through the forms of desire, anger, and so on; yet its equality exists everywhere, due to the nature of the perfectly full self.

Even the slightest lack of full knowledge regarding one's own unsurpassed nature constitutes the imbalance of the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*), and that alone is *saṃsāra*—that is, *saṃsāra* consisting of coming and going and so forth. He confirms this very point with the word "incomplete" (*apūrṇa*).
The conceit of incompleteness is twofold; one pertains to the Light (*prakāśa*).

The second [form] consists of the abandonment of independence, while [the first] consists of independent consciousness; there, the designation as "one" occurs because of the identity resulting from the loss of one's own specific nature.
Because the limited nature (*aṇutva*) is produced within one's own self through the conceit of incompleteness, there is the *āṇava-mala* (the impurity of atomicity). Furthermore,

because of the longing for that incomplete form to become complete— and according to the principle that "here, mantra is the expression [of that longing]"— there is the *māyīya-mala* (the impurity called *māyā*) arising from the perception of duality.
"Right here, the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is called *māyā*, which bestows birth and experience;
whereas in the non-awakened agent, there is the *kārma* [impurity]. These three [impurities] exist solely through the power of *māyā*.
Thus, up to this point, there has been the emergence of the impurity of action (*kārmamala*) due to the grasping of auspicious and inauspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
This very point has been reinforced by the statement beginning with "even in the slightest degree" (*aṇumātram api*), and it is to be understood through subtle observation.

Upon the cessation of that inequality—which consists in the non-recognition of one's true nature—[that is, upon the cessation of the inequality of that unsurpassed [Self], because of the absence of the three-fold impurity (*mala*); due to the absence of impurity, the mental fluctuations such as anger and delusion [cease].
They are indeed of the nature of the fully perfected consciousness of the Lord Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka. As it was said by the venerable Somānanda-pāda:
thus—likewise—
"I, the Supreme Śiva, abide in pleasure— which is the effect of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas in succession— as well as in pain and delusion. Thus it is said.
"Even in suffering, through expansion and by means of the application of fortitude for the sake of stability," and so forth.
For the mental states such as anger [arise] from identity with the wonder of consciousness; otherwise, they would not exist.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for them to attain their own essential nature independently, those very goddesses who are the deities of the instruments (*karaṇadevatā*)—
who are the rays of the sun that is Śiva and who manifest various divine sports— are likewise the internal mental fluctuations such as anger and the rest.

Possessing innumerable forms acquired through their various mutual interminglings, they assume specific gentle or fierce modalities appropriate for each respective rite— such as expulsion (*uccāṭana*), killing (*māraṇa*), pacification (*śānti*), and so forth—

according to the distinctions of *kṛtyā* and other such categories. [The distinction of *kṛtyā* is to be inferred by oneself from such statements as "Vāmā is so called because she vomits forth (*vamana*) transmigratory existence" (*saṃsāra*).]
The powers (śaktis) attend as deities (devatās). As it has been said:
"Those functions which are proclaimed for the mantra directed outward are proclaimed as the powers of this [mantra] when directed inward."

Thus, those to be worshipped have been described as being present in the scriptures such as the Mata and others, and as constituting the retinue of the venerable Lord Bhairava-bhaṭṭāraka. As it has been said:
"Kākavaktrā [is used] for eradication (*uccāṭana*)," and so on; having begun thus:
"Those very rays of the God of gods are the sustainers of the letters beginning with *ka*."

And so forth. However, those whose true nature is not fully understood conceal the wonder of consciousness— which, even within conceptual thought, has non-conceptuality as its sole essence— by entering into a state of doubt and distress through various forms of conceptualization, consisting of diverse clusters of syllables and letters, appearing as most terrible deities.
They bestow the state of being a beast bound by the snares of saṃsāra. As it has been said:
"The mistresses of the sacred seats (pīṭheśvarīs), who are most terrible, delude [beings] again and again.
Likewise:
"Causing the individual souls (*aṇu*s) who are completely absorbed in sense objects to fall lower and lower," and so forth. Likewise:
"The mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) arising from [the Absolute]—[the mass of sounds beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*. Of the group of powers (*śaktivarga*)—"

Through the *kalās* (energies) of the *ka*-group—that is, the letters beginning with *ka*—the group of powers (*śakti*) becomes an object of enjoyment. Having lost his sovereign power due to these *kalās*, he who has fallen into that state is known as a *paśu* (bound soul).
(p. 44) Thus it is said.
Having their true nature known, those very [energies], by the reasoning already stated, bestow the state of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā). It has been stated accordingly:
"When, however, in one place" [the term *ekatra* refers to the general *spanda*; "of that" refers to the group beginning with *ka*; "in the wheel" refers to the series from *a* to *ha*].
Then, having become firmly established, he who governs both dissolution and emergence attains the state of the enjoyer; thereafter, he becomes the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara).

Thus, the thorough knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpa*) consists precisely in this: that within these mental states (*vṛtti*)—namely, those such as anger and the like—which at the moment of their arising are of a single, non-conceptual form (as it has been said: "When, even in the states of contact with the knower who is the foremost of all knowledge...").
And she, remaining as she is, perceives that [object] through repose in it, and likewise in the fruit.
Thus, even as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises, although it is colored by various specific words composed of a collection of phonemes (*varṇa-rāśi*),
it is not joined with such a wheel of powers (*śakti-cakra*) whose nature is a mass of phonemes—
that [wheel] which constitutes the prior, non-conceptual, and unitary linguistic usage of the subject whose nature is conceptualization.
One might object:
conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are not distinct from experience or from other conceptual constructions; rather, they are that very same single [entity]. (p. 45)

The Lord of the wheel of consciousness, which has attained the name of "the manifest" (bhūta) and so forth through the differentiation produced by the coloring of existence with His own sovereignty—thus, liberation is indeed identity with the *khecarī* state, and that is precisely the thorough knowledge of the nature of the Absolute (*anuttara*).
[Regarding the term *anuttara*, this is the intended meaning here: it should not be thought that [liberation] is merely one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone.

Liberation is therefore [attained] through Khecarī; for Khecarī is said in the Āmnāyas to be the state of Śakti, since the nature of the Absolute (anuttara-svarūpa), which transcends all paths, is liberation here, and that is accomplished only by Khecarī, whose form is the most subtle reflective awareness (vimarśa). [It is] eternally arisen.
