Through the union and absorption (*samāpatti*) with Parameśvarī within the self of Śiva, there arises the establishment of the bliss of the reflective awareness of both. For Śiva consists of the emission of the potency of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*), which is the nature of supreme speech; and by the emission of Parameśvarī—which is replete with the "flower" consisting of the density of that potency—[there is the manifestation of that light whose nature is the Absolute (*anuttara*)].

Vīrya is the throbbing [of consciousness], and external vīrya is that which exists through identity with it as a dense essence; and that flower, characterized by the universe, is the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā) well-known externally,
and it is joined with such a creation— a creation consisting of action— that is full and manifold.

For indeed, whatever among all the internal and external organs enters therein, that very thing resides within the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) on earth, by virtue of being the most internal of all.
Because it exists in the present, it is called "middle";

however, that which has not come to rest therein does not become a sky-flower (*nabhaḥ-kusuma*). By this statement, one should not think that the sky-flower is something entirely distinct [from the non-existent], for that too—

"Because it is one with light, it is thus. That which is called *ojas*—the essence that vitalizes all limbs and exists as the conscious self in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—resides within all limbs as their animator;
and because its power is inseparable from them, it further manifests through the doors of the senses, such as sight and hearing.

The form that nourishes (*vṛṃhaka*), upon entering into form, sound, and so forth, becomes an awakener of the fire of desire in the form of the agitation of *vīrya* precisely because of its nature as a nourisher. This is the intended meaning here:

regarding that web of *kalās* which consists of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and which has the nature of sound and so forth, as well as the form of the ear and other senses.
From that union which arises from the mutual friction of the absence of subject and object—

according to the principle that "the fire named Śuci is produced from the friction of the Moon and the Sun"— the bliss of emission (*visargānanda*) unfolds through entry into the central channel (*madhyadhāmānupraveśāt*), as a semblance of that [ultimate state].
The meaning is that another [means], O Ānanda, by which one practices also becomes a cause for entering into the consciousness of another.
As it has been said:
"From conversation, from the touch of the body... [and so forth].

And so forth. Furthermore, by means of even a single form—such as color (rūpa) or another—the capacity to produce the aforementioned agitation, which effects all objects of experience, belongs to everything when augmented by previously accumulated power;
this is because everything is essentially identical with everything else.

(47) Even through recollection, conceptualization, and so forth, agitation (*kṣobha*) certainly arises by virtue of the expansion of infinite objects such as sound that have entered the mind consisting of all things (*sarvamaya*). Only that which possesses the fully nourished great potency (*mahāvīrya*) consisting of all things brings about the creation of nourishment (*puṣṭisṛṣṭi*), and not that which is incomplete.

Nor is it diminished, as is the case with youth and old age when they have reached their natural limits; for even when there is an agitation of *vīrya*, because *vīrya* is its own nature, it remains essentially the form of the Great Contemplation (*mahāvimarśa*) consisting of vibration that is not limited by space or time, which is the very self of the perfect consciousness of Bhairava. [The intention here is as follows:]
Pāśava knowledge is said to correspond to the degree of contraction,
whereas the knowledge of the Lord (patijñāna), which sublates it, corresponds to the degree of expansion.
Such is the method of the Siddhānta. In that regard, it is said:

"The universe shall be fully gratified by means of the desired Śiva-liṅga. However, in the Kula and other systems, this worship of the liṅga is prohibited; therein, regarding the worship of the liṅga—

They say that the supreme Śiva-liṅga consists of all the paths because it contains within itself the entire expansion of the paths through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Others, however, maintain that the body itself consists of all the paths;
therefore, direct realization is easily attained right there. What is the use of an external liṅga and so forth, which would otherwise be logically untenable?
As they say:
"Having abandoned the Omniscient One who dwells in the house of the cave of the heart and is all-pervading,
the one of limited intellect bows down with the hope for Śiva to a stone and such things that are inauspicious yet praised as auspicious."

Thus [it is said]. Here, however, in this supreme non-dual vision of the Trika system, there is no purpose whatsoever served by either its affirmation or its negation. Furthermore, the presentation of the Kula system that has been made here is solely for the purpose of demonstrating superior knowledge (*abhijñā*), as well as for the sake of illuminating the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), since it is stated that "the Trika is superior to the Kula. As it has been said:
Bhaṭṭanāyaka also, with this very intention, said:
"O Lord, how much fruit could this neuter Supreme Brahman bear,
were it not for Your beautiful Śakti who impels its manly power?"
Thus: Sovereignty consists of the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti), which brings forth happiness; for even the form of the eyes [is such].

By means of the technique of separation from that great emission (*mahāvisarga*), which consists of the agitation of its own vitality (*vīrya*); [the meaning here is as follows: in the supreme Light, the ultimate emission, which is like a waveless ocean and is not yet affected by the operations consisting of the desire to manifest and so forth at the prior limit, [this occurs] precisely from the play of the first manifestation].
Because there is no object of reflection external [to consciousness], the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cit-parāmarśa*) flashes forth, by means of which its sovereignty arises everywhere.

Then, through the very majesty of its own sovereignty, the Supreme Lord—whose essence is the light of the Absolute (*anuttara-prakāśa*)—conceals His own nature by ascending through the stages beginning with the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
Emission (*sṛṣṭi*) is the externalization of [objects] in the form of blue, pleasure, and so forth; persistence (*sthiti*) is their relishing for some time;

withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is the assimilation into one's own self; dissolution (*laya*) follows from that, due to the pride of satisfaction in thinking "this object has been known"; and grace (*anugraha*) is resting within one's own self by dissolving even that externalized form.
And it is said:
"The supreme emission is separation; the entire universe is said to consist of that.
Thus, it becomes a bestower of bliss. And [this applies] to sweet songs and the like for the ears, and likewise for other sense faculties as well.
It does not experience the state of complete fullness of creation solely because of its surging within itself; thus,
it is like stones, which lack the joy of passion consisting of the agitation of such vitality because they are not augmented by that vitality.
Even the most exquisite form of a young woman, and even the sweet, low-toned singing of a full-hipped lady’s voice,
does not culminate in complete bliss; and to the extent that it fails to augment [the soul], to that same extent [it remains incomplete].
For indeed, when there is a total absence of aesthetic wonder (*acamatkāra*) on all sides, there is mere insentience;

it is only the immersion in supreme wonder, consisting of the agitation of *vīrya* (vital energy), that is called "sensitivity" (*sahṛdayatā*). It is only for one whose heart is nourished by the infinite expansion of *vīrya*—which has been established through the habitual practice of attachment to this enjoyment—that [this state exists].

This very excellence of wonder exists even in suffering; for that which is established within—the bliss of a beloved son and so forth—is of the nature of *vīrya* (vital energy). Through the awakening of such states as weeping, which resemble intense contemplation (*bhāvanā*), it attains an expansion characterized by agitation, thinking, "This shall never happen again."
The true nature of suffering consists of a particular wonder arising from the power of detachment. As it has been said:
"Even in suffering, by means of expansion... [and so forth].
When, however, there is the complete filling of the winds and other elements within all the channels of the senses...
When one enters the state of the great central Suṣumnā, one attains identity with the agitation of one's own power;
then, as duality dissolves on all sides—(p.
Upon entering the wonder of the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*) consisting of the reflective awareness of the full weight of one's own power—
by means of entering the union with the *rudrayāmala*, which is the nature of the bliss of the perfect emanation,
and through the process of the differentiation of emission (*visarga*) which is the potency of that great mantra.
There is the manifestation of the state of Bhairava, which is free from waves and consists of the firm foundation; for thus, at the time of trembling,
even that which is of the nature of both genders— being the form of the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī)—
obtains its support through the strength of the vigor and energy of that [Bhairava].
The bliss of internal touch, characterized by the desire to arise from the agitation of all-encompassing *vīrya*, is indeed witnessed by one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*).

And this [bliss] is not merely established within the imagined body; rather, through the instruction on its direct realization, it leads to the attainment of the stable state (*dhruvapada*) reached by the separation of the emission (*visarga*) of such great mantra-vigor (*vīrya*).

There is an entry into the form of the Supreme Goddess Parā, who is the sovereignty of bliss arising from the union of Śiva and Śakti, whose nature is the supreme Brahman, and who is the creative power. This will be stated:
"Then one should worship the emission (*sṛṣṭi*)."... [text omitted] ...[text omitted]... [text omitted]... [text omitted].
And so forth. Likewise—(p.
51)—just as [the tree] residing within the seed of the nyagrodha... * * * * * * * *...
And so forth. Likewise—so forth. It is also stated elsewhere:
"From licking, churning, and striking, through the recollection of the fullness of a woman's pleasure..."

O Mistress of the Gods, even in the absence of external power (or: even in the absence of external means), through the immersion into the nature of Śakti preceded by recollection and due to the intensity of contemplation, there occurs an overflowing of bliss; such is the meaning.
Thus, for when that touch is recollected from memory, and within the field of that touch,
it is reflected as a central form by the power of the *apara-ātman* (the lower self) through the tube (*nāḍikā*),
then even in the absence of the primary *śākta-sparśa*, there exists the vitality (*vīrya*) consisting of the *śākta-sparśa* functioning within it.

This is with the intention that she becomes an agitator (*kṣobhakārī*). Likewise, that bliss of the reality of Brahman which concludes with the agitation caused by the union of powers and the immersion into power— that bliss [is the same as] that which arises at the end of the immersion manifested through the joy of sexual union.

But that happiness which is free from the mental preoccupation with women, men, and so forth, and is established solely in one's own self—that is called "one's own" (*svākyam*); it should be contemplated as belonging only to oneself and not derived from anything else. However, union with a woman is indeed the cause of its manifestation;
this is the meaning. Thus, it is called "one's own."
Thus it is said; and so too by the Great Hero, the Blessed Vyāsa—(p.

"Of mine"— that is, of me whose nature is the Supreme Brahman— "the Great" (mahat)— meaning the gross, which, being perceived as an object of knowledge, constitutes the "womb" (garbha), namely the transferral of one's own potency characterized by pure consciousness—
from that, from the essential nature which is perceived as "this-ness" (idantā). This is the intended meaning here:
Reflecting upon the nature of the Supreme Brahman, I illuminate the reality characterized as Prakṛti;

for even when it appears as "this-ness," it lacks luminosity without the penetration of the light of Consciousness (citprakāśa), and while its nature as Brahman is thus established, it is nevertheless called "gross" because its nature consists of limited objects of knowledge.

The Great Brahman, which consists of the "this-ness" (idantā) that serves as the cause for the differentiation of all entities in the entire world, is my womb, acting as the locus of origin for me who am desirous of creating the universe. That womb is the Great Brahman; into it I place the seed.
From that, O Bhārata, the origin of all beings arises.
Thus it is also sung. And by the venerable Somānanda-pāda in his own commentary:

O Lord, tell this secret, this great secret, to me, your own master.

It is "secret" (*guhya*) because it is not manifest; for it remains within *māyā*—the cave consisting of the non-recognition of one's own true nature—even while it exists there. Regarding the statement "it remains," the intended meaning is this: since the Self is by its very nature light, it is indeed always manifest; it does not fail to manifest in any respect whatsoever, and thus it is said to be "not manifest."
The meaning is that it has not attained the state of being fully grasped by the heart; thus, it is unmanifest. And yet, it is great and not secret, because it consists of such wonder for everyone.
It is the Blessed Lady, Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā) herself, characterized by the non-differentiation of the divisions consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

In the *māyā* triangle, the power of the Supreme Lord (*parameśa-śakti*)—which consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and which apprehends differentiation as it is intensely reflected therein—is *māyā*. Consequently, in reality, it is indeed *vidyā* (knowledge).
For how could that which is the ground of birth (*jananabhūḥ*) be *avidyā* (ignorance)? As for its status as *avidyā*, that is...
Excluding the category of insentient objects yet to be created, this very [consciousness] is called *prakṛti* in the Sāṃkhya system, as stated in the *Pañcastavi*:
"Whom the sages declare to be the ancient *prakṛti*..."
I, having no other refuge, take shelter in that Goddess whom those who know the secret of the Vedas call "Vidyā," whose form and seal are half-blossomed Śaṅkara.

Thus [it is said]. And the Goddess Māyā is such because she is the nature of the unfolding "this-ness" (idantā) veiled by "I-ness" (ahantā), appearing clearly in the form of the cognition "this is I. For this very reason, her status as the "vital potency of mantra" (mantravīryatva) has been described elsewhere;
for it is when a mantra rests upon this state that it possesses the capacity to bestow its appropriate fruit.
And it is said elsewhere:

"One should not employ a mantra in the person (puruṣa), nor in the supreme reality (para-tattva), nor in the power (śakti). In the principle of the person, the mantra becomes inert; in the supreme reality, it is fruitless."
Thus it is said; and likewise in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"This *yoginīhṛdaya* is the *liṅga* characterized by bliss;
through the union of the seed (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*), it gives birth to an ineffable consciousness."
Thus it is said:
"It exists"— even *māyā*, the ground for the birth of the world, is in reality nothing but *vidyā* according to the principle stated above.

Because it is not fully known in its suchness (*evaṃbhūtatva*), and because the three corners consisting of the subject and so forth are concealed by the majesty of non-duality (*abheda-māhātmya*), it is called the "Great Cave" (*mahāguhā*).
And that very [cave] is in reality the locus of worship, the trident (*triśūla*) in the sense of the Triad (*trika*). As it has been said:
She is the triangle, the Great Vidyā, the triple-folded one, and the abode of all aesthetic flavors.

This very state is the "state of emission" (*visargapada*); by means of attaining that abode, the stream of bliss of the Kaulika power known as Sovereignty (*svātantrya*) flows forth—thus he says, "the state of emission."

Her state as the *visarga* (the creative emission) is explained in the *Tantrāloka* as follows: "And that very [state] of hers is the condition of *visarga*, which is an overflowing state that, through the process of the arising of bliss,
culminates in the fully manifested power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)."
Thus, by virtue of its surging forth in succession, the universe, even while surging outward, appears ever-new; and it has been stated elsewhere:
"By the stream of the bliss of emission (*visarga*) resulting from absorption into this *liṅga*..."
Once sprinkled, that entire universe eternally experiences protection.

Thus, the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is obtained here through contemplation alone. "All flavors" means the nature of both enjoyment and liberation. The greatness of creation here lies precisely in the absence of duality. Therefore, one should worship the Triad.

The definition is as stated in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:

Thus it has been said:

"By means of its nature as expansion" (*prasarātmanā*)—that is, by way of its own surging forth in the form of vibration (*spanda*).
As it has been said:
"The unified form of those two is known as their *saṃghaṭṭa* (union/conjunction)."
That very power is called the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti), from which the universe is emitted.

"That supreme Kauliki power which is described as the internal desire to emit (*visisṛkṣā*), that very power, by virtue of agitation (*kṣobha*), certainly attains the nature of emission."
Thus it is said. In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
the Śakti-kuṇḍalikā and likewise the Prāṇa-kuṇḍalikā.

Thus, assuming the state of the visarga through its form— since the visarga itself consists of the power (śakti) of the letter *ha* which is the nature of Kuṇḍalinī— it again exists as the bindu, whose essence is the realization of non-difference from that very expansion of power.

It proceeds in the form of a human being. Likewise again—just as previously, having emitted everything that was to be done into the fire of emptiness—this is called the *āṇava* [stage], characterized by the resting of the mind; immediately after that.

The state of being oriented toward objects such as those seen or heard within one's own consciousness is called the awakening of the mind (*cittasaṃbodha*); it consists essentially of the fullness of the unfolding of power (*śāktollāsa*).
Therein, due to being oriented toward that [reality], from the collision with that object, and because of its firm rooting in the heart,
there occurs an immersion into Śiva through fullness, resulting in the dissolution of the limited mind.
This supreme emission of Śambhu, known as the dissolution of the mind, arises from the limited state that is conceivable through the orientation toward future existence, as previously described.
Thus, this will be further clarified very shortly in the context of that previously mentioned form of the Great Supreme Bliss (*maheparamānanda*). As for this which [is now stated]:

Likewise, regarding "mine" (*mama*), which denotes a connection to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), that which is secret within this state of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*) is said to be "I" (*aham*). For instance, in the thought "this appears as mine," the word "this" (*idam*) refers to one's own self.

Because it is an unreal construction (*asatkalpa*), my own manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), having entered into the form of vibration (*spandana*) through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), is to be designated as having the single essence of the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*). One must discern for oneself that there is neither a process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) nor a process of withdrawal here; this [reality] shines forth.

Thus, that which is manifestation has as its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) once again the singular essence of the "I-sense" (*ahambhāva*); and that "I-sense," by way of withdrawing all objective phenomena, is precisely of the form of *mah-a*, as stated previously. As it has been said:
The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of "this," which is initially fragmented,
is that repose within one's own essential nature— the reflective awareness "I am this."
Thus it is said elsewhere:

"The determination 'this is a jar' appears as the power of the Supreme Lord, like the Self itself, transcending name and form; it does not appear as a mere 'this-ness'. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.20)
Thus it has been stated by the venerable Somānandapāda in his own commentary:
"That which is seedless (abīja) is the nature of pure Śiva."

And so forth. That very point has been elaborated by us. Likewise, "one's own" (*svamama*) means that for whom "mine" (*mama*) does not exist at all, because the universe is of a single nature with the burden of the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*), such that nothing exists as something separate from him that could be connected to the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*) which is the life-breath of a distinct designation. [This applies] to those initiated into other scriptures...

Although for those who are *vijñānākalas* and *pralayakevalins* there is no sense of "mine" (*mama*) as something separate, nevertheless, at the time of awakening, that which was capable of differentiation must indeed exist; for through its expansion, the ascension of the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) occurs. To eliminate that [sense of "mine"], the word *su-* is used in the sense of "well" (*susthu*). As it has been said by me myself in the *Stotra*:
Foolish beings constantly fall into a state of wretchedness because they think, "Nothing is mine.
Since they respond to everything with negation, saying "Not this, not that," it is said: "I am all; everything is mine."
"I have taken up this entire, heavy burden."

60) Thus [it is said]. He whose "māna" (measure/cognition) is this knowledge—beautiful because it is entirely free from even a trace of the turbidity of the stain of duality—and which is non-dual in nature due to its instruction on the ultimate reality.

Because its nature is solely self-luminous: *amā* means "without *mā*. Here, *mā* refers to that in which *māna* (measurement) and *niṣedha* (negation) do not exist; because it is eternally risen (*nityodita*), there is no dissolution (*saṃhāra*) therein. That Blessed Lady is called *amā*. Wherein *mā* is auspicious and eternally risen—that is *māyā*, wherein the conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) exists.

The term *tādṛśīmā* is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) within another possessive compound. For the Supreme Lord, even in the conventional usage of means of knowledge and so forth, is entirely composed of supreme power because He is in every way non-dual;
thus, this is an address to Himself. (1-1/2)

O Lord of Gods, tell me of that power residing in the heart, who is Kaulikī, the Mistress of the Kula.
By which I obtain satisfaction. || 2 ||

The meaning is that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the locus of support for everything—such as blue, pleasure, and so forth [where "blue" refers to the external and internal object of apprehension, and "body" refers to the subject; the meaning is that consciousness is the foundation for both]. Furthermore, the supreme locus of support for the body, vital breath, intellect, and so forth, is the heart which is the self of consciousness. Its various distinctions are fashioned by its own innate sovereignty.

This power, consisting of radiant manifestation, resides within the diverse cognitions of jars and other objects; she is the mistress of the *kula*, the bestower of radiance upon the body, vital breath, pleasure, and so forth; she is the vitality of the circle of deities beginning with Brāhmī, and she takes the form of the "Middle" (*madhyama*) situated in the center of the entire network of channels of the senses.
The self of the *janana*, the *sthāna*, the *karṇikā*, and the *liṅga* exists there. And in that very *kula*, there is the *kaulikī*, who is born of *kula* and whose form is *kula*;
or rather, she is that which arises in *kula* and whose nature is *akula*.
That in which the Kaula exists internally through identity is the Kaulikī; for the Kula indeed becomes such only when it has ascended into the light of Akula. As it has been said:
"Also, by the touch of the power of one's own Self" (Svacchandatantra, Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava, Chapter 8, Uddyota).

Thus, having taken hold of that power, the mantras, endowed with the power of the Omniscient One, proceed toward their respective functions, just as the sense organs of embodied beings do. (Svacchandatantra, Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava, Kārikā 10)

Thus [it is said]. This is an address to the Lord (Īśa) of the gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others. The venerable Somānanda-pāda also reads: "Tell me that," and he explains it as "therefore" (tasmāt). Alternatively, [he explains it as]:
"Tell me that by which I may obtain satisfaction consisting of supreme bliss."
The syntactic connection is: "I exist as the essence of the sovereignty of supreme non-dual bliss. There is also a reading *brajāmi* (I go).

By the word *aham* (I), that which is the very life of all subjects (*pramātṛ*) is constantly referred to; and by means of this instruction on the nature thus described, one recognizes one's own essential form as the Lord (*īśvara*).
It has already been made clear that one finds satisfaction consisting of the state of fullness. As it was stated by the venerable Somānanda in his own commentary (*Svavivṛti*): [p. 63]
"Knowledge is the movement of iron within the heart," and so forth.
Thus, for those whose minds thirst to drink the nectar of Śiva—
In order to forcibly tear asunder the knot in the sky of the heart of those in whom existence has been established by Śiva for the constant destruction of inauspiciousness,

Thus, regarding this *Praśnasarvasva*:
Śrī Bhairava said—“This has already been explained; what is the point of repeating it? Bhairava is, by nature, the one who sustains (*bharaṇa*).”
"Bharaṇa" (sustenance) means the supporting of the universe within oneself, as well as its nourishment by way of being fixed upon the wall of one's own Self;

for it has been stated elsewhere that "by this very [Self] the universe is sustained through the union of supporting and nourishing. Likewise, because it manifests everywhere as consisting of the universe, it is both the support and the nourishment of that [universe]. Thus, the universe...

(p. 64) Therefore, this is the intended meaning here:

The meaning is that this power of will (*icchā-śakti*), as it unfolds because its nature consists of acceptance, is also nothing other than the supreme (*parā*) and unsurpassed (*anuttara*) form; he states the reason for this very point by saying, "non-different from Bhairava. The sequence therein is as follows: when [the will] is oriented toward emergence, it is that very supreme [will]; when oriented toward the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), it is *paśyantī*; and when that [same will] is oriented toward the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), it is [the state of] stability.
Madhyamā abides [in the state of] Vaikharī. The Blessed Consciousness, as it unfolds from its own essential nature, is called the Power of Supreme Will (parā-icchā-śakti), inseparable from Bhairava.

Realizing his own self alone in its absolute isolation, he should remain resting in his innate bliss. Then,
according to the principle that "prior consciousness has transformed into the vital breath," when the vital breath— which is of the nature of the means of knowledge—
arises from the heart to the *dvādaśānta* by way of exhalation (*recaka*), there occurs, through some degree of outward orientation, [the following]:

Having emerged from one's own bliss which is regarded as the subject (*pramātṛ*), one should remain in the state of blisslessness (*nirānanda*). 2. Then, when the object (*prameya*) consisting of the *apāna* breath arises again, one should contemplate the bliss produced by that supreme object, so that even during the stage of the emergence of the object, one may abide in supreme bliss (*parānanda*). 3. Furthermore, from that...

Having rested for a moment in the heart, one should abide established in the bliss of Brahman through the friction (*saṃghaṭṭa*) consisting of the mutual fusion of the various objects of knowledge appearing as blue, pleasure, and so forth. 4. Even from that state, one should be intent upon swallowing the flood of both the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge.
Devoted to their union, he should contemplate the bliss recognized as the subject;

he should reflect upon it as being essentially the repose within his own self alone, and thus abide in that which consists of great bliss (mahānanda). 5. Even beyond that, because it is the nature of the unifier of all this, he should abide in the world-bliss (jagadānanda), which is the nature of the light of the Self. 6.
As it is said in the *Tantrāloka*: "The nature of universal bliss (*jagadānanda*) is that in which there is no differentiation whatsoever, from which everything radiates,
and which is nourished by the supreme nectar of unextracted consciousness."

"That which possesses no primary connection whatsoever with meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the like—this very bliss of the world Śambhu has declared to us. [Regarding the definition of happiness, p.

Since whatever happiness there may be is, by entering into the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*)— the supreme abode of great bliss and tranquility— attained as a limited form through being perceived in such a manner; as it was said by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa:

"I bow to that God, the ocean of bliss, whose single drop (*bindu*) is whatever joy whatsoever is seen here in the three worlds, consisting of existence, non-existence, and super-existence. (Verse 61) Thus,
according to the previously stated method, it is that very form which is called *maha-a* that is to be worshipped by her.
For that which is the "I" of the Supreme Lord, expanded by His own creative wonder (*svacamatkāra*), is indeed His Śākta body,
and it is said to be the form of the Supreme Goddess Parābhaṭṭārikā. Therefore, she alone— the Supreme Goddess— perceives everything,
abiding through her very existence known as hearing (*śravaṇa*).

The sovereignty known as the synthesis and contemplation of formless unification— which culminates in the mass of phonemes consisting of one's own successive and manifest vibrations within the cavity of the ears— is indeed that [sovereignty]. For without it,
even while hearing specific sounds merged in a general clamor, the cognizer employs the expression, "I do not hear."
70) However, since the synthesis has as its object merely the general clamor, the conventional usage "it was heard right there" occurs.
In reality, that sound of clamor, upon entering the space of the auditory organ, does not enter into the individual phonemes.
Thus it would be, because there would only be a confused clamor (*kalakala*) consisting of phonemes exceeding those [specific] letters.

Therefore, a single sentence-sphoṭa (*vākya-sphoṭa*), which is devoid of succession and whose unreal parts are merely conceptualized, produces a cognition regarding its own denoted object of such a nature.

Those various castes, who are absorbed in primordial nature and whose sole foundation is conceptual construction, do not direct their intellects toward that ultimate reality; therefore, enough with talk of them.

Thus is the doctrine of *sphoṭa* accepted by the grammarians. Furthermore, when there is a desire to express specific phonemes (*varṇa*), there would be a non-arising of a confused din (*kalakala*) precisely because of the absence of its cause;
for even though it might be the effect of a word consisting of distinct phonemes produced by that desire to speak.

Because the production of a word consisting of homogeneous phonemes is impossible [in that manner], those very same phonemes, when they reach a state of synthesis (*saṃkalana*) through that distinct form, are what is denoted by the term "clamor" (*kalakala*). For one who is intent on attending to that synthesis, there would indeed be a perception of some degree of clarity; thus, it is synthesis alone that is effective here.
And it is that very Blessed One, the Supreme Goddess Parā herself, who performs this synthesis. As it has been said:
"Having seized that power, the mantras... (Spaṣṭapada 2.10).
And so forth. In reality, indeed, the forms of hearing, seeing, speaking, grasping, and so on, belong to the Blessed Lady alone.
As it has been said:
"That by which one perceives form, taste, smell, touch, sound, and sexual union..."

"By this very [Self] one knows; what remains here? (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3)—thus it is stated by the Supreme Lord in the Vedānta. However, "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) does not merely consist of listening to phonemes in their distinct, indistinct, high-pitched, or faltering forms. For instance:
The venerable Supreme Lord himself has described this very point in the *Śrī Svacchanda Śāstra* at the occasion of determining the divisions of recitation (*japa*):
"That which is heard by oneself alone is known as 'whispered' (*upāṃśu*)."
For it is stated here regarding the middle stage (*madhyamāpada*) that "the self alone hears [it], and no other," (p.
72) due to the clarity of the effort of the places of articulation and so forth, through the conjunction and separation of the teeth, lips, and other parts.
Even if one utters a sound very softly, it may still be heard by someone standing nearby; thus, there is inevitably the occurrence of being accompanied by sound.
That which is heard by others is declared to be "accompanied by sound" (saśabda).

For it has been stated that "there is no distinction here such as proximity and so forth. However, when there is contact between the tongue, lips, and other organs— which are the domain of the mere perception of another subject— if the hearing belongs to oneself alone and not to the other, nevertheless, this results in the very state of *madhyamā* with respect to the phoneme.

Because there is no acquisition of an external self-nature; for indeed, due to the impact of the vital air (*vāyu*), [the sound] is produced as a distinct phoneme (*varṇa*), yet in that case, the impact of the vital air would not extend to the point of attaining externality. Even the movement of the lips and so forth would not enter into the constituent part of the phoneme therein, but rather it would be merely momentary and grounded in its own self.

But when there is a conjunction with the effort of clearly manifesting the *sthāna* (articulatory place) and *karaṇa* (articulatory organ), which serves as the locus for the simultaneous gestures, winking, and manual operations [of the speaker], then even during the production of the phoneme (*varṇa*), [the word-meaning is understood].

Even if there were a distinction between high and low pitches and so forth among sounds due to their relative intensity, such that they might be heard from far or near, they would nonetheless be heard by others; therefore, this is simply the state of *vaikharī*. Enough of this digression. That very [state], characterized by hearing, is the Supreme Goddess.

By means of the method of address (*āmantraṇa*), she is clearly stated to be of the nature of *Śakti*. [The phrase] "clearly stated to be of the nature of *Śakti*" is further elucidated with reflection by the words beginning with "nara-śakti" and so forth. In that context, *Nara* is characterized primarily by difference (*bheda*), *Śakti* is characterized primarily by both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), and [Śiva] is characterized solely by non-difference (*abheda*).
Regarding the word "Śiva": as it has been stated, "And when its manifestation is divided, its body is declared to be threefold.
Here, its nature as Will, Knowledge, and Action is easily understood according to the sequence of emanation; for all this [is Śiva].
In that context, that which is merely the threefold form abiding within itself is primarily characterized by a purely insentient nature—(p.
74) the intention of the word "primarily" (*mukhyatayā*) is this: that which is insentient within itself...

The meaning is that, although [the object] has not yet attained existence from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) and is indeed attached to the light [of consciousness], it is primarily inert (*jaḍa*) because it currently appears as something standing apart [from the subject]. This very [state] is like [the expression]: "The jar, which is not of the nature of the Self, remains"—wherein the distinction between these two is that "jar" is a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), while "this" is an indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpa*). It is exactly this.

The "remainder" (śeṣa) has as its object the first person. Furthermore, even that which appears as "this"—the fulfillment of this fragmented reflective awareness (*vicchinnavimarśa*)—is that reflective awareness which rests in its own essential nature; it is this very "I."
Thus: "In this way, the determination 'this is a jar' appears as the power of the Supreme Lord, which is like the Self, transcending name and form; it does not appear as a mere 'this-ness'."
Thus it is said. Herein is the distinction: those which are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) constitute the cause of differentiation within that which is of the nature of the Person (*puruṣa*).
Furthermore, this capacity for the determination "this is [it]" is, by virtue of its non-differentiation, the very nature of power (*śakti*);
for this [power] is non-distinct from the Self (*ātman*), because it is veiled by the "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*). This is so because it is that which is being addressed.

In the statement "You (tvaṃ) remain," that form belonging to Śakti— which is designated by the word *yuṣmad* (you), which consists of the state of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*) distinct from that [subject], yet covered by the state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*) through address—
is indeed the meaning of the word *yuṣmad*, as well as the reality of address (*āmantraṇatattva*). For instance, just as "I remain," so too...
"This one too"— meaning that for him as well,
the sovereignty of the wonder of the *ahaṃbhāva* (I-consciousness) delimited by our own form exists precisely through the uninterrupted wonder of the "I."
Reflecting thus, he addresses [her] and designates her with the second person according to the actual state of things;
for she is indeed the Blessed One, both supreme and non-supreme in every respect.

Furthermore, in the self-reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-vimarśa*), which is characterized by uninterrupted wonder and independent sovereignty, I abide. And so it is said in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
"The three types of persons—the inferior, the mediocre, and the superior—are all distinct; yet when combined, they become one."
But from me, the Great Person whose nature is self-reflection, nothing exists externally.
That form which appears as "I," seemingly divided like the exclusion of what remains of you, is merely a distinction of parts; for I am one and eternal.
Thus [ends the section on] the arising of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā). In this regard, the supremacy of the Person (Puruṣa) has been stated as follows:
"Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)."

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the use of the word "I" (*asmi*), it is stated that I am superior even to both the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*) forms. [Objection: But surely, in the phrase "I remain," only the egoity (*ahaṃtā*) of the body and so forth is clearly perceived;
how then can there be the arising of the Supreme Goddess (*parābhaṭṭārikā*) here? To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. Furthermore, in this context...
Existence (*bhāva*)—the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is indeed the essence of the entity that is a dense mass of independent light and imperishable.

That very [reality], through its own sovereignty (*svātantrya*), even when assuming the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) regarding the body and so forth, is called "I" (*aham*); this is because it does not abandon its primordial nature, but rather manifests it. As for the body and so forth, however, [their existence] is merely perceptible.
[If] the ultimate reality is characterized by disjunction, how can there be the designation "I" with respect to it? To this [it is replied]:
everywhere, that which is limited, such as the body and so forth, is designated as "I," and this is established through direct perception itself.

Because it would contradict its very nature. Thus, such a form—which consists of self-manifestation (meaning it is self-luminous, and not dependent on manifestation through distinctions of difference or non-difference between the forms of the individual soul and the power)—is of the nature of Śiva; for this very reason, it belongs to this consciousness.

For that which consists of the manifestation of self-awareness, there is neither deficiency nor excess—[in the form of difference or non-difference]. This is because that which is of the nature of non-manifestation does not enter into the realm of consciousness [whereas it is established by implication that that which is of the nature of manifestation does enter into the essential nature of consciousness]; and with respect to that, neutrality also does not exist.

Regarding the word *kiṃcit*— in that which stands as the middle between increase (*upacaya*) and decrease (*apacaya*), and which has attained its footing in an absence that cannot be designated as "this"—
[increase pertains to the light (*prakāśa*), decrease to the jar (*ghaṭa*), and neutrality (*mādhyasthya*) to the "you" (*yuṣmad*)], words do not prevail.

The referents of the word *asmat* (we/us) consist of the uninterrupted nature of the awareness of that [Self], while the referents of the word *yuṣmat* (you/they), even when interrupted, are likewise so; for this very reason, *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are said to be without gender (*aliṅga*). However, through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of number and other attributes belonging to the body, and because they encompass powers such as the "supreme" (*parā*) and "non-supreme" (*aparā*), their connection with number is indeed justified.
For instance: one should contemplate as a single unity the infinite bodies and so forth, which are the manifestations of difference fashioned by one's own sovereignty;
and [one should likewise contemplate] "we two," "you two," "we," and "you," as well as the increases and so forth pertaining to the body.

They cannot even be figuratively described as such, because it is impossible for that which is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa) to possess deficiency or excess; for everything is indeed of the nature of everything.
Thus, even insentient beings like men, having abandoned their former forms, become partakers of the Śākta and Śaiva natures. Listen, O stones! I am Meru, the king of mountains.

Because there is the cognition, "I am Caitra," and "I speak," even that which consists of the power (śāktam) and has the form of the object denoted by *yuṣmad* (the second person pronoun) indeed assumes the nature of the individual self (*narātmakatām*). This is because one understands [the meaning] even through the non-addressive mode, as in: "O you who have abandoned fear and the power of fortitude, you [are such]," having set aside the form of the power. By the word *bhavān*, the feet are the teachers.

Because cognition exists through such specific cognitions as "I" and so forth— which have as their object the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*) consisting of the human nature appropriate to the subsequent state— even for one who has abandoned the Śākta form, there would also be the nature of Śiva in the form of "I."

Having cast aside the very nature of body and mind in his beloved, through the conviction "I am indeed He," he enters even the form of Śiva as a body consisting of *nara* (the individual) and *śakti* (power), as if its conscious nature (*cidrūpa*) had been abandoned. For in such expressions as "Who am I?",
"This is I," "Oh, I!", "Shame on me!", or "Oh, for me!", the sense of "I" is made subordinate and remains uninterrupted.

But primarily, sovereignty is that wherein a fragmented "this-ness" (*idantā*) is perceived, which is the emergence of the goddess Aparā in such instances as "O, I! and so forth; this is indeed the touch of the vibration of the Parāparā Śakti belonging to Śiva. However, each preceding state is invariably present in the subsequent one; thus, the form of the individual (*nara*) is [perceived] through a clearly manifest cognition.
One would indeed be able to ascend the path that balances the Śākta and Śāmbhava [powers], but not by ascending in the reverse order;
for [the ascent] consists of clear perception through the non-abandonment of each respective nature.
Because it consists of three aspects, each of these triads assumes the form of one, two, or many. For it has been said:
"A single reality becomes twofold, and being twofold, it becomes manifold.
Indeed, when there is a state of oneness, because there is no counter-correlative, and when the possibility of a counter-correlative to Śiva-nature arises, that is Śakti-nature.

In the state of multiplicity, there is indeed differentiation; yet the human self-nature is one alone, just as [the word] "jar" can stand as "a jar," "two jars," "jars," or even "jars, cloth, and stones. Furthermore, [the forms] "stands," "stand," and "stand" [are used] by means of that very same [self-nature], for this is simply the manifestation of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). As it has been said:
"Having made the manifold one, who would not be released from bondage?

For this very reason, when there is a simultaneous reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the human (*nara*), power (*śakti*), and Śiva within a single locus, there occurs an entry into each subsequent essential nature; for that [subsequent nature] is, in reality, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the former. And that...
The very sequence of cognition— “you two remain,” “he and you two remain,” and “he, you two, and I remain”—
is followed by the grammarians through their technical definitions (*lakṣaṇa*), which have as their essence uncreated linguistic conventions (*akṛtaka-saṃskāra*); and so it is.

Even in vernacular languages such as those of the Buddhists, the Andhras, and the Draviḍas, where not even the name of refinement remains, this very same verbal sequence prevails; and this verbal sequence,
following the internal realization from its very root, exists because that realization is of the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

One should understand that it possesses such a nature, as stated by me myself. Therefore, in every respect, these are indeed uncreated; as it has been said: "Without them, there would be no word, no object, nor even the comprehension of consciousness."

Thus it is said; and also in the *Śrīmālinītantra*: "O Śambhu, just as that single power of Śaṅkara remains presiding over the entire aggregate of individual souls (*aṇu*), so has it been described to you."
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrītantrasamuccaya*:

"This entire universe is always pervaded by Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, in every respect, both for those who follow the sequential path (*kramin*) in their worldly conduct and for those who possess all-encompassing knowledge."
Thus [it is said] on page 81.
That very [reality], consisting of the nature of Man, Power, and Śiva, has been demonstrated through the instruction of the tradition for clear comprehension:
"Man, Power, and Śiva"—this is the all-enduring sequence of realization.

"Created by the sovereign freedom of the Supreme Lord’s will"—enough of this [discussion] which captivates the hearts of only a few fortunate and learned connoisseurs who have been purified by the descent of the supreme *śakti* and possess the requisite instruction.
[The term *sahṛdaya* refers to sensitive listeners; "only a few" is as it has been said:]
"There are hundreds of worshippers; there are thousands of devotees.
But those who are vessels of grace and full of confidence are two or three, not five.
[This was said] as a digression following a further digression. "Listen, O Goddess, for that has been explained"—this refers to what was stated regarding the subsequent [section] as well.

To the question "How is it unsurpassed? the reply is as follows: even that which is proximate to the "surpassable" (uttara) is "unsurpassed" (anuttara) according to the sequence previously stated; for the surpassable also exists only through identity with the state of being unsurpassed, and not otherwise.
For this very reason, without even taking up the surpassable—using the genitive case in the sense of disregard—the form is indeed "the surpassable."
Not having attained that state, it is indeed of unsurpassed form; for this differentiation, being of a subsequent form, is absolutely non-differentiation.

Having resorted to the earth [resorting = taking as a basis; likewise = in the form of differentiation], it would exist in such a way that even the determination of the other [determination of the other = the restriction of difference;
others = distinct entities] is established in the other.
As long as another is not made one's own, it is impossible to act [for their sake], because an unenlightened person regards another as merely "another."

Thus, it is said. Likewise, even for the subsequent portion of the text—[the phrase "of the subsequent" refers to that which is about to be stated; "anuttara" means transcended]—it is unsurpassed (*anuttara*), and therefore it cannot be transcended even by that. Even by the *paśyantī* [the phrase "even by the *paśyantī*" refers to the fact that the reality of luminosity (*prakāśatattva*) is essentially reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and that very reflective awareness takes the form of the first expansion].
As it has been said:
"But Paśyantī is undivided, with all succession withdrawn;
she is the light of her own nature within, subtle, and abiding in the form of speech."

Thus, it is that very [power] which exists in the mind—whose nature is the desire to communicate meaning (vivakṣā) and whose form is consciousness—that is called the "intermediate" (madhyamā). And this is eternally one and common to all, situated between the prāṇa and apāna breaths. As it has been said:

That very sound, existing in the form of consciousness, is here designated as *madhyamā* by virtue of the speaker's intention; it is further described through the sequence of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *marut*.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, when that very [power] reaches the vocal channels and becomes differentiated by the locations of the throat and so forth as the specific phonemes beginning with *ka*, it is called *vaikharī*;

it is this very [power] that takes the form of a literary work (*grantha*). Therefore, since this [work] is of the nature of its manifestation (*prasara*), how could it be possible to determine [the ultimate reality] by means of it?
And it is said:
"Vaikharī speech, which assumes the form of articulated phonemes, occurs when the breath is released through the [various] locations [of articulation];
it is bound to the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa) of the speakers."
Thus,
because the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) is the primary [emanation], and because my own [work] is also subsequent.

This alone is the unsurpassed ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Just as the divisions of the directions and so forth are known by means of the light of a lamp or the rays of the sun, so too, O Dear One, is Śiva known through His power (*śakti*), which consists of the impelling of the trident and other such functions.

Thus: that which is the supreme immersion (*samāveśa*) by means of the trident—the three powers having become merged (*lolībhūta*)—as it has been said: "Therefore, the three powers have become merged; that is the trident.
By quickly entering into that, the yogi becomes stainless (*nirañjana*)."

Thus. What is that unsurpassed place of rest? To this he says: from which this *kaulika* procedure (*vidhi*) arises—*kaulika* meaning consisting of both *kula* and *akula*, as previously explained; and being that which is being performed, it is a "procedure" (*vidhi*), whose nature is the Great Emanation (*mahāsṛṣṭi*) [the Great Emanation being the nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*)].

Since [the Absolute] has issued forth from that which contains within it hundreds of millions of infinite cycles of emanation and so forth, this very [Absolute] is the unsurpassed; as it has been said:
"Salutation to that Universal Self, who is eternally composed of all things. (p. 84)

In this regard, since all this multitude of effects originates from a single agent, the statement "from whom all" establishes the universal agency of the one reality; likewise, the statement "in whom all" establishes its omniscience with respect to this entire collection of entities that appear as utterly distinct.

The meaning is this: within that luminous Self—which has as its sole nature the state of being the single cognizer persisting through all states such as pleasure and so forth, existing as such-and-such by virtue of its own self solely on the basis of being merely that which is being experienced—this very multiplicity resides, by whose power it manifests in this way; [this is expressed] by the phrase "that which is everything."

By the phrase "independent of any other material cause or entity distinct from his own mere will," its independence is stated; and by the phrase "he who [shines] everywhere," the meaning is that since he alone shines forth within every object of knowledge, there is no modification of his essential nature. Furthermore, by the phrase "he who is eternally identical with all," it is meant even when no effect is being produced.

The intended meaning here is as follows: "Everything is one; the omniscient, the creator of all, devoid of material cause and devoid of limiting adjuncts, eternally manifests as the self of all"—thus it is stated in the commentary by the illustrious Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. Everything... [repeated].

Thus it is said. For indeed, this entire universe—consisting of consciousness, mind, vital breath, body, pleasure, pain, the senses, the elements, jars, and so forth—is contained within either the one [consciousness], which is the subject as emptiness (*śūnyapramātā*), or within the other, the supreme sovereign Bhairava-consciousness. [Now, is it not the case that...]

All this is of the nature of light alone; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the world being blind. Why, then, was it said "in consciousness, by way of a non-dual form consisting of awareness"? The intention here is as follows: although it is true that nothing manifests without the existence of light, nevertheless, those [objects] are mutually...
[They are indeed separate]; however, in the supreme nature (*anuttara-svarūpa*), there is no mutual separation, and thus it is "supreme" (*anuttara*).
Although it exists as a non-dual form consisting of consciousness (*bodha-ātmaka*), [it remains so].
Form never sets, for if it were to set, it would follow that it would no longer manifest; nevertheless, there is no mutual exclusion within it, because the Universal Self— the pervasive,
blissful consciousness shining as the very self in all beings— is present therein.
Śiva is one whose flow of desire is unceasing and whose vision and action are ever-expanding.
When he remains absorbed in the experience of mere bliss of consciousness,
his will is exactly that much, and his knowledge and action are likewise that much.
At that time, he exists in the state of equilibrium of the three extremely subtle powers;
supreme, indivisible, and consisting of the bliss of the nature of consciousness.
Thus, in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*: "If these entities were not established therein [in Śiva], then even the initial synthesis and so forth would not be capable of impelling the senses;
therefore, the entire collection of entities is non-different from the mere supreme reflective awareness of 'I', in which the appropriate notions of 'this' and 'that' have not yet arisen."

Indeed, all this [universe] has attained rest within that very Śiva— who consists of the thirty-six principles,
whose nature is the consciousness of universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*), who is the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), and who is primarily characterized by supreme power—
even though it was emitted by his own power, it remains therein, within the nature of the specific vibration of Bhairava (*bhairavaviśeṣaspanda*), which is primarily characterized by power.
It should rest in its own essential nature; that indeed is the state of things being established in their own intrinsic being (*svabhāva*). As it has been said:
"In which all [is contained]... This very reality, consisting of Śiva and Śakti, is both the universal and the particular, and though it is of a single essence, it possesses these two forms.

That which is presented as distinct by the Supreme Lord Himself for the sake of entering the means of instruction, is in reality, however, one alone—the unsurpassed (Anuttara), whose essence is the power of sovereignty consisting of the "I" (Aham), autonomous and composed of consciousness.
Abiding in what kind of own-nature? In my heart-space; that which is called "mine" (mama) is this very heart.

The locus, foundation, and abode of all entities—indeed, of everything from blue and so forth down to the very smallest insect—is nothing other than the cognizer himself, for no form such as blue exists apart from being established within a portion of consciousness.

That which is the state of being mounted upon an uninterrupted fragment of the wonder [of consciousness], such that "blue has appeared to me," is precisely the nature of blue and so forth. Of this "mine" (*mama*), which is the heart of all infinite entities such as blue, there is a void (*vyoma*);
therein, the universe—which consists of the sense of "mine"—is completely dissolved (*vītam*, meaning specifically gone or departed). It is perfectly [dissolved].

Therefore, it is maintained that the void (vyoma) consists of the nature of emptiness because its own distinct individual form has been abandoned; and therein lies the "void" of even that heart— which is the "I" (ahaṃ), the abode of ultimate support, and whose self is consciousness consisting of the supreme and non-supreme, both distinct and non-distinct from the notion of "mine" (mama)— through the process of dissolution (saṃhāra), which is expressed as *ma ha a*.

The individual soul (*nara*), dissolved within the power of the *bindu*— the syllable *ma*— having entered the *kuṇḍalinī*, which is the form of the *kalā* of the syllable *ha*, becomes thus absorbed in the syllable *a*, which is the uninterrupted, all-pervading, and perfectly full, unobstructed wonder; this very state is my own heart-space (*hṛdvyoma*), because of which this [is so].
That very [reality] wherein [the world] has issued forth and wherein it comes to rest is eternal, its nature unobscured, self-manifesting,
undeniable, and unsurpassed. As it has been said:
In that wherein all this effect resides and from which it has emerged,

Thus: for even that which is considered an obstruction by virtue of its being a veil is, when manifesting through its own sovereignty as that very veil and so forth, none other than the Supreme Lord whose nature consists of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyā*). Here, the particle *yat*—which functions in the sense of all case endings—remains fixed in this specific sense due to the suitability of its connection with the subsequent sentence.
It functions in the sense of the ablative and the locative. This is indeed the direct meaning—without even the discernment of subtle objects:
that which is this emanation of the *kaulika* creation, and that which abides in the space of my heart, that alone is the Absolute (*anuttara*). Thus, of that very same...

The proof of the thesis (*pakṣasādhana*) is the proposition (*pratijñā*); the thesis is that which possesses the doubtful probandum (*saṃdigdhasādhyavān*), as for example: "This mountain possesses fire. In that very context, the reason (*hetu*) is that which indicates the mark (*liṅga*) for the sake of another's understanding, as for example: "Because it possesses smoke. In that same context, the example (*udāharaṇa*) is the cause for clear comprehension, as for example: [the instance of a kitchen, etc.]

The application (*upanaya*) is the presentation of the probans (*sādhana*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), based on the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the kitchen and other such places—namely, "and this [mountain] is likewise.

The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the presentation of the probandum (*sādhya*) in that same subject—namely, "therefore, it is so. For those who possess firm *śaktipāta*, [the goal is attained] by the conclusion alone.
