As for what the venerable Śrī Somānanda said:
The letter *a* is said to be Śiva, and the letter *tha* is called Śakti; by this demonstration from the Āgama, the word *atha* alone is the Absolute (*anuttara*).

This being so, according to the logic of a "conclusion established by the context" (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*), that which was previously stated—even though a sequence of priority and posteriority is not possible—[is now established].

"In the same way, there is not even the slightest suspicion regarding [the attainment of] silence and so forth," they explained in the first chapter (*ullāsa*) everywhere, with the intention that the phonemes *tha* and *ha* possess equal pervasion (*samavyāptikatā*) when one effect is accomplished, all other effects are accomplished of their own accord; this is what is called *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.
Because it is of the nature of non-difference from the power of creating an infinite-infinite array of objects that is ever-expanding.
Furthermore, because the meaning of the word "atha" consists in its being based upon the supreme *nāda* (sound), which is the life-force residing within all beings,
we have not analyzed that in detail— since we are not directly cognizant of such scripture, whereas they [the masters] are so.

The fact that the Sūtra-text is capable of withstanding hundreds of various arguments has already been indicated by those who have directly realized the scriptural tradition; even the demonstration of the distinctions among the *dhūli* [particles] is merely the exposition of the meaning of the *Cūrṇi*. With that very intention—that is, with the intention of establishing equal pervasion—it was stated by them (i.e., by the venerable Somānanda) from this point onward.

"From that" means from various scriptures characterized by the *Parātriṃśikā* and so forth; and "from that" [it is] spread out. We, however, being purified by those teachings and desiring the purification of our own selves through the unraveling of the knots of their texts, remain entirely indifferent toward such matters as these which have been determined by them, as well as regarding the distinctions between the *dhūlis* and so on.

Even the dependence on imagined conventional signs (*sāmayika-likhya*)—where "conventional" means "indicatory"—might occur for someone [since the arrangement of phonemes is entirely different in all regions, it does not apply to everyone]. (p. 101)

Regarding the means (*upāya*), the distinction of time (*kālabheda*) should be understood in exactly this way. It is not, however, intended for disciples existing in all places and times; thus, we have not elaborated upon this at length.
For those who have entered into the logic of direct experience, that [means] is ineffective, and it is easily accomplished through their own conceptualizations.

And it remains so for others who are ignorant of this instruction; here is the distinction: "Like a drop of water fallen upon a stone heated by the summer sun, the song of instruction never produces an internal impact in the foolish."
And so it has been said: "The words of instruction, even when accepted as objects of knowledge by others, are unable to take root in the hearts of those with deluded minds."
Do the streams of rain from the sky, though clinging closely together, bestow moisture upon the lotus petals?

Thus, even that instruction is ineffective; enough of this which causes an obstacle to the subject at hand. Let us follow the main topic: [the term] *athādi* refers to those vowels of which *a* is the first, or alternatively, those of which *atha*—with the letter *tha* added for the sake of easy pronunciation—is the first.

Regarding the word "first" (*ādya*) here, it does not refer merely to a fixed position, nor even to proximity and so forth; rather, "first" means that which exists at the beginning. Nevertheless, this ground of Parāvāk is determined here as belonging to these phonemes.
In that very state, their form is non-temporal, eternal, uncreated, and consists solely of consciousness (*saṃvinmaya*).

Within this body of consciousness, the state of being the self of all things is perpetually manifest; and she who is thus the Supreme Goddess, the Most Venerable Parā, even while partaking in such unsurpassed non-duality, [manifests as] Paśyantī and the other levels of speech.

[The *parā* is according to the analogy of the liquid inside a peacock’s egg; the *paśyantī* is according to the analogy of the seed-vessel of a banyan tree; the *madhyamā* is according to the analogy of a bean sprout; and beyond that is the *vaikharī*.
She is the nature of the expansion of the venerable goddess Parāparā and others, having internalized within herself all those various infinite diversities.
For it is not logical that what does not exist there could exist anywhere else; and as one reflects upon this, one perceives the first [level of speech],

called *pratibhā* (intuition), according to the analogy of the fluid within a peacock’s egg, then the *parā* (the supreme) according to the analogy of the seed-vessel of a banyan tree, then the *madhyamā* (the intermediate) according to the analogy of the *māṣa-śamikā* plant, and after that, the *vaikharī* (the manifest).
The Blessed Consciousness is devoid even of the slightest trace of the impurity of contraction; for indeed, whatever exists, whether moving or unmoving, is, in its ultimate and imperishable form,
essentially composed of the very substance of *vīrya* (vital energy).
That [consciousness], at the time when hundreds of objects— ranging from those about to arise to those that are extremely indistinct, more indistinct, and slightly indistinct— are being polished,
perceives each of those infinite [objects] individually.

By virtue of being manifested through its own manifold variety, it remains indeed within consciousness—which is the divine Lord Bhairava-Bhaṭṭāraka—when firmly established through an excellence of focused attention. [The intention here is this:

the established doctrine states that "the determinations of objects reside in consciousness," and that is not...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be fragmentary at the end. The translation reflects the available portion.*
These entities are established not merely by resting in pure consciousness whose nature is valid cognition (*pramā*) despite its diverse forms,

but rather through the medium of various cognitions whose nature is valid cognition— such as ascertainment (*niścaya*) and so forth— if these entities abide within the single essential nature of "I" (*aham*); otherwise, for insentient objects and their respective cognitions, [such establishment would be impossible].

There would be no coherence whatsoever among those conceptual constructions and determinations, which occur sequentially in space and time and are established solely in their own individual forms. And this has been stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
When entities, through the various gateways of their distinct cognitions, come to rest within a single cognizer, this state of "knowability" (jñāteya) becomes possible.
Likewise,
for objects that possess a sequence of space and time and which terminate within themselves, [the cognition is simultaneous].
This [state] is to be accomplished by a single manifestation; otherwise, what kind of integration could there be?
Thus, in this manner,
within the all-pervasive [consciousness] which is inlaid with the manifestation of objects that appear as exceedingly distinct,
worldly transaction— whether impure or pure— is experienced.
Thus, this has been stated as "with such attentiveness. With this very intention, it is said in the *Śivopaniṣad*:
"The consciousness of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings;
however, for yogins, this distinction lies in their attentiveness toward that connection."
Thus, the stage of omniscience— uncontracted in its ultimate reality, unartificial in its nature—

is indeed ascended by those purified by the favor of others, through whose form that non-doubting state has been ground, polished, and refined by the friction of the whetstone of the sequence of practice.

Even for those possessed by doubt—doubt being a stain synonymous with trembling and other such states—their consciousness appears contracted by the mere object that momentarily manifests. This is the intended meaning here:
for one perceiving blue, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), consisting of sixteen *tuṭis*, arises until the point of immersion into the object of knowledge; therein, the first...

The first *tuṭi* is of a single nature, devoid of division; the second is of the nature of the emergence of the subject (*grāhaka*); the last, however, is non-different from the object (*grāhya*) and consists of that; the penultimate, however, is of the nature of the subject as it becomes manifest. As for the middle twelvefold [cycle], its half is of the nature of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*), which veils conceptualization; therein, one is [the *tuṭi*] by way of its own essential nature.
In the conceptualization that is to be covered, there is the desire to open (*unmimipiṣā*), which is the state of opening (*unmiṣattā*);
and this, because it consists of a manifest activity, is composed of two moments (*tuṭi*), since it lacks the nature of a single moment of vibration (*spandana*).
Furthermore, there is the state of having opened (*unmiṣitatā*) and the capacity to perform its own function.

Thus, due to the fivefold nature of the objects to be concealed and their essential form (*svarūpa*), there are six moments (*tuṭi*) that are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Following that, there are six *tuṭis* consisting of: the state of the non-conceptual being destroyed (*dhvaṃsamānatā*), its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), the desire of the conceptual thought to emerge (*unmimiṣipā*), its emerging state (*unmiṣattā*), its fully emerged state (*unmiṣitatā*), and the capacity to perform its own function (*svakāryakartṛtā*).

It has been stated that the nature of the grasper is no longer counted; thus, when there is a decrease in conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there is a corresponding decrease in the *tuṭi*s. This being the case, as long as there is a decrease in duality—which is essentially the clear sense of "I" and "this"—the pair [of *tuṭi*s] diminishes by two at a time, until the immersion into Śiva consists of only two *tuṭi*s. Among these, the first *tuṭi*...

The second [tuṭi], which is full in every respect and permeated by the instruments of all-knowingness, when practiced, conduces to omniscience and omnipotence; however, the first does not. This very point has been handed down by Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa as "the falling away of the tuṭi" (*tuṭipāta*);
the meaning is that the "falling away" (*pāta*)—that is, the diminution—of the first *tuṭi* is the subsequent *tuṭi*, the second. But it is not...
It is artificial. As the venerable Kallaṭapāda has said:
"Upon the falling away of a *tuṭi*, there is the attainment of omniscience and omnipotence.
Thus, although this object is of the sole nature of self-luminosity, it is [perceived] through reasoning—

It is demonstrated as follows: whatever [cognition] possesses an unshakeable correspondence— attained through the force of its truth being rendered exhaustive by the capacity for causal efficiency arising subsequently from its own power— and which appears as a contradiction...
Just as the non-conceptual form of consciousness— which precedes the conceptualization of blue and so forth that is being conceptually constructed in a sequential order—
is inseparable from the appearances of blue, yellow, and so on, which are considered to be contradictory to those respective objects of conceptualization; so it is.

Just as in the case of variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), it is not that the variegated form does not appear—since that would contradict direct experience (*saṃvitti*) and because what is insentient (*jaḍa*) cannot be manifest; therefore, this form is of the very nature of cognition itself. Nor is there a difference in cognition due to a difference in forms, because a single variegated form lacks a plurality of forms, just as blue is one.

The aspect has blue as its intrinsic nature; likewise, the aspect of a single variegated [object] has variegation itself as its intrinsic nature. And cognition, when operating upon that which constitutes its own essence, operates entirely upon it, or else does not operate at all—it does not operate partially, because that [aspect] is partless. As for these [supposed] parts:
The meaning is that they do not appear as mutually distinct; thus, there is no such thing as "variegated form" (*citra-rūpa*).
For even though there is a difference between the objects of cognition, such as houses and so forth, for Śikharaśvāmin, there would be only a single appearance of the city.
The point is that even in the case of "dark-blue cognition"—that is, non-conceptual knowledge of blue and so forth—there is likewise no differentiation.
That which arises from the consciousness situated at the peak of variegated cognition— such as the awareness of deep blue and so forth—
is not divided from the manifestations of blue, yellow, and other colors that are its contrary forms; rather,
it consists of those very [colors] such as blue and yellow, produced by the emergence of its own infinite inherent powers.
Even though it is preceded by the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it does not become [conceptual]— just as the cognition that directly perceives blue [is non-conceptual]—

and this [cognition], such as the flash of intuition (*unmeṣa-pratibhā*) occurring in the interval between two cognitions of conceptual constructions regarding what has set and what is about to rise, indeed exists.
That which is proclaimed in the verbal tradition [the verbal tradition being the treatises on grammar] is non-conceptual;
it precedes conceptualizations such as "blue" and the like, which are accompanied by correspondence or contradiction.
Therefore, it consists solely of an undivided manifestation of that [object] immediately following it—and this applies to both.

The interval between two cognitions is undeniable; it exists precisely because of the difference between those two cognitions, and it is itself of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-ātmaka*). Otherwise, if that interval were not conscious, the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of consciousness would be destroyed. [Regarding the phrase "destruction of impressions":
this means that new and ever-new appearances would undergo arising and passing away at every moment, resulting in the collapse of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-hāni*). And therefore...
When a certain object has been previously grasped, that consciousness which was formerly directed outward possesses an inward-facing nature consisting of pure awareness (*cit-svarūpa*).

The power of memory (*smaraṇa-śakti*) is that which, even at a later time and throughout various states, reflects upon that inwardness residing in its own self while simultaneously perceiving the outward-directedness toward that specific object.
Likewise, synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) consists in the attainment of a memory that has come to possess a single object; thus,
for all disputants, there is no possibility of synthesis such as recollection and so forth for a subject (*dharmin*) designated as "intuition" (*pratibhā*).
p.
107) There is no dispute [on this point], for it has been stated in the *Sūtravimarśinī* by this very author:
"Without whom nothing at all would exist, even all philosophical views (*dṛṣṭi*)."
We praise that auspicious Śiva, whose nature is unceasing awakening.
Thus, there is no lack of proof; and because it does not depend upon the time of the acquisition of linguistic convention (*saṃketa-vyutpatti*), it is indeed non-conceptual (*avikalpa*).
For the connection with an innate and non-conventional reflective awareness (*tathā-parāmarśa*) is inseparable from the nature of consciousness, which is distinct from the insentient (*jaḍa*).
[But surely, how can there be a reflective awareness in the Blessed One, whose nature is pure consciousness, that is equivalent to conceptualization?]
Could this be so? To this he says: "Inert," and so forth. And it has been said:
"They know that the essential nature of manifestation is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); otherwise, even if it is colored by an object, light would be like an inert thing such as a crystal."

Thus it is said. Nor should it be argued: "How then could that not be of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? For it does not possess the same status as conceptual construction, because no differentiation (*bheda*) is manifested therein. And so it has been stated: "That reflective awareness of the 'I'-notion, though its essence is light, is yet the body of speech."
That conceptual construction is not tenable; it is a definitive determination that projects a duality.

Thus: there is no equality with conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), because [conceptual thought] does not manifest difference; rather, it would bring about the existence of objects by having obtained the essence of difference. Furthermore, conceptual thoughts do not arise without non-conceptual [awareness], because they lack autonomy, and this lack of autonomy is due to [the absence of that non-conceptual awareness].
Since it has the recollection of conventions and so forth as its means, and since such recollection of conventions and so forth cannot exist without prior experience,

and because— according to the previously stated reasoning— consciousness lacks delimitation by time and other factors, this sovereign intuition (*pratibhā*) of the Supreme Lord is of such a nature, being conceived solely through the power of our [authoritative] statement.

Although its nature is undivided, it is indeed the self of all; even while abiding in the middle, it is the very ground for the production of various conceptualizations of past and future forms. Thus, according to that view: "For if the object were to appear as having a nature distinct from cognition..."
Would this [object] be perceived even in the absence of cognition? But such is not the case; therefore, there is indeed no difference between cognition and the object. As they have said:
"Because of the rule of simultaneous perception, there is no difference between the blue and the cognition thereof."

Thus, it is cognition alone that appears in various ways everywhere; there is no such thing as an object distinct from it. Therefore, the entire conventional usage of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the act of knowing (*pramiti*) is subsumed within cognition itself.
For its taking on the form of the object is the *prameya*, and its being the cause of the grasping subject-form is the *pramāṇa*.

"And self-awareness is the fruit. As it has been said: "That which appears is the object of cognition; that [same appearance] is the means of cognition, and furthermore, it is the fruit. Because of the awareness of the form of the apprehender, these three are not made separate from one another."

Thus, because the vision of reality has been distorted by the play of the impressions of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyāvāsanā*), knowledge itself appears as if it possessed the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject; however, upon the cessation of ignorance, this becomes purely transparent, or rather, it is nothing at all. As it has been said:
There is no other experience for the intellect, nor is there any further experience of it;
because it is devoid of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, it shines by itself.

Thus: "Likewise, although the nature of the intellect is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinctions of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness, to those whose vision is distorted."
Thus, seeing that this is indeed mere consciousness, devoid of both object and form,
one casts off the succession of suffering and attains fearless Nirvana.
Thus is the doctrine of the Sugatas. Furthermore, by those skilled in discernment, it has been accepted that the *ālayavijñāna* alone is the [source],
and its status as being in agreement with the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arising immediately thereafter has already been demonstrated.

Thus, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). Furthermore, in that which performs the differentiation of a conceptual construction appearing as a single unity: "That which is cognized by a cognition is not distinct from it, just as the self is [not distinct] from knowledge; blue and other objects are cognized [by knowledge]. For if there were a difference, its status as being cognized by knowledge would not exist, because of identity (*tādātmya*)."
Because there is no cause for restriction, if one thing were cognizable by another with which it is unrelated, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Thus, since the relation—which is the pervader and the cause of restriction—is not perceived in the case of difference, the property of being cognizable (*vedyatva*), which is excluded from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) of difference, is pervaded by non-difference (*abheda*). And this which...
The appearance of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the cognition as distinct from one another is an error, like the appearance of duality in a single moon. As it has been said:
"And this distinction would appear in non-erroneous cognition, just as the two [moons] appear in the case of the moon."

Thus: [it] either always or at some time exists in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) which is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), and its exclusion from that is not doubtful; therefore, it is neither contradictory (*viruddha*) nor inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). (p. 110)

The exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. For instance, just as the act of cutting is connected with and divided by that which is to be cut, so too the act of cognition will be connected with and divided by the object of cognition; thus, the opponent’s position is that the exclusion of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) from the counter-example is also doubtful. To this—

Since the rule of the simultaneous apprehension of blue and its cognition is established by the mere fact that cognition is self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedya*) and cognizes another (*parasaṃvedya*), the opponent’s position is that because an external object does not exist, cognition does not become a cognizer of another. [This is stated] with reference to the property of the example, such as variegated cognition (*citrājñāna*), and so forth.

In this very way, the defects of the reason (*hetu*), such as its being unestablished (*asiddha*), are indeed avoided; and when the defects of the reason have been removed, defects of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and so forth simply find no room. Since much of this has already been determined by others, what is the point of the trouble of merely repeating it? This much, at least, is established:
That which is intuitive, which encompasses all objects of experience,
which exists before, after, and within them, and which is the essence of all— [in that state],
for one whose body has dissolved into her, she shines as the Supreme Power.
Exhaustion would occur—that is, it would reach a state of dissolution—would this be brought about by the power of non-existence? [Regarding "non-existence":
as others have said, "One should meditate on non-existence until one attains identity with it."]
Thus [it is said].
(111) Without beholding the veil of the enjoyment of others' wealth and pleasures within his own body, life-force, and so forth, he experiences an incomparable despondency in his heart.
If the Supreme Goddess, who is the essence of the birth of the entire universe, has indeed entered within, then— alas!— may she shine forth like a full oblation.
As it is said in the *Spanda*:
"Lassitude in the body is a thief; its course arises from ignorance.
If that [ignorance] is destroyed by the unfolding of [consciousness], how could such lassitude exist without a cause?"
Thus:
"Since the emergence of another thought occurs for one who is intent upon a single thought, that should be known as 'unmeṣa' (the opening); one should recognize it by oneself."
And thus it is said:
"The auspicious ones maintain that the root of the impurities of illusion and karma is indeed the impurity called 'ignorance' (ajñāna), which is the individual soul (māṇava)."
That very seed of the ancient tree of worldly existence is, in the supreme fire that consumes consciousness, burnt away in an instant.
As they have said:
"They maintain that ignorance is the impurity, the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra.
This very point has been stated.

"If that [glāni] were destroyed by its own unfolding (*unmeṣa*)... and so forth. It has been explained exactly in this way; otherwise, how could there be any connection between what is being said? For instance: the destruction of exhaustion (*glāni*) occurs through this [unfolding], and the departure from ignorance (*ajñāna*) occurs through this [exhaustion], while the destruction of ignorance occurs through its unfolding (*unmeṣa*). What, then, is connected with what?
It would be essentially a description of the king:
he who is elevated by the wind of his own excellence, who is upright,
who has cast off all impurities, and who is difficult to overcome.

Thus, the Blessed One, the ground of supreme speech (*parāvāgbhūmi*), contains within herself the unfolding of the venerable goddesses Parāparā and the others, who arise from the power of her own sovereignty and are situated in the levels of Paśyantī and the rest;
and by virtue of containing them within herself, she is the manifold expansion of all beings, worlds, and entities, fashioned without dispute.
Its essence is the wonder of the unity of awakening;

its true nature is that supreme reality, manifested as the marvelous being of such a kind through the appearance of the Supreme Lord, the venerable Bhairava; it is the stainlessness of one's own self—

(p. 113) By means of the passage beginning with "Now, the primordial [power]" (*athādyā*), the Blessed One definitively establishes in its entirety the Great Creative Power (*mahāsṛṣṭiśakti*)— which consists of the unity of infinite creation, maintenance, and withdrawal reflected in a mirror, and which takes the form of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.
It is established. Thus, [it being established that everything exists right there], the meaning of the text is determined as follows:

the Śiva-tattva consists of the letters from *a* to the *visarga*; the five elements consist of the letters from *ka* to *ṅa*, corresponding to earth through ether; and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) consist of the letters from *ca* to *ña*, corresponding to smell through sound.
The five organs of action (karmendriyas) begin with *ṭ* and end with *ṇ*;

the five instruments of cognition (buddhikaraṇas), beginning with the sense of smell and ending with the ear, begin with *t* and end with *n*; the pentad consisting of mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the individual soul (*puruṣa*) begins with *p* and ends with *m*; and the letters from *y* onwards are denoted by the term "air" (*vāyu*) and so forth.

The principles (tattvas) called Rāga, Vidyā, Kalā, and Māyā, which end in the letter *va*, are "retainers" (*dhāraṇāni*) because they cause [the soul] to hold onto—that is, to conceive of itself as—distinct [from the Supreme]. There are two causative suffixes (*ṇic*) here due to the dual nature of the relationship between the instigator and the instigated;
for indeed, all of them are "held" (*dhriyante*)—meaning they maintain their own existence—within their very own selves.
All entities reside within the state that is the self-luminous, supremely perfect, and all-pervading Bhairava-nature; as it is stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*: "in the self of Śiva. (p. 114)

The Self alone— whose nature is its own essence— is Śiva, whose body is consciousness that shines forth within all existents [“whose body is consciousness” means one who has made all objects of knowledge his own],
whose flow of will is unimpeded, and whose powers of vision and action are ever-expanding.
Thus it is said; as stated in the *Spanda*:
"In which all this is established... and so forth. In this way, one perceives those entities that are sustained by manifestation within one's own self, which is luminous.
It maintains itself through its own lack of self-luminosity— by means of its nature as insentience— as "this-ness" (idantā),
as stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"For those things augmented by the state of 'this-ness' which have reached the level of the object of knowledge..."
Because the essence of all phenomena is awakening, one perceives them exactly as they are.

Thus, by bringing about the state of being the locus of existence, the Supreme Lord reveals [the world] and then again covers it precisely with the sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*). Therefore, this state of the Lord Sadāśiva, consisting of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), is intimated by a single *ṇic* suffix; and therein, that which belongs to the sphere of "this-ness" (*idantā*) is [subsumed] by "I-ness" (*ahantā*).
That covering (ācchādana) is established when there is the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā)—
[that is,
it is established within the friendship of "this-ness" consisting of the forms of Vidyeśvara and so forth, and not otherwise].

Furthermore, in relation to the pure, supreme Lord’s nature consisting of consciousness, this form called "thisness" (*idantā*), which consists of the manifestation of difference, is not possible; thus, since that which is to be concealed is impossible, the concealment of the *ahaṃbhāva* (the sense of "I") by virtue of it is also impossible, and consequently, such a cognition of the Lord is impossible, and in its impossibility—
Nothing at all would appear— because of the absence of a cause, as has been stated more than once— and yet this world does appear.
Although it is not distinct from that [supreme] light, it manifests externally solely through the power of the Supreme Lord,
because no other cause is possible and because within one's own consciousness, consciousness itself is manifested as being composed of everything.

Thus, the world, which is one's own essential nature, though appearing as differentiated, shines within the "I" (ahamātman) which is identical with the Light itself, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). By this much, the following has necessarily been implied:
that it is the Lord alone who perceives certain objects of knowledge, distinct from Himself, as "I," and who is that very [Lord].
Whoever is the experiencer is also, by virtue of manifesting, identical with his own self; thus, he rests within his own self upon such powers (p.
By means of which [impurities], he would at that very moment attain the state of having the distinction between the object of cognition and the subject of cognition;

and since it is through passion and the like that he becomes such, it is passion and the like themselves that, by the aforementioned reasoning, become the instigators toward the Lord who maintains the existing entities. Therefore, it belongs to Him alone...

Being the sole cause for the designation of masculinity, when a second *ṇic* suffix arises, these [meanings] are expressed by the word "dhāraṇa" (sustaining). Even upon the occurrence of the *ṇic*, there is no loss of the connection with the meaning of the root (*prakṛti*) in any case; for indeed, the state of being sustained belongs only to that which is manifest as being sustained, and this is the technical term "manifestation" (*prakāśanā*).
This is logical, as it was stated by me myself in the *Śivadṛṣṭyālocana*:
"Even that which is sent forth must possess what is called 'capacity'. Bhartṛhari also says:
For when there is an instigation of one who has not yet begun to act, the imperative (loṭ) is prescribed after roots such as *pra-chād*;
but when there is an instigation of one who has already begun to act, then that is the domain of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

Thus, in this way, by the word *dhāraṇā*, it is precisely those principles (*tattvas*) well-known under the name of *kañcukas* in other scriptures that have been described here; as it has been stated in the *Śrītantrasāra*:

Just as the bonds of a sacrificial animal hold it fast, so do the principles such as Vidyā, Māyā, and Niyati—which consist of one's own self—bind the individual soul; therefore, these must be purified with diligent effort.

Thus it is said. As for the fact that the venerable Śrī Somānanda used the word *dhāraṇā* (retention) to designate the ancillary limbs (*aṅga*) by resorting to an alternative interpretation [meaning by explaining them in another sense], his intention therein was merely to demonstrate that all the views of other schools are visible within himself; for such is his style.
"Śailī is that which resides in moral conduct (śīla); it is activity preceded by concentration, according to Kayyaṭa; others say it is composition; still others say it is one's own doctrine.
He who does not know his own positions and the positions of others in their entirety—
How can he, who is himself sinking in the ocean of doubt, enable others to cross?

Thus, the five principles beginning with Śādi and ending with Kṣānta are known as Mahāmāyā, Vidyeśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śakti. For instance, between the principle of Māyā above and the principle of Vidyā below, there must necessarily be another principle wherein the Vijñānākalas reside.
In this regard, the sequence stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* is as follows:
"The loss of freedom for consciousness and the lack of consciousness for freedom—
this is the twofold *āṇava* impurity, resulting from the abandonment of one's own true nature."
Even though they possess the nature of pure consciousness, those who do not exercise supreme agency have been created by the Lord as distinct from Himself due to the absence of that agency.
And these, being solitary consciousnesses whose nature is the non-cognition of Śūnya and the rest, are the agents known as the Pralayākalas;
such is the established doctrine, as has been stated.
Above Māyā and below Śuddhavidyā reside the Vijñānakevalas.

Thus it is said. For instance, in the absence of Mahāmāyā, the Pralayakevalas abide in the realm of Māyā, while the Vidyeśvaras and others abide in the realm of Vidyā; so what could that [realm] be other than the station of the Vijñānakevalas? Therefore, even for those who have fallen from the realm of Vidyā, this [state remains].

Because the manifestation of diverse objects of cognition situated within the mass of differentiated entities does not arise, and because the impurity designated as "māyīya" does not manifest there, it is said in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* that the *vijñānakevala* is joined with only one impurity;
thus, its dependence on the *āṇavamala*, which consists of ignorance, is described therein. These very [entities]...
Awakened by the grace of the state of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), they partake in the nature of the mantra and its lords and so forth; for it is said elsewhere:
"He attains the status of a *mantra* through the awakening bestowed by Ananteśa.
Thus it is stated in that very [text]:
"He awakened eight *pudgala*s who were *vijñānakevala*s."
Having thus appointed [him] to the state of a Lord of the Great Lords of Mantra (*mantramaheśvareśa*) by means of such passages,

and also by means of other passages such as "In some scriptures, however, that Great Māyā [is so called] by way of metaphorical designation due to the absence of the impurity of differentiation (*bhedamala*)."

In some cases, [the principle of *vidyā*] is determined as being merely a residue of the *vidyā*-tattva; however, due to the obstruction caused by the presence of the impurity of ignorance (*ajñāna-mala*), it is sometimes treated as a tail-end of the *māyā*-tattva, as in certain scriptures where the *rāga*-tattva is not mentioned separately because it is attached only to the individual soul (*pums*). Or, for example, in these very *Śrītrikāgamas*, *niyati* and *kāla* are not treated separately.
In this system, these two have been described; furthermore, the fivefold Brahman—beginning with Vidyā and ending with Śiva—will be determined here.

Moreover, the "greatness" (*bṛhattva*) and "expansiveness" (*bṛṃhakatva*) of these principles (*tattva*s) arise primarily from their transcendence of duality and their status as the agents of the birth of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Thus are they.
(120) The thirty-four principles (*tattvas*), existing in the form of the creative process (*prakriyā*), partake of the letter *a* alone as their primordial form.
Regarding this, the following is investigated: first, the principle of Śiva [is located] in the *a*-group, then the elements (*bhūtas*), and so forth.

Up until the end, where the *śaktitattva* [is reached]— what kind of sequence is this among the sequences of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), cognition (*jñapti*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and descent (*avatāra*)? And in all the scriptures, such as the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*, the *Siddhātantra*, and the *Svacchanda*, [the sequence begins] from the letter *kṣa*.

Regarding the phrase "starting with," the sequence here is as follows: on the earth [tattva], there is the single syllable *kṣa* alone, consisting of a word and a mantra; in the principles from water up to the unmanifest (*avyakta*), there are twenty-three syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *ṭa*, which constitute two mantras of four syllables each and five syllables [in total].
In the [principles] beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Māyā, there are seven phonemes from *dha* to *na*; these constitute two mantras as words:

one of five syllables and the second of two syllables. Furthermore, in Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, there are three phonemes, *ga*, *kha*, and *ka*, which likewise constitute a mantra of three syllables as a single word. In the Śiva-tattva, however, [there is only one].
The single reality of phoneme, word, and mantra consists of the sixteen vowels;

and because power (*śakti*) is predominant, it is one alone, for power cannot be distinct from the possessor of power—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, by adding one [vowel] to each of the thirty-four principles beginning with Earth (*kṣiti*), starting from the letter *kṣa*...

Since it is appropriate for the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) during the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*) that the thirty-sixth principle— which was previously considered all-pervasive and endowed with power— should consist of the sixteen vowels from *visarga* onwards in direct order (*ānulomyena*), ending with the vowel *a*. And it has been stated elsewhere:
Then, having established the state of being a single syllable for each respective principle (tattva) starting from Kṣama,
it is declared that in the supreme Śiva-principle there are sixteen syllables, including the visarga.
Thus, from [the beginning] up to the end of the *avarga* group (p. 121), the arrangement of the principles (*tattva*) starting from the earthly (*pārthiva*) and ending with Śiva has been described.
Regarding the first *dhārikā* (the sustainer): this is the doctrine of Maheśvara, as stated in the *Śrīpūrva*:
"The *dhārikā* is the pervader (*āpyinī*), the cognizer (*boddhrī*), the purifier (*pavitrī*), and the provider of space (*avakāśadā*)."
Thus, one principle is held to be pervading therein;
one should contemplate each individual letter, word, and syllable separately.
And in that very same place, furthermore, according to the *Bhinnayonimālinī-bhaṭṭārikā*— [regarding the term *mālinī*:

as stated by the illustrious Rājānaka Jayadratha on the occasion of its commentary— "That whose *yoni*, characterized by the letters beginning with *ka*, is *bhinna*, meaning differentiated by the vowels"].

In this context, the *mālinī* mantra denotes Śakti, while the *mātṛkā* mantra denotes the Possessor of Śakti (*śaktimān*). Among these, the *mātṛkā* is well known. As for the *mālinī*, it is as follows: na, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, tha, ca, dha, ī, ṇa, u, ū, ba, ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, i, a, ba, bha, ya, ḍa, ḍha, ṭha, jha, ña, ja, ra, ṭa, pa, cha, la, ā, sa, aḥ, ha, ya, kṣa, ma, śa.
"Aṃ ta e ai o au da pha. Also, in the *Trikahṛdaya*:
"But Nādinī, located at the tip of the crest-lock, is designated by the syllable 'na'.
Thus it is said that the Blessed Mālinī is indeed the primary Śākta form.
Through the friction of seed-syllables and matrices, she is the wish-fulfilling cow of all desires; this name is significant in meaning:

she is joined with the garlands of Rudra’s powers, she blossoms with fruits, she is the female bee of the resonance that destroys the coolness of saṃsāra, and she bestows both supernatural attainments and liberation.

"Endowed with the power of giving and taking," because of the traditional rule that *ra* and *la* are interchangeable; for this very reason, even a mantra whose ritual procedure has been lost becomes complete through this placement (*nyāsa*).
Even a "smeared" (*sāñjana*) mantra—such as those of the Gāruḍa or Vaiṣṇava traditions—attains the state of being "unsmeared" (*nirañjana*) and becomes a bestower of liberation.
Even for those [letters] beginning with *pha*, which have attained their respective internal states through the placement of the Mātṛkā whose source is undivided—
*phe* is taught as the earth-principle (*dharātattva*), [and so on] in successive order from *ca* to *ña*.
By the passage beginning with "The twenty-three *āvādīs*," the application of the principles (*tattva*) starting from the earthly element is described. Furthermore, in that very same place,
according to the three *Vidyās*— [the phrase "according to the three *Vidyās*" refers to...]— the application is again set forth.
O Goddess, that power of the Creator of the universe which has been described as inherent (samavāyinī) becomes His will when He desires to emit [the world].

Thus, because its nature consists of the first surging forth and it has the inherent disposition to overflow outwardly, it is called *parā* (the Supreme), being the abode of rest for the subject; from that [state], there arises the well-ascertained cognition: "This object is thus and not otherwise."
Making [the world] known here in this universe, she is called the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
Thus, wherever the rays consisting of will and action, which were interwoven within, converge,
there the All-pervasive Lord alone unfolds.
Such is what is called the "supreme and non-supreme" [will]. Furthermore,
when [the will arises] again with the thought, "May this object become thus," and they bring that object into being at that very moment, it is called "action" (kriyā) in this context.
Thus, that which consists of the manifold variety of various subjects, objects of knowledge, and so forth, is called the "lower" (apara).
As stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:
"That by which this world, from Śiva down to the earth, is both sustained and perceived as being of the nature of non-conceptual pure consciousness alone..."

And the Supreme Lord illumines; that is His supreme power (*parā-śakti*). That by which [He illumines] through both difference and non-difference, like a mirror and an elephant and so forth, is the supreme-non-supreme power (*parāparā-śakti*).
That by which [He illumines] solely through difference, characterized by mutual distinctness, is the inferior power (*aparā-śakti*).
Thus, regarding the description of the three sciences in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (p.
in the Niṣkala [state], there is the single-syllable word; in the two [states of Śakala and Śaktopāya], there are the two pairs consisting of the tri-syllabic and the single-syllabic.
Thus, according to the Parāparā-bhaṭṭārikā: "In the Śrīmanmālinīvijaya,
for the purification of the path regarding Māyā and in the rite of initiation in all respects,
the wise one should employ the Aparā mantra in those ritual acts where no specific mantra has been mentioned."
One should join [the principles] from Vidyā up to Sakala in that same manner as the Parāparā;
above Īśvara, one should not join the group of eight beginning with Niyati.
Furthermore, the wise one should not perform the six-limbed rite above the Sakala level;
rather, whatever is enjoined by the ritual rules should be performed with the Parā [mantra] in the Niṣkala state.

Thus, for those possessing extremely subtle discernment, the fundamental meaning here is indeed easily understood and need not be further determined; however, for others, even the presentation of logical arguments would be as useless as grinding what has already been ground. [This concludes the exposition of the principles (tattvas) beginning with the earthly, in the sequence starting with the syllable *oṃ* as the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), *aghora* as the principle of Śakti (*śaktitattva*), and so forth.]

Furthermore, in that very same place, according to the reality (*tattva*) of the Śrī-vidyā, there is the establishment of the *mātṛkā* of the non-differentiated womb beginning with the letter *pha*, by which one attains a state within another reality.
Regarding their names as well: the principles of the elements (dhātutattvas), beginning with the letter Ca and ending with Ña, are indicated in successive order,
consisting of twenty-three vowels and so forth.
By such statements as these, there is the application of the principles (*tattva-yojanā*). Furthermore, according to the intention of the venerable Aparā-bhaṭṭārikā:
"Two cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*) are pervaded by [the first] half [of the power], and two [others] separately by each [of the remaining halves];
this pervasion of Aparā has been declared in reverse order. [The summary of the meaning here is: the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)—
The meaning is that the triad of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) should be understood in their reverse order.

By such statements as these, the placement of the principles (*tattva*) is as follows: the two mundane cosmic eggs (*prākṛtāṇḍa*) are within the syllable *phaṭ*; the illusory egg (*māyīya*) is within the syllable *huṃ*; and the power-egg (*śāktamaṇḍa*) is within the syllable *hrīṃ*. Furthermore, in the determination of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the venerable Supreme Goddess (*Parābhaṭṭārikā*), it is said: "The triad is pervaded by the letter *sa*, and the fourth by the trident."

The supreme pervasion (*parā vyāpti*) is declared to be that which transcends everything through emission (*visarga*). Furthermore, the intention behind explaining this is as follows: when purification is achieved by means of one form, the Guru, possessed of continuous contemplation (*anusandhānavān*), should perform the purification while internally including other modalities within that very same state.
He states that even when there is no capacity for inclusion, there is another sequence:
"But when there is no capacity for inclusion, the subtle [seed] is purified within the subtle;
for that, being pure, does not produce a subsequent continuity because it has become a seed."
Thus; and all this is well known in the *Trikasāra*.
Thus, the application of the ritual procedure has been described in a different manner; furthermore,
it is [also] presented according to the intention of the venerable mantras such as Mātṛkā-sadbhāva, Ratiśekhara, Kuleśvara, and others.

In one way and another, even within the *paratantra* [dependent nature], much that is largely erroneous has been described many times; yet here, all of that is seen to be entirely otherwise—thus, this great upheaval, like a disturbance in one's own camp, has arisen among those who know the scriptures, threatening total destruction. And not...

This is conventional (*sāṃketika*): by means of a form constructed according to the whim of people, things are described here in various ways so that they may be consistent [with local usage], just as the Southerners designate boiled rice by the word *caura*,
whereas the Saindhavas use that very same word for a thief, and designate boiled rice with the word *krūra*.

But the Kashmiris [prefer] husked barley, wheat, and rice-grains—because, since conventional designations (*saṃketa*) are unstable and lack ultimate reality (*apāramārthika*), they are useless for establishing the relationship between the purified and the purifier; thus, there would be nothing but indefinability. Furthermore, even a convention does not possess ultimate existence (*paramārthasattā*); indeed, that which is called a "convention" is not [ultimately real].
Another [author] says: "Indeed, no convention established by the will of the Blessed One is well-known apart from the will of the Supreme Lord" (p.

If it is argued that this is because the attainment of results such as pacification (*śāntika*) arises from the performance of rites like nourishment (*āpyāyana*) based on the letters of the name, the script, and so forth— then, if all things could be accomplished by a single convention (*saṃketa*), what would be the purpose of relying on other conventions? Or, if one does rely on them, [what is the point]?

Even that [scriptural authority], preceded by the establishment of an infinite variety of conventions— pertaining to one's own scriptures, other scriptures, worldly usage, attendants, teachers, and those composed by great masters, as well as those fixed for each individual and so forth— is certainly to be examined; there is no utility in merely [accepting] it, for the accomplishment of the task is achieved by this much alone— even by those whose bellies are like the hollows of blind wells, devoid of letters.

If it is argued that "what is being spoken and what is being heard is indeed beautiful; does the unimpeded will of the Blessed One not transcend the path of critical inquiry?"—then enough with this false exertion consisting of memorizing, reciting, explaining, and investigating the text; this [objection] must simply be abandoned.
One should remain taking refuge in silence despite the heavy burden;
it is the will of the Blessed One alone that shall deliver one from what is to be delivered. It is His will alone, consisting of grace, that brings such contemplation to its ultimate conclusion.
127) Indeed, by those who merely stretch out their feet while lying down comfortably, and who eat without reflecting for themselves...

Or else, one should remain with a mind turned away from the cultivation of an intellect capable of the most subtle discernment—an intellect produced by the supreme Lord’s grace, which becomes increasingly intense according to one's own degree of self-reliance. This must always be kept in mind: we do not abandon this much; therefore, having understood this point, please remain here for as long as it takes.

We set aside all these various objections in their entirety; for, in reality, they do not apply to the Supreme Lord as the ground of the supreme Word (parāvāk), whose essence is absolute freedom— consisting in the power to accomplish the impossible—
and which is not tainted even by the slightest atom of a particle of dependence, as has been explained almost previously.
This has already been reconciled; nevertheless, it is avoided in detail:

as for what was said—that this sequence beginning with "from that [Śiva-tattva] comes Earth" and so forth—there is no such sequence. We say that this which is without sequence is the supreme, sovereign freedom of the Supreme Lord, which is manifold and which internalizes infinite variety.

That very reality is the form of the three-fold object; for this is the case: that which is the non-supreme, the supreme-non-supreme, and the supreme Bhairavī, the sovereign power of the Lord, exists as a state transcending even the Sadāśiva-tattva and the Anāśrita-śakti-tattva.
p.
128) Since that which ends with it is also included within the category of the seat, this sequence is for the purpose of reviving the divine body,
as is the case elsewhere.
Thereafter, one should place the great preta, laughing and unconscious,
red in color, possessing great luster, and adorned with three eyes.

Namely: at the root of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) is the root, the bulb (*kanda*), and the root-essence (*āsāramūlaka*); at the end of the uvula (*lambikā*) is the staff (*daṇḍa*) extending to the end of the *kalā*-tattva; the knot (*granthi*) consists of *māyā*; the fourfold seat (*catuṣkikā*) is the lotus of *śuddhavidyā*; and right there resides the venerable Lord Sadāśiva, who is himself the Great Preta.

Because it is intensely dissolved, because it is primarily characterized by awakening, and because it consists of the dissolution of the body— which is of the nature of the object of knowledge— and the reflective awareness of the *ānanda* (bliss), [the consciousness] has arisen there and emerged through the aperture at the top of its head.

Having established as the seat within this differentiated reality— which consists of the triad of Parā, consisting of Nāda, Antavartinī, Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā, extending to the end of the twelve [tattvas], and above that, the three pure lotuses and the Unmanā state—
the deity who is the supported, according to one's own preference, by way of being the presiding pervader;
"Having visualized it, one should worship. Regarding this, there are intermediate verses:
"This twelve-finger span is the tip; the triple-pronged [trident] flashes from its base.
Reaching the tip of the wheel of the Goddess, having abandoned sequential order, one attains the state of moving through the sky (khecaratā)."
This Khecarī consists of filling the space from the Mūlādhāra up to the tip of the sky at the end of the twelve finger-breadths;
she is so called because of her movement and abiding in the void, and because she consumes her own nectar.
Thus ends the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). For instance:
"The Lord, the Great Preta, laughing, insentient"—by this, the seat ending with Sadāśiva is established within the wing of the End of Sound (*nādānta*).
Having stated that "all this, as summarized in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra, constitutes the seat," [he continued].
"One should contemplate the three prongs of the trident of power (*śakti-śūla*) arisen from its navel"—
by this, the three prongs consisting of Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā have been described; therein also:

This supreme seat (paramāsana) is described as having the form of the three white lotuses of the states of *unmanā*, *ūrdhvakuṇḍalikā*, and the supreme abode (*paramadhāma*), because it reaches the limit of the Supreme (*parā*). Furthermore, the Goddesses abide above that;
thus, this is the supreme abode of the very power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), known as Paśyantī.
The form known as *nāda* exists precisely as something to be transcended, as it is stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"Now, that power of knowledge of ours which is the nature of Sadāśiva—
that is the state of *paśyantī*, the supreme [state] for the grammarians."
Thus:
for the intellect, as the visionary (paśyantī) with Rudra as its deity, rests within the inner self;
it ultimately comes to rest in the power of knowledge of Sadāśiva alone, which is the very nature of the power of Anāśrita-Śiva.

Regarding the two deities Brahmā and Viṣṇu associated with the mind (*manas*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* states: "In that state where there remains only the status of being a subject, Rudra is the presiding deity;
when the expansion of distinct objects of cognition occurs, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are cited."
Thus it is said. On this point, those who desire discernment should consult the *Tantrāloka* itself.
In the stages of *vaikharī* and *madhyamā*, the positions of the Lords Īśvara and Sadāśiva correspond precisely to the stage of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

[In Sadāśiva, which is indeed the principle of Īśvara,] it is established by scripture and reinforced by self-awareness that this is the supreme ground of *Pratiṣṭhā*. Above *Paśyantī* lies the ground of *Parā*, the Blessed Lady,
wherein everything shines forth as non-dual alone, and where the sequence, though discernible by subtle intellect, is contemplated.
For although the manifestation as non-dual persists both in the stage of Vidyā and in the stage of Māyā,
the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) therein is otherwise: in the stage of Vidyā— [in the case of the Lord Īśvara]—
the entire collection of subjects and objects manifests as "this," whereas in the stage of Sadāśiva— [in the case of the Lord Sadāśiva]— it merges into the single "I" which is the Self.

That which is covered by it is then reflected upon as "I am this. Thus, within the common substratum of the conscious self—[the auspicious power of knowledge]—both are reflected and appear as non-different; this is what is called grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For this very reason, in the state of Īśvara...
In the state of Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, all entities attain the supreme condition, just as they do on the path of Māyā.
Having abandoned both Śuddhavidyā and Mahāmāyā, she herself is indeed the state of Īśvara.
She is not the other—that is, she is not the Aparā-śakti; rather, she is the Parāparā-śakti. As for the statement "that which," he states the reason for the possibility of her being *parā* (supreme):
because the state of being *parāpara* (both supreme and non-supreme) has been shown there in the principle (*tattva*) of Īśvara.

Therefore, supremacy (*paratva*) is established in the state of the Lord (*īśvara*). Regarding the *Īśvaratattva*, it has been stated by the venerable feet of Utpaladeva—[the phrase "it has been stated" is to be construed as "and as having both supreme and non-supreme forms"].
As it was said:

In this state, the "inferiority" (aparatva) of entities arises from their appearing as non-self (anātmatvena), while their "superiority" (paratā) arises from being veiled by the I-consciousness (ahantā); thus, that indeed is the intermediate state (parāparadaśā).

Thus: "Otherness" (*paratva*) is fullness (*pūrṇatva*), which is the "I" (*aham*) independent of anything else; "non-otherness" (*aparatva*) is incompleteness (*apūrṇatā*), which is the "this" (*idam*) dependent on another. In the very same way, it is stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) of the cognition of 'Being' (*sadvidyā*) and the cognition of 'this' (*idamdhiyoḥ*) is [the relation between] 'I' and 'this'."

When light rests solely within itself, not directed toward anything else, that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) characterized by resting in the luminosity of one's own self is called "I" (*so'ham*). However, that which is directed toward another is called "this" (*idam*), and it, in turn, comes to rest in a form that is merely its own self-luminosity, no longer directed toward anything else.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*): therein, in the first reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there is the *śiva*-principle; in the second, the state of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*); but in the middle form, that reflective awareness which proceeds according to the maxim of two scales held in perfect equilibrium as "I" and "this"—that belongs to the Lord Sadāśiva and the venerable Lord Īśvara. However, the distinction between them is caused by the "darkness" or "lack of darkness" of the aspect of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*). As for those...

The two cognitions "I" and "this"— which, in the subject of illusion (*māyā-pramātṛ*), have distinct substrata, namely the "I" as the grasper and the "this" as the grasped— the unification of these two in a single substrate in the form of a relationship, by means of their negation [as separate], is true, pure *vidyā*, as distinguished from impure *vidyā*.

The [consciousness] residing in the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) is indeed different. In that regard, when it causes the "this-portion" (*idam-aṃśa*) to manifest within that very locus which is the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-rūpa*)—the locus of the "I" (*aham*)—then, because of its lack of clarity, there is the state of Sadāśiva (*sadāśivatā*), expressed as "I am this" (*aham idam*).
However, in the case of "this is I" (*idam aham*), it occurs when the locus has become clear in the "this-portion."
"When I infuse the reflective awareness of the 'I' (ahaṃvimarśa), that is sovereignty"—this is the distinction.
This [claim] is consistent with the suspicion of a reversal of the scriptures that has been demonstrated.

Thus one should not think; for regarding the nature of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) in the case of the Mantramaheshas and others—[Utpaladeva Mahodaya says in the *Ishvarapratyabhijñākārikā*: "The word 'mantra'..."]—its form, although its ultimate reality is nothing but pure consciousness (*bodha*), is nevertheless distinct from that whose ultimate reality is a consciousness other than itself, such as "I" or "this," which is [merely] this very [object].

[The word "again" (*punar*) indicates that this predominance of the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*), which is distinct from the "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) occurring above, is why the name "Mahāmāyā" has been assigned by others; as it was stated in that very context: "it is indeed the cognition of difference. Thus, for the *vijñānākala*s, consciousness (*saṃvit*) exists even in a form whose ultimate reality is pure awareness, yet [it appears as] "I am not this" (*ahaṃ nedam*).
Due to the lack of awakening of consciousness, there is the notion "I" alone; therein, for those who are *pralayakevalins*, there is the unawakened state of "this is I.

Here—in this context of the *māyā* level, which includes both the *pralayākala* and the *sakala*—although such a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the very life-force of consciousness, exists through the appearance of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*) within the *māyā* level, it remains precisely of that same unawakened nature.
Nevertheless, for one who employs that linguistic convention—
whether [the object] has acquired its existence through the grace of that [convention], or whether it is non-different from it— for such a subsequent reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

"This is the body and so forth, this am I who am the knower, this is the pot and so forth, this is that which is the object of knowledge"— such worldly discourse, consisting of conceptualization (*vikalpātman*), occurs precisely through the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) characterized by differentiation. However, since no other cause for such a state is perceived there, even if a cause were to be postulated, once again...
Because it culminates in nothing other than inseparable from such a realization, that very self of non-conceptual consciousness possesses such power;

and precisely through the possession of such power, it consists of that infinite variety—thus its sovereignty would be established as unfailing. And within this state of being, sovereignty is inseparable, because:

In this way, such a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is indeed possible even within the *vaikharī* self, or within the abode of *madhyamā*, which consists of *māyīyavidyā*, despite the fact that [there] luminosity exceeds [reflective awareness]. But here, in supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvid*), just as there is luminosity, so too is there reflective awareness consisting of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Therefore—like water in water, like fire in flame...
In every respect, entities appear as consisting solely of non-differentiation from the flame; they do not appear even in the manner of a reflection.
However, to the extent that this Supreme Goddess herself is defined for the sake of instruction, she becomes so constituted by the postulation of lower levels of existence.

And thus, this nature of Bhairava, consisting of speech, is self-established, beginningless, primordial, existing everywhere at the beginning and everywhere at the end; what else, then, could be said of it?
It reveals its own self-luminous nature through identity with the expansion of the essence of reality,
and likewise contemplates it; and that contemplation, even while not departing from such wonder,
is the direct realization of future infinite creations and dissolutions numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of parārdhas.
In manifestation, it must be exactly as it appears; and if, during the process of creation,
one were to reflect upon an initial or intermediate state through that very manifestation,
then because the suspicion and possibility of the subsequent deviating from the former would not have been removed.

How could that which is incomplete— shattered by the mass of other natures that have not yet been realized as non-different from it— be the fully manifest Great Abode of Supreme Bhairava? It remains stained by the traces of differentiation, beginning with the lower level of Paśyantī and ending with the rest, which have not yet been transcended.
By virtue of not nourishing such an object,
that certain form— which is merely a name— would become the form of the Supreme Goddess Bhūtirāja.
And in the absence of such an ascent into the stream [of consciousness], this which is unfolding would not appear or manifest at all;
let there be no incompleteness, let the mass of established entities not be undermined by talk of non-duality,
let the state of being grounded in Bhairava not cease to exist, and let it not bear the stain of duality.

It is appropriate to say that supremacy consists in mere naming; this very point is established and becomes coherent if, appearing first and foremost as the end of all things, such a manifestation should fix its footing there through reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
for that is the final portion which, in that manner, maintains its own essential nature.

Even that preceding part, which appears and is being reflected upon as having internal divisions consisting of its own infinite prior and more prior portions— accepted as being inseparable from its own essential nature— is indeed complete,
because of its identity with the essence of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the full manifestation that has already occurred, following upon the back of the subsequent part.

Not abandoning its fullness of subsequent forms, and itself manifesting while encompassing the internal portions of its own preceding and even more preceding stages— drawn forth by force through its own inseparable nature— it appears and, when reflected upon, remains likewise undivided; thus it is.
In the differentiation of the appearances of those respective second, third, and subsequent parts— which follow from the appearances of each preceding part—
there occurs the acceptance, by the force of conforming to the non-deviation of the essential nature of the state of Bhairava, of one's own respective preceding parts.
Even each single marvel becomes supreme and full, as soon as it exists in a form that is most proximate to one’s own self-luminous innate sun; or rather,
that very body called Bhairava is the abode of rest in one’s own will, which is itself skilled in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that.

Become intent upon *prasaṃkhyāna* (discriminative discernment); in a forest region— whether devoid of the limitations of adjuncts such as the heart, the mountain, and the tree, or even possessing them— your gaze, remaining unbroken from afar,
attains this very state of non-fragmentation toward the entry into the consciousness of Bhairava.
One should attain the state of tradition;

one should cast the gaze upon a place such as one devoid of trees, mountains, or walls, and so forth. Otherwise, in the event of a partial descent, starting from the first part, or else [one may proceed] without parts at all.

What then is the distinction of this [consciousness] from other cognitions that are considered incomplete because they lack mutual awareness? The distinction of a cognition regarded as complete from other cognitions regarded as incomplete lies, as it were, in its capacity to encompass the wonder of infinite variety within itself.
May those who possess the supreme teachings understand this for themselves.

But when the lotus-heart of a bound soul (*paśu*) has blossomed by the rays of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) from the Supreme Lord, [he is not moved] even by hundreds of our words, nor even by needles of extremely sharp meaning.

Whether it be a division or an expansion, even in a jar, the gaze can be cast in this very same way as [upon the Self]. For there too, non-conceptual consciousness (*avikalpa-saṃvit*) falls instantly only upon the final part;
thereafter, however, conceptual cognitions arrive gradually from the penultimate part down to the innermost depths, becoming increasingly internal and more internal still.

And since they enter [into it], what need is there for anything else? Thus, here too, it is established that the Śiva-principle is eternally free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), yet the source of conceptual construction, possessing the essence of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), beginningless, and the primordial ground of all; there is no disagreement on this point. However, it becomes fully manifest in such a way only when it rests upon the very last level, the earthly plane (*pārthivī bhūmi*).
For if consciousness (*saṃvit*) were to manifest and reflect upon the earth even as an object (*viṣaya*) through non-difference,

it would have to be occupied with both the manifestation and the reflective awareness of the entire essence of that [earth's] own nature; and its true being (*svarūpasatattva*) consists in a state where the non-difference— preceded by that [manifestation]— is unestablished yet of a single flavor, fashioned by the freedom (*svātantrya*) of its own perfectly expanded [nature].

[It is] that which consists of the existence of the sovereignty of consciousness (citsvātantrya), which is contracted by the power of manifestation; it is characterized by the non-differentiation between the subject of Māyā and the external circle [of objects], and it comprises the primary matter (pradhāna) and its derivatives, such as the intellect (dhī).

The earth exists as subsisting upon the group of elements beginning with ether and ending with water, which have issued forth from the category of subtle elements (*tanmātra*)— the root cause of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) whose nature is the transformation of that [Prakṛti]— by virtue of being situated at the lower level.
For as long as it persists through its own projection, it remains possessed of its own essential reality for that duration.

Because they possess five qualities, they must draw forth the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); and as those [subtle elements] are being drawn forth, for the sake of establishing their own essential nature, they are preceded by their own prior [causes], which are linked to a continuous succession of other primordial foundational causes that were previously drawn forth.

It is logical that the very roots themselves would not lack the nature of the causes intended as the material cause (*upādāna*) when the effect exists; however, one might perhaps say that instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) and the like do not persist in some way. But this [objection] undermines the subject at hand and has been extracted from another treatise devoted to explaining those [causes].
This has already been extracted by us and is not elaborated upon here. Thus, first of all, the earth,
and then likewise water— which appears in its entirety as its own essential nature— is, when being contemplated,
made into the mantra of the wonder of contemplation (*vimarśa*) by means of that manifestation.

In this way, one should indeed fulfill that which possesses the existence of the refinement of the reality (*tattva*) of the earth; the meaning is that finally, that very Blessed Lady of Full Consciousness is none other than Śiva himself. By this very [means], p.

O Brahmin, according to the method of the reasoning of the *upadeśa*, it is established in the scriptures that even a mere portion possesses the form of all things, and that within each single principle (*tattva*) there exists the nature of being composed of the thirty-six principles. And thus is the teaching of the venerable *Spandaśāstra*:
When one remains pervading all objects as if out of a desire to see them, then what is the use of much speaking? One will understand by oneself.
Thus, this must be made to penetrate the heart; that very point is indicated here by the final quarter-verse. What more need be said?

That which cannot exist without something else is, for its part, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that thing—just as *śiṃśapā*-ness is the essential nature of a tree. [In this case, *śiṃśapā*-ness does not occur anywhere other than in a tree; wherever there is...]

"Śiṃśapā-ness exists here and there, and tree-ness [exists] there"—thus, śiṃśapā-ness is the essential nature (svarūpa) of tree-ness, because śiṃśapā-ness does not occur without a tree; therefore, it is its essential nature.
Now, one might ask: how can one thing be the essential nature of another, given the contradiction with the principle of necessity? To this, he says:

Regarding the statement that "the nature of the Supreme Lord is not such that it is non-existent," it is as follows: here, it is not the case that wherever there is "treeness" (vṛkṣatva), there must be "śiṃśapā-ness" (śiṃśapātva), because that [śiṃśapā-ness] is absent in trees such as the *vānīra* and others; thus, treeness is not the very nature (svarūpa) of śiṃśapā-ness.

That which, within the manifestation of necessity (*niyati*)—which is itself the concealment of the supreme Lord’s freedom (*svātantrya*)—does not become its own true nature for as long as [it persists], [is the object of knowledge].

Without that [preceding element], the subsequent one simply does not exist; just as the exclusion of "śiṃśapā-ness" does not occur without "tree-ness," so too the subsequent principles, such as earth, do not exist without their respective preceding ones, such as water. Thus, they are merely its own essential nature (svarūpa).
For earth cannot exist without water, because hardness is observed precisely through the act of supporting (dhṛti). In this manner, [the sequence continues].

How could the gross elements exist without the subtle elements? Those [subtle elements] also cannot exist without the unfolding of the senses; the senses likewise cannot exist without that kind of determinative cognition (adhyavasāya); and all of these, along with their subsequent manifestations, cannot exist without being rooted in a subtle causal form that is fundamentally undivided.

Even the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is an object of enjoyment; without an enjoyer, how could it—being merely a recipient of the distribution of that enjoyment—exist? And how could it exist without the network of bonds (*pāśajāla*), such as time (*kāla*) and portions (*kalā*), which are contracted by that very contraction and consist of consciousness (*saṃvit*); for how [could there be] a division of consciousness, which is by nature indivisible?
Apart from that sovereignty which is the cause of contraction— also known by the synonym *māyā*— and apart from sovereignty itself,
which, in its state of contraction, depends upon the essence of contraction and the various degrees of that contraction,
[there would be nothing] except for the forms that are slightly contracted, uncontracted, slightly expanded, or fully blossomed.
(141) This entire world,
as it manifests, could not exist at all— indeed,
nothing whatsoever could exist— without Bhairava, whose essence is independent and perfectly full manifestation.

This sequence of principles is established by one's own direct experience (*svasaṃvit*). Regarding the *Śruti* as well, the meaning is this: one should consider that the earth also has the nature of water. Why? To this it says: "without solidity. The intention is this:
if the earth did not have the nature of water, it would lose its very stability; for solidity is...

Hardness and mutual cohesion are produced by water alone. Where could even the primordial earth exist without being of the nature of water? Even if one were to say this, would it not cause [the opponent's position] to be cut down?
On the contrary, it would serve only to nourish the supreme consciousness whose essence is the venerable Lord Bhairava, who consists of all things in their fullness.

And all this— beginning with the venerable Parāparā and others, and including Paśyantī and the rest— arises from the convention of existence according to the distinctions of the principles (tattva) that are slightly manifest,
more manifest, and so forth; for while differentiation is indeed indistinct within "I-ness" (ahantā), it is [distinct] within "this-ness" (idantā).
However, the distinction between the categories of reality is even more clearly stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:

"In this context, the 'inferiority' (*aparatva*) of entities arises from their appearing as non-self; whereas their 'superiority' (*paratā*) arises from being veiled by the 'I-consciousness' (*ahantā*). This, indeed, is the intermediate state (*parāparadaśā*)."
Thus, she shines there in the great splendor of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā), with a body suited to that very light.
For in that state, wealth would never reside in the hand of one who is destitute, even if it were to come into being in the future. Indeed... [p. 142] ...how could it be?

How could the distinction between the supreme (*parā*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*), and so forth, be subsumed within the supreme state (*parā-daśā*)? For when differentiation arises, then the designations such as *paśyantī* and so on occur; but when there is no arising [of differentiation], how can those designations apply to it?
To this, he says: "even though it is yet to be," and so on. "First" means even in the absence of its future existence. [This refers to the] reality (*vastu*).
Even that which is final would indeed appear in the first manifestation;

however, with respect to its essential nature as a single flavor—the clear form of that differentiation—it possesses a state of "future-ness. For instance, [if it were not so], how could such things as "Kalki will arise" and "he will slay those devoted to unrighteousness" appear in the Purāṇas, if they had not been manifested?
If it is argued that "the sun was fixed in a certain creation and likewise performed its function," then is it that very same one, or another?
If it is another, then it is unmanifest [the intention being: "if it is another, you have arrived at our own position by your own statement"]. If it is that very same one...

How can there be a division of time? If it is argued that [the Self] is not limited by time, how so?
