If you say "because of its nature as consciousness (cittva) and because it possesses the form of the universe (viśvarūpatva)," then, in the case of the conscious Self which is not limited by time—being eternally inseparable from the power of the universe and possessing the manifestation of contraction and expansion through the force of its own sovereignty—it would follow that it possesses the contradictory forms of both withdrawal and emanation.
Everything exists within the Supreme Lord, whose body consists of that [reality], the venerable Bhairava, who never departs from our hearts and the tips of our tongues.
Thus, why is this very principle being presented by us not accepted with a lack of hesitation, or why is it not determined and discerned by you yourself with an even more open throat? Therefore,
this Śiva-tattva is without beginning or end, manifesting of its own accord.

Having inwardly embraced the entire collection of principles— which have as their sole ultimate reality the Self, whose essence is sovereignty consisting solely in absolute independence and fullness— and because that Supreme Consciousness is eternally arisen,
non-contradictory to all things, and the benefactor of all, it does not admit of designations by means of words denoting [limited] states.

It is established that as long as [the deity] remains seated in the form of Bhairava, unconditioned by time, he exists through the very process of the Great Emanation (*mahāsṛṣṭi*) and so forth appropriate to this scripture,
and not through the sequence of the Limited Emanation (*mitasṛṣṭi*) and so forth; this is precisely what our teachers have taught regarding the practice of *saṃpuṭa*.

The tradition (*saṃpradāya*)—because of the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*) of every single reality (*tattva*) as well as the entire multitude of realities by means of pure supreme existence (*śuddhaparasattā*)—will be explained further as "the manifestation of parts and sub-parts, consisting of the outlining of differentiation, beginning from the state of Paśyantī. [The word *iti* indicates the cause. From that point onward indeed...
The relationship between the object of purification and the purifier (śodhya-śodhakabhāva)—
as stated [on page 144]—
is a systematic arrangement that cannot be denied. Thus it has been said.

O lady of excellent vows, all that which begins with the earthly element and extends up to Sadāśiva— knowing that here the sequence of ascent occurs through the relationship of the purified and the purifier—
is to be understood as being of the nature of Prakṛti, joined with both destruction and origination.

Perceiving this and so forth, the true nature of the venerable Parāparā—the self-power of the supreme power (paraśakti) itself, which is like a mirror—is that very form of the venerable Parā in which she alone shines, like a reflection; and as for that [which is said]: "Now, even in the case of the venerable Parā, according to the principle of difference-and-non-difference..."

The conceptualization of a reflection certainly exists; however, since that too must be explained by the very term "reflection," one might ask: why is this mode of expression restricted solely to the *parāparā* [level]? To this he says: "And that which... for in that context, the intention is that the form (*rūpa*) in both the original object (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*) is one and the same, having unity as its ultimate reality (*ekatā-paramārtha*). Thus, the form is eternally the supreme reality of oneness in both the original object and the reflection.
That which is merely a touch upon the surface, like a reflection on a mirror, is not said to be "reflected" [as it has been stated by this very author elsewhere:
"For this is the definition of a reflection: that which cannot manifest as distinct, but manifests only through its intermingling with another, that is a reflection"].

Because its true essence consists solely of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), it nevertheless appears there in various ways—as this or that—just as a face appears with distinctions such as front and back, left and right.

"Through successive transformation, this very thing is that very thing, and that very thing is this very thing"— this refers to the Supreme Reality within the power that is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara-śakti).
They say that, without abandoning its own nature, it possesses a resemblance to another form,
having the character of a reflection, like the surface of a sword or a mirror.
Thus,
because it is impossible for it to be mixed with anything else, its differentiation cannot be manifested;
they call this a "reflection," just as a face [is reflected] in a mirror.

Thus, regarding the true nature of the reflection (*pratibimba*), the principle that "it has neither location nor form" and so forth should be understood here. That which is called "reflected" possesses qualities identical to its source and is not of a different genus; and thus, within the stainless mirror of *parāparā*, whose true nature is *paśyantī*— [The text continues: ...the principle that "it has neither location nor form" and so forth should be understood here. That which is called "reflected" possesses qualities identical to its source and is not of a different genus; and thus, within the stainless mirror of *parāparā*, whose true nature is *paśyantī*— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment containing a repetition of the phrase "na deśo no rūpamityādinayo'tra boddhavyaḥ" and a partial sentence regarding the mirror of *parāparā*. The translation reflects the available content.)
[That reality], filled with the complete totality of the principles (tattva) beginning with Earth and so forth, according to the aforementioned sequence;
[in which, through the distinction between cause and effect, the thirty-sixfold nature resides within each single element in due order];
and which is internally embraced by such an innate, uncreated, ultimate, and imperishable reflective awareness (parāmarśa).
Even while existing as such through its own nature, the body of the venerable Parā-Bhaṭṭārikā, by casting forth a reflection, perceives that which is to be perceived—

earth, water, and so forth— as being of a single supreme essence; for it does not allow for any alteration of its own nature, nor does it admit any other mode of awareness, yet it does so by way of weaving together the threads of differentiation as they thus manifest.
As long as one reflects upon that which is of the same class and stainless, so long does a reversal of the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, arise—
this should be understood as a reversal of their own essential nature— namely, that the principle of Power (śaktitattva) exists within supreme consciousness.
That very earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*) which exists within the supreme-non-supreme self is the power-principle (*śaktitattva*);
thus, starting from the letter *kṣa*, there is the abiding of the principles beginning with earth. But as for the venerable Lord Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka, he says:
"Now, just as the pervasion of two principles by the letter *kṣa* and so forth is established by logic according to the different tantras, so too it is in the *avarga*."

To explain why it is said to be "pervaded," he says "by the Lord" and so forth. He is eternally full, infinite, and absolutely independent; he never undergoes any transformation at any time. The reason for this is stated as "due to the absence of anything exceeding the nature of consciousness" and so on—this has been stated many times. Regarding the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) within the Supreme Self:

The principles (*tattva*) are nothing other than the single reality of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and this reflective awareness is the ultimate reality whose form consists of the powers from *ka* to *kṣa*. Therefore, there is absolute non-duality therein.

However, in the "Supreme-Non-Supreme" (*parāparā*) state, there is a nature consisting of both difference and non-difference according to the analogy of reflection; and that [state], consisting of supreme-non-supreme reflective awareness, is composed of the letters from *ka* to...

As long as she maintains a body garlanded with the phonemes beginning with *kṣā* and ending with *m*, bearing within them the reflections of reality established in the Supreme Goddess situated above her,
so long does she abide in those very [phonemes] which constitute the ultimate realization of the non-illusory, non-Vedic, and other [traditions], beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣā*.

The principles (tattvas) are established through the inversion of the upper and lower, by virtue of the majesty of the nature of the upper source and its lower reflection; this is the intended meaning. From that [arises] earth.

There is nothing contradictory in [the letter] *kṣa* and so forth being considered the form to be purified (*śodhya*), because even there the supreme state (*paradaśā*) does not depart; for this very series of letters beginning with *ka* arises therein from the predominance of its own portion (*svāṃśa*) and from the manifestation of the state of Madhyamā situated within that own portion.

And because of the inclination toward the form of *vaikharī* existing as its own nature—[the word "inclination" (*prāvaṇya*) means being attached (*lagnatva*)]—the state of being letters, mantras, and words is the function of the portion to be purified. Let this incidental matter rest; for this has already been determined by me in the commentaries (*pañcikā*) on the *Śrīpūrva* and other scriptures, even though it was stated there.

The status [of these systems] is established differently according to the venerable Śrī Mālinī-bhaṭṭārikā and otherwise; let those who belong to the Supreme Lord— the knots of whose ignorance have been severed by the teaching of the Trika— reflect upon this, having determined it as it is being described, after transcending the ultimate limit of Paśyantī, which consists of the power of Anāśrita.

That Paśyantī, which is the very nature of power belonging to the Unconditioned, is itself the supreme pinnacle and the state of the inception of all entities. Your honors ought not to forget what was stated regarding the three deities within the supreme consciousness of the Supreme Lord; and thus:
The state of the Middle Path (madhyamā), which abides within the supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*)— the locus of the unfolding of the venerable goddess Parāparā— is here contemplated.

To that extent, within one's own office—the sovereign state whose nature is the power of action—the denotable is superimposed upon the denotative, which consists of a cognition that conceals the clearly manifest object; and even there, the denotative is superimposed upon the denotable.
Since everything is the denotable and everything is the denotative, if everything is indeed the self, then it is thus.
Superimposition (*adhyāsa*) can be established through the mutual concealment and blending of successions, but not otherwise;
for even if a cloth is deficient by only three or four finger-breadths, it cannot conceal another cloth.
Furthermore, the state of being the self of the universe would result from the mutual intermingling of the essential natures of the seeds.
The vowels possess the nature of denotators (*vācaka*), while the consonants, which are of the form of the womb (*yoni*), possess the nature of the denoted (*vācya*).
This is because they sequentially consist of the essence of Śiva and Śakti; thus, it is said here that the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Śiva and the womb is Śakti.
Thus:
"In that way, due to the distinction consisting of seed (*bīja*) and womb (*yoni*), [the letters] are of two kinds;
the vowels are considered the seed, and those beginning with 'ka' are remembered as the womb."
Thus, according to the determination of the venerable *Pūrvaśāstra*, Śiva alone—without relinquishing his status as the subject (*pramātṛ*)—is the signifier (*vācaka*);
and Śakti alone, who penetrates the objective aspect (*prameyāṃśa*), is the signified (*vācyā*). For even though there is a distinction, [Śiva] is the signifier.
It manifests as nothing other than the uninterrupted nature of the subject, which consists of both the object to be conveyed and the conveyor;

this very state of solidification (*śyānata*), whose essence is Śiva and which takes the form of the vowels as seeds (*bīja*) and the consonants as the source of power (*śākta-yoni*), proceeds from the seed itself into the source—this we shall determine immediately hereafter. For this very reason:
If there were a state of mutual intermingling between the seed-syllable, which consists of vowels, and the womb, then alas, the production of all fruits would occur without effort;

thus, liberation and worldly enjoyment would both become drawn out and ripened [only after a long time]. Since the phoneme of the seed is likewise within itself and the phoneme of the womb is likewise so, what could distinguish one from the other? This is what is being stated.
Let it not disturb us that we maintain this single Speech, which is of the nature of consciousness and contains within it infinite variety; as it has been said:
"There is no cognition in the world that does not follow from words."
All knowledge is understood as if it were permeated by sound.
Likewise,
if the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness,
manifestation would not be manifest, for it is that [speech] which performs reflective awareness.

Thus, even within the sphere of conventional practice belonging to the realm of illusion (māyīya), that which consists of the clarity of worldly, sequential phonemes and words is of the very nature of a single, unitary reflective awareness (ekaparāmarśa).
Speech, which consists of the nature of light and performs reflective awareness, has been established here by others through effort;
moreover, for those who rest upon the continuous stream of instruction to this extent, it is accomplished without effort.
Thus, we have not labored here in vain.
An insistence has been established merely for the purpose of manifesting the purification of the body through visiting the teacher’s house as a grammarian;

in exactly the same way, the resolution of objections regarding the distinctions of sequence, non-sequence, priority, and posteriority is already established even in the case of the *navātmapiṇḍa* and other such *mālāmantra*s. Thus it is with the Bhagavatī.

*Mālinī* itself is the mantra of Power (*śakti*), namely *hrīṃ na pha hrīṃ*; *hrīṃ a-kṣa-hrīṃ* is the designator of the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*). *Na pha* is for the sake of the entire creation filled with the intensity of ten million-fold immersion (*koṭisamāveśa*).
Thus, in the *Bahurūpagarbha*:
"The syllable *na* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* are the garland of the head;
then the head itself; the eyes are *u* and *ū*; *ī* is the upper and lower [eyes]; *ghr̥* is the nose; and *ṇu* and *ṇū* are the two ears."
The *ba* and the *ka*-group are located in the mouth, the teeth, and the tongue, as well as in speech;
*va*, *bha*, and *ya* are in the throat and the right shoulder and so forth; and *ḍha* and *ḍha* are in the two arms.
Ṭha is in the two hands; jha and ña are the branches; jra and ṭa are the trident and skull-bowl.
The letter *pa* with *ha*, *ṛ*, *ta*, and *cha-la* represents the breasts; the letter *kṣī* with *ra-ma-sa* and the *visarga* represents the life-force (*jīva*).
The vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be intent upon that; the letters *ṣa* and *kṣa* reside in the belly and the navel.
The letters *ma*, *śa*, and *ta* are located in the hips, the private parts, and the pair of thighs, as well as the knees.
The letters *e* and *ai* are likewise the shanks, and the letters *da* and *pha* are the feet that follow them.
Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Above the two ears are the two *ṇa* sounds; there, the ear-lobes enter into union with the *u* and *ū* vowels.
This is the true essence of the power (*śakti*) that is the primary, ultimate, and middle locus. For this very reason, it has been said: [Page 151]
In the Śrīpūrvaśāstra,
for the sake of those who follow the mantras and tantras in order to achieve their desired results,
one should install the Mālinī [alphabet] with its distinct *yoni*s for the purpose of constituting the body of Śakti.
Thus, the fact that their origins are distinct has been determined; this also applies elsewhere:

"Neither in the individual soul (puṃs), nor in the Supreme Reality, nor in Śakti [is there such a thing as immersion]. As for that immersion which is manifest during the unfolding of the body's dissolution, [it occurs through Śakti]."
This world, which emerges while being veiled by the sense of "I," is joined with objective existence.
This manifest and unmanifest sign (liṅga) is the potency of mantra, both supreme and non-supreme;
it arises from the union of the individual soul (nara) and power (śakti), yet remains distinct from the form of Śiva.
As it has been stated elsewhere:
"A mantra applied to the principle of the individual soul (puṃstattva) becomes inert, while one applied to the supreme principle (paratattva) is fruitless;
however, when applied to the Śakti, it bestows the fruits of all actions."
Thus it is said. Herein is the distinction:
elsewhere, the birth of accomplishments (*siddhi*) arises from the manifest (*vyakta*), and liberation (*vimokṣa*) results from both the manifest and the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
From the unmanifest comes the primordial power (*bala*) of the Supreme; however, this discussion does not apply to the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
Thus one should install the mantra:
"Because of their insentience and lack of activity, they do not bestow worldly enjoyment or liberation."

Thus, this being the case, because everything has everything as its essence, whatever is expressed here—namely *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *tha*, *ca*, *dha*, *ī*, *ṇa*, *u*, *ū*, *ba*, *ka*, *kha*, *ga*—is [in reality] the Supreme Consciousness (*parasaṃvit*), with respect to which these are sequentially [manifested].

The auditory organ (*śrotra*) has as its nature the form of sound (*nāda*), which is of the nature of the womb (*yoni*). Because it brings about the nourishment of the immortal (*amṛta*) within the Self alone, and because of resting therein, it is said to be "of the nature of the immortal. As it is stated elsewhere:
"Having fallen upon the ground that nourishes the fourfold seed (*bīja*), and having attained fullness, it suddenly..."
Having attained the state of being composed of the essence of the *rasana* (tasting) faculty whose nature is grasping,

and having become a specific odor in the form of the earth, it resorts there to the status of the instrument of touch; and this much is the power-based (*śākta*) and generative (*yauna*) abode, presided over by the seed-syllable of Īśāna within the instrumental power in the self of speech.

Then, reflected back from that [consciousness] by way of being the seed for the upward ascent through the unfolding of the power of the instruments (*karaṇa-śakti*), it rests upon the womb of Śakti in the form of *buddhi*; having entered the wombs of earth, water, and fire,
it exists within those very seeds in the form of the *paśyantī* state, which has the nature of grasping and takes the form of the hand.

Having extended into the earth of the Cākṣuṣī, Śuddhavidyā— being similar to that— abides in the organ of smell, which is the final of all organs; having ascended by means of the seed-syllable of Īśāna and having taken hold of the power of hearing through the conjunction of the Unmeṣa and the upper seed-syllables, it reaches the source of the organ of bliss.

It becomes composed of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā; thus, what is described here is the Śiva-tattva, which is unlimited because it pervades all— beginning, middle, and end— and possesses infinite power.
p.

153) In the *Mālinī*, by following the other consciousness (*apara-saṃvit*) which is struck here, and by following the existence consisting of *paśyantī*, there is, in sequence, *vāyu* and *māyā* [corresponding to] *pa* and *gha*; *sādākhya* and *nabhaḥ* [corresponding to] *kha* and *lā*; and *īśvara* and *icchā* [corresponding to] *ca* and *ṅa*.

Śuddhavidyā consists of Śakti; Anuttara is indeed the independent sense of "I" (ahambhāva). A is called Śiva; Māyā is Bha; Śuddhavidyā is Ma; Rāga is Sparśa; Kāla is Ya; Pāyu and Ahaṃkṛt are Ḍa; Niyati is the letter Ḍha; the hands and Manas are the letter Tha; the organ of bliss and Buddhi are Ṭha; and Puruṣa is Ña.

The letter *ja* is the intellect (*dhī*), form (*rūpa*), and destiny (*niyati*); the letter *ra* is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛta*) and the form of destiny (*niyatirūpa*). The letter *ṭa* is the mind (*manaḥ*), the organ of the feet (*pādendriya*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*). The letter *pa* is the ear (*śrotra*), the mind (*manas*), and the hand (*hasta*). The letters *dha-la* are the skin (*tvak*), taste (*rasa*), time (*kāla*), and the power of Śiva (*śaivī*). The letter *ā* is the tongue (*rasanā*) and the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*). The letter *sa* is the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*), the splendor of knowledge (*vidyātejas*), and the power of emission (*visargaśakti*). The letter *aḥ* is speech (*vāk*) and the two hands (*karau*).
Ī, water, and *pāyu* (the anus); *ha*, *māyā*, and *vāyu*—these six constitute the organ of bliss (*ānandendriya*) and that which is called *sādākhya*;
*pṛthivī* and *kṣa*, the feet; *pumān* and *śabda*, he is the sound; *śa*, *kalā*, and *nabhas*, touch;
*baindhavī*, *śiva-śakti*, *aṃ*, form, the nose, and the skin; *ta*, taste, *śiva-śakti*, *sāttvī*, *e*, and smell.
p. 154) That very [vowel] *ai* is *nabhas* (ether); likewise, *o* is wind and fire; *au* is taste and water; *aḥ* is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛt*) and the anus;
and *pha* is earth. And herein, as previously stated, is the arrangement of the body—thus it is.
The state of being the self of all things in their entirety would be fully realized; for it is Parābhaṭṭārikā alone who, according to the stated method,
while casting her own reflection into Paśyantī, at that very same moment [at the very time of casting the reflection into Paśyantī],
[establishes herself] in the intermediate abode (madhyamadhāman) which is situated in identity with her own Self.

Attaining diverse origins, due to the infinity of the variety arising from the mutual intermingling of the seeds of those various wombs, she partakes in innumerable divisions according to the distinctions of the persons belonging to this or that family and so forth; thus, she is indeed Mālinī, as has been stated.
One should worship the goddess Mālinī, whose form is surrounded by infinite bodies of the Kula and by the Kula-śaktis themselves.
And by this very sequence, the yogi intent on practice becomes a possessor of various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) within the external worlds, the *tattvas*, and the bodily wheels (*cakras*).

In whichever body or vital breath (*prāṇa*) it occurs, just as certain medicinal herbs, having grown, perform only a specific effect, so too is it with certain [mantras]. [Now, one might object: "If this is so, then because everything would be dependent upon one's own will, everything should bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*); why then has a restriction been established? To this, he says "just as" and so forth. Just as certain medicinal herbs, having arisen, perform only a certain specific effect, so too is it with certain [mantras].

Even if a certain accomplishment (*siddhi*) were to be bestowed through the arising of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), or through the application of mantras, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth,
it would still not transcend the operation of necessity (*niyati*); for indeed, in every scripture, [the results] are described differently,
preceded by different arrangements of phonemes.

The *prastāra* (the systematic arrangement of phonemes) has been described as a collection of phonemes formed according to a fixed sequence, which follows the precedence of specific phonemes based on the primacy of the respective Lord-phonemes appropriate to each individual consciousness; and from that very [arrangement], the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*) has also been described— namely, that which consists of the form of the *mātṛkā*.
In order to demonstrate that which bestows the radiance of mantras augmented by such heroic giving (*vīrya-dāna*), [it is shown] because,
in the *Śrī-nityātantras*,

there is a predominance of the entry into the nature of the supreme sound (*paranāda*), which is the cause for the predominance of the deluding seed-syllable (*mohana-bīja*) consisting of the letter *e*.

The reading *hetuparanādātmā* is also accepted by the wise with the intention of referring to the ultimate meaning (*uttamārtha*), and not in consideration of the immediate context. Following that, the arrangement occurs precisely according to the sequence from Śrī-mantra to Pha;
this alone is the [order] for the Kula-men and the Kula-energies (*kulaśakti*) here.
The intention regarding the placement [of the letters] is as follows: the fruit is not merely the concealment of the phonemes, mantras, and so forth;
for it is stated thus in the *Śrīvājasaneyatantra* after the phonemes have been placed appropriately:
This divine wheel of the Mātṛkās, the abode of Viṣṇu’s feet,
when fully understood from the mouth of the Guru, severs the bonds of the bound soul (paśu).
Thus it is said; likewise, in the *Śrītrikahṛdaya* as well:
"Of wheels, tridents, lotuses, and so forth; of living beings, rivers, and men;
of weapons and powers (*śakti*s), and of whatever else."
That which is the abiding of the phonemes is their potency residing in the mantra;
by that being protected, they are protected, while the remaining phonemes are merely themselves.

Thus it is; for instance, even when there is a change in a single syllable or mora of mantras, those very same [mantras] undergo alteration in the scriptures through the divisions of Āṇava, Śākta, Śāmbhava, and so forth— just as, for example,
the seed-syllable *māyā*, the *praṇava*, and all the seed-syllables of immortality (*amṛtabīja*) [are altered] in the Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva [traditions].
Just as it is taught in the Vāmā and other scriptures, or in the *Kaulottara* and others regarding the Lord of Four Kalās (*catuṣkalabhaṭṭāraka*),
and in the venerable *Ucchuṣmaśāstra*, here too, for the purpose of revealing the many varieties of the Kula person (*kulapuruṣa*), the method employed by those who are proficient is set forth.
(157) The former [syllables] are for others, and the latter are for those who are not others, just as with the back;
and the former also, according to their sequence, are considered the rule for the *mātṛkā*.
In this very same manner, according to the nature of their different origins.
This supreme Uttaramālinī is the Goddess who is beyond numbering, such as the Śākta and other categories.
Thus, among the abodes (dhāma) situated above and below, which are enumerated according to their divisions:
one is the Bindu; furthermore, among the others, that which was previously mentioned moves toward the end.
Having placed that number which is on one's own back aside, one should cast it into one place;
from this [total], the number resulting from the other desired touched [numbers] is obtained, and the process is repeated again.
As it has been stated regarding the procedure for the realization of the infinite nature of the *kula-śaktis*:
by this very procedure, those *kulapuruṣas* who are practitioners of *śakti-yoga* become devoid of [limited] authority, as it is said:
"In the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as soon as it is born, [the power is] fully present."
Three and a half crores of mantras, appointed by Śiva,
having bestowed grace upon the multitude of souls, have gone to the state that is free from affliction.

Thus, they are the Great Lords of Mantra (mantramaheśvaras), but not the mantras themselves— for at the time of their own dissolution, there is an absence of reaching the state beyond affliction (anāmayapada), and no extraction of mantras occurs from them, precisely because that would be fruitless.
"In the Kali age, however, [the letters] from *na* to *pha* reside within the womb of the undivided.
Thus, in this way, the Blessed Lady Parābhaṭṭārikā, possessing various divisions of words, is primarily present through the Middle Path (*madhyamā*).

O Blessed One, by its very mode of being, Mālinī is indeed infinite; for even though her own essential nature manifests a manifold variety (vaiśvarūpya) as demonstrated through enumeration, she likewise exists within herself as the self of all, due to the predominance of three aspects, and thus possesses the nature of phonemes (varṇa), words (pada), and mantras. And this—

It should be understood that this occurs by way of being the instrument of purification (*śodhanakaraṇabhāvena*). For the fetters (*pāśa*), which manifest as the aspect of *paśyantī*, are indeed subtle and thus constitute the objects to be purified (*śodhya*); for they possess the nature of fetters only so long as they remain latent within.
However, in the state of *madhyamā*, which consists of the unfolding of ever-arising expansion through the flow of *śakti*, there exists only the status of being the instrument of purification.

Just as the external gross impurity [is removed] upon the removal of the internal latent impurities, so too is the state of *vaikharī* contemplated within the consciousness of that Supreme Goddess; for it is not impossible for *vaikharī* to exist therein. To illustrate: although children, even with two or three years...

Although their places of articulation (*sthāna*) and organs of articulation (*karaṇa*) have become manifest, nevertheless, their arising—occurring either month by month, day by day, or moment by moment—attains an increasingly superior form; this much is established.
In that regard, if, in the state of the middle way (*madhyamā*), such an expansion of the manifest articulated speech (*vaikharī*) were to become clear...

If there were no manifestation of the portions of phonemes— which are the undivided [unity of] places of articulation (*sthāna*), instruments of production (*karaṇa*), and phonemes (*varṇa*)— then there would be no difference in the linguistic proficiency of a child born on that very day, one born a month ago, or one born a year ago; it would be merely the intermediate [unmanifested] state.

If it is asked, "How is it distinguished by proficiency? let that first be examined: one becomes proficient while merely hearing those words and seeing their meanings; and one would reflect upon the phonemes even as they are being heard.
Yet these [phonemes] consist of *vaikharī* speech, and in them, this [consciousness] is indeed embodied, like one blind from birth.
Therefore, the *vaikharī* speech—which consists of internal positions (*sthāna*), articulators (*karaṇa*), and so forth—is indeed present even in the mute;

likewise, the fact that consciousness is the self of all has been stated by the Blessed Lady herself. And thus, the very state of *vaikharī*, having attained its expansion within the substratum of *madhyamā*, [manifests] in its own part.

When the manifestation of the mutual variety [of things] occurs within the Self, and the clear emergence of the relationship between signifier and signified has arisen, as long as one remains having internalized the web of objective reality (tattvajāla), so long is she the Aparā-Bhaṭṭārikā;
when there is the emergence of the state of Madhyamā within her, she is Parāparā; and upon the emergence of Paśyantī, she is the Blessed Lady in her essential nature.

And the Goddess—thus, by virtue of being the purifier, she abides as the threefold state itself; for the purifier is the self of the universe (*viśvātman*), whose form is pervasive (*vitatarūpa*), and it has been stated that pervasiveness (*vaitatya*) occurs in this very manner. (p. 160) [The act of] purification...

However, instrumentality belongs only to the agent— the Lord who, having assumed contraction through His own sovereignty, rests within the majesty of His power; whereas the state of being purified belongs to that which is of the sole nature of contraction,
[purified] by the non-distinct Supreme Bhairava-Bhaṭṭāraka, who is the single form of the Triad transcending the thirty-seven [principles].

The essential meaning here is as follows: from the differentiation inherent in the first manifestation (*prathamāsūtrita-bheda*) within the abode of *paśyantī*— which is the form of the power of the bound soul (*paśuśakti*) expanded by the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) of Sadāśiva, whose nature is unshakeable (*akṣobha*) and who occupies a rank equal to the supreme and non-supreme deities (*bhaṭṭārikātulyakakṣya-parāparadevatā*).
The loss of freedom for consciousness, and the lack of awareness even regarding that freedom—
this is the twofold atomic impurity (āṇavamala), arising from the forfeiture of one's own true nature.

The very manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is that which is called *māyā*, which bestows birth and experience; whereas *kārma* (karmic bondage) resides in the agent's lack of awakening. Thus, this triad [of bonds] exists solely through the power of *māyā*.

Thus, it has been stated that while this collection of bonds (*pāśasamūha*) is gross, the web of bonds exists even above in a subtle form; this was indicated by the first aphorism. This is the determination regarding the web of bonds of the individual self (*narātman*). As it was said by the venerable Śrī Somānandapāda in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
May Śiva, who has entered our very form, protect himself by means of his own self through the supreme power; salutations to that pervasive Self!
Thus, in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* (p. 161), it is stated that within the entire complex of ritual actions, there is an indication of this very nature;
and therein also, there is a progressive dissolution even of the objects to be purified and the purifying agents.
Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon.
Thus, this stream is of such a nature that even the purifier and the act of purification are themselves merely the object to be purified;
for it is stated in the venerable *Ṣaḍardhaśāstra*: "There is indeed a simultaneous existence of the excellence of all three;
for while speaking of one thing, one conceptualizes another, and while talking of one thing, one perceives another quite beyond conceptualization."
But here, through the cultivation of the oral instructions of the tradition of experience— namely, that "the Blessed One is indeed Bhairava himself in his full extent"—
this reality, which consists of one's own consciousness, cannot be denied; therefore, it is not simultaneous, but rather occurs in such a manner.
If it is argued that "it is unperceivable due to its subtlety" and that there is only a misconception of simultaneity—

like the piercing of a hundred petals of a *śirīṣa* flower with a needle— then what indeed is this terminology? If you say "simultaneously" means "at the same time," then according to the aforementioned reasoning, what time can there be for that consciousness which is inward-turned and whose nature is pure awareness?

Because it possesses the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consisting of the appearance and its absence of the coming and going of the vital breath that takes the form of the object of knowledge, [the Self], although situated within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object of knowledge, [remains unaffected].

If it is argued that "it is knowledge that would overflow"—then whether the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) exists as consisting of light within itself or otherwise, what specific distinction of it has been stated by way of knowledge? Furthermore, the entire argument concerning the collapse of mutual dependence due to the difference between the existent (*sat*) and so forth, even as it is being asserted, would necessarily result in being expressed solely through the medium of knowledge; and thus, that very same fault remains.

Even when a multitude of hundreds of flowers and sprouts is said to be "many," because of their connection with parts ending in atoms (*paramāṇu*), it would follow that there is no action anywhere; nor could there be a synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) in the absence of cognition, whether that synthesis be a variety of memory or memory itself.

If it were dependent upon experience, there would be an absence of experience [itself]. I have already examined this at length in my *Padārthapraveśanirṇaya-ṭīkā*; so what is the use here of this web of futile talk, which results only in obstructing the instruction at hand? Thus, the Goddess [is present] in the form of the purifier (*śodhaka*).

And it is there that the Bhagavatī, who is both supreme and non-supreme, abides— the state of the powers (śaktis) such as Aghorā and the rest— through the conjunction with whom the Vijñānākala practitioners and yogins become Aghora and the others in the form of Mantramaheśvaras and so forth,
solely by the grace of the powers such as Brāhmī and the rest.
The *sādhaka-aṇavas* are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others; for the Supreme Lord Bhairava-bhaṭṭāraka,
whose body is completely full and overflowing with the mass of all powers (*śakti*), [manifests] Brāhmī and the other [goddesses] by means of the deployment of his own powers.
What else is there but that he acts out of his own sovereignty? In this way, even the purifier possesses the state of being the object of purification; this is another excellence.

According to this established principle, because the object of purification, the act of purification, and the purifier everywhere possess a threefold nature, the triad is invariable, as I have stated myself in my hymn.
Thus, there is no infinite regress, because all of this consists solely of the supreme consciousness of the Lord;

this is precisely how one should consider it. Furthermore, even purification—and ultimately even the purifier—is itself the object of purification, because when the aspect of duality surges forth, they are of the nature of fetters. And so too is the act of purification.
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the fire itself— which is non-different from the Bhairava-consciousness capable of burning away all impurities—
is indeed the very fullness (*paripūrṇatā*) in its penetration into everything, as he will state on page 164.
"Thus, he who knows in truth," and so forth. Because those deities, such as Parā, Aparā, and others, consist of the single essence of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*) and are the self of all,
there are eight Yoginīs of great power born from the limbs of the Supreme-Non-Supreme (*parāparā*).

By such statements, the infinite range of signifieds and signifiers found in worldly conventions and other treatises is also included. Thus, by encompassing the infinite conventions—past, present, and future—this relationship between the purifier and the purified is established; there is neither an infinite regress, nor an over-extension, nor an excessive pervasion.
It is established that the conventional is not ultimately real; this being so, we now follow the subject at hand:

the connection is that the vowels beginning with ‘A’ themselves, through their association with time, are those which are proclaimed as the Moon and the Sun within that [reality]. By the word "that" (tat), the *akula* which consists of Bhairava, mentioned in the preceding verse, is referred to.
Therefore, it is indeed *akula*, having internalized all conceptualization (*kalanā*). Herein lies the power of *Kula*—[here meaning *akula*].
"That which remains as the singular form of pure consciousness is itself the state of the Fourth (*turyatā*).
And just as in the statement "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," the state of the *Vijñānākala* is indeed the state of the Fourth, if...

The meaning is this: in that case, if there were no power consisting of temporal succession (*kalana*), what distinction would there be between the Fourth State (*turya*) and that which transcends it?
Likewise, in the *Spandaśāstra*, it is said:
"Then, in that Great Void where the moon and sun have dissolved..."
Like one in the state of deep sleep, the deluded person becomes awakened and unenveloped.
Thus, by means of that power residing within the womb, the supreme light contains power within itself;
this is the intended meaning. For the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), which consists of conceptualization (*kalanā*), enters into that [light].

Even that which is called "beyond the fourth" (*turyātīta*), though agitated by the dust [of phenomenal manifestation], is not something distinct— because it is entered into the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-pada*) and because its continuity with the fourth state (*turya-anantaratā*) is likewise identical— and this reflective power (*vimarśa-śakti*) is the supreme Goddess (*parā parameśvarī*).
As it was said by Rājanaka Aṅga in his hymn:
"O Three-eyed One, you alone are seen as the manifest Lord capable of governing or knowing the three worlds."
The power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti), having manifested identity,
nevertheless reveals the defect of duality even within that very difference.
Thus, the state of the venerable Lord Bhairava— which consists of unsurpassed sovereignty—

abides as fullness, as thinness, as both, and as neither; for it exists by having drawn everything within the embrace of its own self, being "full" because there is nothing external to its own nature that has become a burden.

Since no being whatsoever exists [as a separate entity], emaciation and fullness are established as distinct; and because there is emaciation, there is likewise the nature of both and the absence of both. In that regard—(p.

In this regard, there is no stain of succession or simultaneity arising; for succession and simultaneity depend upon creation and so forth, and creation and so forth are nothing other than the self-reflection of one's own nature—this is the intended meaning.
"To such an extent" means to the extent of [dimensions] such as fullness or thinness. And its sovereignty is precisely this:
The reason why there is "identity with this" (*aitadātmyam*) even amidst the appearance of distinctions such as creation and so forth is that [the Self] is "perfectly full" (*paripūrṇa*);
the sense is that even distinction is non-different from the Light. According to the method of the aforementioned teaching, this much [is established]:

the supreme Goddess-consciousness (*parābhaṭṭārikā-saṃvid*) is the singular essence of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of its own nature, which consists of the arising and dissolution of infinite future [manifestations].
Because it is non-dual,
this Lord Bhairava is independent, perfect, and all-pervasive;
there is nothing that He would not manifest within the stainless mirror of His own Self.

According to this principle, as long as there is the manifestation of succession and non-succession within the very nature of the Self—which cannot tolerate either succession or simultaneity—[one should not think: "In succession, sovereignty is indeed fragmented; how then could simultaneity not exist? For simultaneity exists precisely through its dependence on succession; thus, there is no fault. for that long...

In accordance with that, this sequence should be investigated; as for the non-sequential (*akrama*), however, since it exists only as preceded by that [sequence] within consciousness itself, it is presented for the sake of demonstration. [Regarding the question, "How then are sequence and non-sequence [distinguished]?", it is said here: "the utterance of the non-sequential."]
—[Regarding the passage beginning with] "pratipādana" etc.: Let it be so;
since [speech] is in every respect sequential, this entire reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which consists of the nature of speech (*vāgrūpa*), is likewise sequential.

Thus, being of the nature of internal consciousness, it is indeed without succession; therefore, this Supreme Goddess Parābhaṭṭārikā, who belongs to the Supreme Lord, is always of such a kind and is thus manifold in this very way. Consequently, designations such as "at" (beyond) and so forth are made according to that sequence.
In this manner, [the power] consisting of will resides within the self of the Supreme Lord.

The power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), in which the expansion of objective phenomena has not yet unfolded, and whose essence consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the nature of such dense internal consciousness, is called "A. That state, by its very condition, is designated as "Will" (*icchā*); because there is no predominance of objects of desire, it is therefore essentially nothing other than the reflective awareness of the supreme reality (*anuttara-sattā*).
As it is said in the *Mahārthamañjarī*:
"That which is 'existent' (*sann*) is the illumination of the heart; it becomes the agent of the act of becoming (*bhavana*).
That very [agent] is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the act..."

Thus: although this Supreme Lord, who is constantly aware of His own nature, may follow after the powers of *kula* even while contemplating a form consisting of the state of the power of *akula*, nevertheless, there must indeed be a distinction for Him due to that awareness of *kula*. This is the reality of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), namely Bhairava.
(168) "Just such" means that very [reality], which consists of mutual orientation, is of the nature of vibration (*spanda*), and is the surging forth of one's own self.
But when, through the expansion of the fragrance arising from the nature of his consciousness,
there occurs the production of various effects in the form of manifold artistic arrangements for the purpose of creating diverse works;
"The mind being turned upward is the first *tuṭi* of the Will.
Thus, it consists of vibration (*spanda*) and has the nature of mere external orientation;
it may either consist of the mere Will that has not yet delineated the object to be created, or it may take form through the delineation of each respective object to be governed.

There is a twofold division of this [power]: she who assumes the nature of effort characterized by agitation, or she who possesses sovereignty through the form of fire. As it has been said regarding the Middle [Power]: "She is either merely the nature of will alone, being distant from that which is to be created, or else, having attained the state of effort, she is proximate."
In this regard, its nature as Īśāna is as follows: the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), expanding further, has issued forth as *ā*;

it is the fullness of will (*icchā*). That very will, desiring to grasp through the sovereignty that consists of the future power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), takes the form of Īśana as *ī*. But when the power of knowledge unfolds, it consists of the unfolding of all objects of desire as *u*.

Thus: the very act of unfolding (*unmiṣattā*)—even for those things that are unfolding—is, by virtue of contraction, a state of being diminished through the internalization of all existence within the unsurpassed consciousness (*anuttara-saṃvit*). This occurs despite the fact that [the unfolding] consists of a single form that transcends the unfolding of the entire nature of the inner vital breath (*prāṇa*), while the multitude of objects appears as portions of differentiation that are almost indistinct, being directed toward the sphere of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The letter *ū* is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) belonging to the supreme deity who has the form of the essence of the bodiless one (*anaṅgadhairavīrūpa*); she whose thighs are raised (*ūdhorūpā*), who carries the entire mass of phenomena (*ūḍhasakalabhāvarāśi*), and who is perfectly manifest and pervasive.

Thus, these are the two powers of Bhairava, the Supreme Lord. The first is called *icchā* (will), which is a formative impulse (*kalana*) consisting of repose in one's own bliss; it is "full" because its nature is the fulfillment of one's own essence, and it is "of the nature of Soma" because it exists together with Umā, being non-different from the lunar power.

Regarding that which will be stated as "one should sacrifice the emanation there" in the context of what is designated as the Great Emanation (mahāsṛṣṭi): the second [state], however, is the solar form (*sūryarūpā*)—which is one's own essential nature (*svarūpabhūtā*)—intensified by the entry into the emission of the mass of the existence of its own nature; yet, precisely because of that emission, it becomes attenuated, its function being the manifestation and expansion of the circle of existents (*bhāvamaṇḍala*).
The power of the Great Withdrawal (*mahāsaṃhāra-śakti*), whose nature is the desire to withdraw the family-consciousness (*kulasaṃvit*), is called Knowledge (*jñāna*); and therein,

by virtue of reflecting upon its own previously expanded form, it exists within itself in a sequential manner as a pair consisting of the natures of Moon and Sun, as well as that which is called "Being" (*bhāva*), whose essence is self-consciousness.
Even the misconception regarding the processes of emanation and withdrawal, which consist of the moon and the sun, arises from observing form;
yet there is no infinite regress here, for this applies to knowledge and will as well.

It must be stated that even for those two— expansion (*prasara*) and non-expansion (*aprasara*)— there would follow the undesirable consequence of having to postulate further internal expansions and non-expansions of will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), and so on ad infinitum; therefore, cease this wandering in the delusions of external error and enter within.

For as long as cognition arises even regarding a jar or similar object, reaching the subtle stage of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), for that very duration the self-luminous knowledge, variegated by the portions of the knowable jar and so forth, manifests itself; and therein,
even the subtle initial flash of the manifestation of the jar and other objects— which constitutes that state of being variegated— must be experienced.

Since the emergence of a single entity is not manifested from anything else whatsoever, it is consciousness alone that possesses sovereignty— the power (*īśana*) consisting of the desire for existence to arise— and this is obtained solely through the means of knowledge that is one's own self-awareness.
Furthermore, the dense, full state of sovereign being, which consists of the accumulation of those entities, is itself also an object of awareness.

Being a mass of bliss within one's own self, one likewise becomes autonomous; thus, even bliss is not to be denied. Furthermore, the Lord Bhairava—the Absolute (Anuttara), the possessor of power, whose essence is the supreme wonder that cannot be designated by words—shines everywhere as the agent, even in that state.

They [the goddesses] exist for those who desire the unfolding of the unexcelled bliss of Īśana, and not for those who are unblinking (i.e., devoid of such desire) regarding the self-reflection of their own essential nature;
for those who rest upon the plane of knowledge by means of investigating its disjunction, they are indeed the Blessed Goddesses. (p. 171)
The powers of consciousness fall together as nothing other than consciousness itself—

because they are non-different due to their perfect fullness, and because any limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*) acts as a differentiator only insofar as it consists of the body and what is cognized therein; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Śrītantrasāra*:

It has been stated that the reality of the shadow of one's own head is such that, just as when one desires to step over the shadow of one's own head with one's feet, the head would not be located in the region of the feet; likewise is this *vaidavī* digit (*kalā*). (The meaning is: the shadow of one's own head...)

Just as [the sun], because it moves ever higher, does not tolerate the treading upon its own feet, so too this power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), because it moves ever higher, does not tolerate dependence upon an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the like. For one who thinks that the nature of the power of knowledge is dependent upon an object of knowledge and so forth— [that view is incorrect] because this [power] is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).
"How can such a mockery exist?"—this is indeed a great delusion on the part of those devoid of self-experience, even at an inappropriate time. As it has been said:
"The power of delusion is so great that it cannot indeed be discerned."
Thus, the meaning is as follows: for those of coarse vision, the manifestation of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is clear when there is the existence of objects of knowledge and so forth;

however, even in the absence of objects of knowledge and the like, for those of subtle vision, the manifestation of the powers of knowledge and so forth certainly exists by virtue of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).

Thus, in this manner, the group of six has proceeded up to the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Now, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), as it unfolds, is investigated: [it consists of] will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) alone.

Action (*kriyā*) consists essentially in the exertion involved in assuming a sequential nature—a marvel consisting of the intermingling and diversity of mutual essential forms. For action indeed consists of parts that are sequential in time. And it has been said by Bhartṛhari:
Whatever is designated as something to be accomplished, whether it be already established or yet unestablished,
is called "action" (kriyā) because it possesses a sequential nature.
Thus: "Likewise,
a collection of parts that arise in succession, though subordinate,
is differentiated by the intellect and designated as 'action' (kriyā)."
And in this regard, the state of being prior and posterior occurs precisely through mutual intermingling. In that process,
whatever undergoes an intermingling mixed with another due to its connection with something else,
it becomes so by way of first invading a nature that is largely void and devoid of reflective awareness.
Just as a frog or similar creature does not leave behind its body among floating objects, so too here the nature consisting of non-transcendent bliss does not depart—
because it is of an indefinable form within all cognitions. Thus,
O small-minded one, this supreme Brahman is for you necessarily but a mere fragment of bliss.
Thus,
when the question was asked, "O Lord, how is the supreme knowledge [attained]?"—
"The supreme light contains power within its womb by virtue of the power residing within it"—this was the reply given. Furthermore, in the *Gītā*:
"I am beyond the perishable, and I am superior even to the imperishable."
Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Thus, it culminates in being the substratum of all—
because its nature is that of the ultimate wall, yet because it is capable of sustaining succession, [it comprises] the stages ending with *saṃrambha*, *icchā*, and *īśanā*.

Capable of flowing forth within its own self, the state of supreme bliss (*anuttarānanda*), that very [power] then, plunging into its own void nature, first enters into a radiant form consisting of light, as in *ṛ* and *ṝ*. For how can the following of *i* and *ī*, as well as the audible presence of the radiant letter *repha* (*r*), be denied?
As the Blessed One Puṣpadanta said:
"Or it is established through the commonality of the word 'empty'.
Indeed, in the state of immobility within the void—[he clarifies this very point by means of the vision of the yogi, beginning with the words "In the void," etc.]—it is in that form.

In the desire to enter [the state], the ascent of the ladder of the perception of radiant form is already established; then, through the entry into the immovable form, there follows the realization of the essence of the earthly form as being of the nature of immovability,
in accordance with the scriptural tradition of the phonemes *ḷ* and *ḹ*, and thus, at the ultimate limit, there is the very nature of sovereignty (*īśana*).
By transcending the essential nature of the self in its state of wholeness, having leaped for a very long distance, it attains a motionless and empty existence.

The *pluta* (protracted) state belongs to the vowel *ḷ*, according to the maxim that "long vowels do not exist for *ḷ*. However, for the vowels beginning with *a*, the *pluta* state is simply the further prolongation of the long vowel; and as per the aforementioned principle—meaning the principle starting with "Bliss is the form of Brahman"—the quality of being long (*dīrghatva*) itself need not be sought separately. Let this suffice.

To that extent, this tetrad is said to be of a neuter nature, like a burnt seed, because it has entered into the state of emptiness; however, this is not because of a total absence of the nature of a seed.
For if these [four] were not of the nature of seeds, then—[they would be] beyond both Śiva and Śakti, who consist of the seed and the womb. (If indeed they lacked the quality of being seeds, then...)

There might be a designation for some third [category]. The meaning is that while the state of being a seed (*bījatva*) consists in both "being agitated" (*kṣubhyati*) and "agitating" (*kṣobhayati*), agitation (*kṣobha*) certainly exists among these [three], yet since there is no "agitating" (*kṣobhaṇā*), there is an absolute absence of the state of being a seed.
Because of the non-existence of even one [of these two aspects], [the author asks] how that absence occurs in the *Śrīpūrva* and other scriptures, and therefore says:

Regarding the phrase "starting with 'pūrva'": because of non-denotation [in that sense], even in worldly pleasures and the like, such a resting point (viśrānti) consisting of bliss (ānanda) exists; thus, it is said that this itself is the fourfold seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*). In this way, will (*icchā*) and lordship (*īśana*) reside within the body of bliss and in the supreme abode (*paradhāman*), which is the unsurpassed (*anuttara*) and primordial state that never deviates from its own nature (*svarūpa*).

Having entered [the vowels] as *a*, *ā*, *i*, and *ī*, but not in reverse order—as it was stated that *a* merges into *i* to become *e*—there is entry into the subsequent syllables and entry into the unsurpassed word.

There may indeed be a distinction: for while there is clarity upon entering the plane of bliss (*ānanda*), there is subtlety when merging into the unsurpassed abode (*anuttara-dhāman*); with respect to that, the Lord, the powerful one among the serpents (*bhujaṅga-vibhu*), has thus instructed.
"The followers of the Sātyamugri-Āraṇāyanīya branch of the Chandogas study [the Veda] with half an *ekāra* and half an *okāra*.
Thus, even in the world, such extensive usage is clearly evident in vernacular dialects and the like."

Even within the Pārameśvara scriptures, that shortness observed in the phonemes *e* and *o* in relation to *ai* and *au* during the application of limbs (*aṅga*), faces (*vaktra*), and so forth, must be understood in exactly this way: this phoneme *e* exists with the intention of *ava*, and *o* likewise; thus the seed-syllable (*bīja*) stands as *e-o*, which is similarly variegated (*śavalībhūta*).
The body of consciousness (*saṃvid-vapuḥ*) likewise remains in that very same form: *a ā e* and *ai*. The same should be stated for the unfolding (*unmeṣa*):

*a ā u ū* and *o*, and *a ā o* and *au*. Although the unfolding, which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), may penetrate into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as it expands, nevertheless, its entry is precisely into both forms consisting of will (*icchā*) and sovereignty (*īśana*).

According to the very principle stated [in the passage], "In the case of desire (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), there is no form of self-transformation (*svaparivṛtti*)," their state remains as such; thus, through the entry into the nature of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*), both desire and knowledge [attain their true state].

Having subsequently abandoned the state of expansion once it has reached its full development, and having relinquished the existence of the vibration of such limiting conditions (*upādhi*), one becomes merged into the unsurpassed state (*anuttara-pada*) with a body that remains as a mere point (*bindu-mātra-avaśeṣa*), consisting of the awareness of the true nature of the Puruṣa-tattva— which is non-dual existence and the ascent of being. Thus, in the letter *au*, it is indeed so.

Thus, the vibration of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is brought to completion; for since will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are included within this very [power], its nature as a trident (*triśūla*) is described in the *Ṣaḍardhaśāstra*. Therefore, among the primary categories, the Point (*bindu*) [is established]; here is the meaning [of this]:
In this context, that which is mere luminosity while the three abodes remain is described in the scripture as the *bindu*; it is considered the *śivabindu*.

According to this principle, when the universe— which, though not distinct from His own nature— emanates for the sake of attaining oneness within itself, then that state characterized by the predominance of the form of the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*) and defined as the immersion into fullness is called the *Śāmbhava* reality (*tattva*).

Furthermore, when the entire universe—which, despite being no different from mere sensation—releases itself for the sake of merging into one's own self as nothing more than a residue of sensation, and [the yogin] emanates it from his own self;

That very Supreme Lord first emits [the universe] primarily as the nature of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), but now he does so primarily through the emission of power (*śāktavisarga*). Indeed, when the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) has reached its fullness up to the letter *au*— that is, ending with *aḥ*— so much of the state of the unsurpassed (*anuttara*) Lord Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka has entered therein.
The triad known as the powers of will, knowledge, and action— which constitute the true nature of the self—
is indeed said by the supreme [teacher] to be the pervasive sovereignty of the Supreme Lord.
Indeed, as soon as the universe, which was non-existent, is brought forth by the power of will (icchā-śakti),
we declare that the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is the cause of its manifestation.
The power of action is the cause for the manifestation of external forms;
indeed, that which possesses the distinctions of beginning, middle, and end is but a single sovereignty.
Therefore, no separate name for these is ever found;
rather, for the sake of clear understanding, they are [designated] as "the desire to emerge" (*ullilasiṣā*), "the state of emerging" (*ullasattā*), and so forth, just as in the root text itself.
These consist of the initial, middle, and final stages of the vibration of the powers whose nature is knowledge and action. The "desire to emerge" (*ullilasiṣā*)—[and the subsequent states]—are...
Their nature is one of radiant manifestation,
clearly characterized for yogis who have ascended to those respective stages as grasped through most subtle discernment—
[discernment being samādhi]— in the Śrī Svacchanda and other procedural scriptures.

These have been described as having the nature of "awakened," "expansion," "obscuration," and so forth [where "awakened" refers to will (*icchā*), "expansion" to knowledge (*jñāna*), and "obscuration" to action (*kriyā*)]. For this very reason, it is stated in the seventh chapter of the *Śivadṛṣṭi-śāstra* (p.
Through the contemplation of the Supreme Self, whose form is filled with the weight of most intense and supreme bliss,
and in whom the triad of powers is dissolved.
And so forth;
even his power has attained the state of universal form, like a lump of clay becoming a jar.
Having thus determined up to this point that there is indeed only one single reality (tattva) and no existence beyond that number—
it is precisely this Śiva-tattva.

The state of Bhairava has been determined as being filled with the wonder of the power of the expansion and vibration of infinite and manifold sovereignty; in that regard, this very sequence mentioned here also applies to the first chapter of the tradition: "As long as that state of transmigratory existence—which consists of the delusion of the non-recognition of identity with Śiva—does not manifest."

Even at that stage, the nature of Śiva as previously described certainly exists; likewise, even though the pentad of powers (*śaktipañcaka*) is of a single form at that time, it nonetheless exists according to the requirements of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) due to its functional efficacy.
For instance, in the state that is both supreme and non-supreme (*parāpara*), that very light which consists of the innate self-reflective awareness "I" (the *aham-pratyavamarśa*) is precisely this.

Because it is independent of anything else, it is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), consisting of liberated consciousness (*nirvṛtacinmaya*), and remains exactly as such. This has been stated [as] "the delight of consciousness" (*cidāhlāda*).

Experience and manifestation occur only within the fullness of pure consciousness-bliss, not in the external; for that very reason, that in which [all things] dissolve is likewise [that same fullness].
By this, "liberated consciousness" is described. As for will, knowledge, and action:

They become manifest in relation to differentiated objects and so forth; however, in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*), only "I am full" shines forth—because it is that much alone which constitutes manifestation. That very [state] is knowledge because it consists of intense impulse (*saṃrambha*); it is action because of its inherent nature; and it is also will, because one accepts it as being of that very nature.

He says, "It remains as it is," meaning that its will (*icchā*) is "only so much" (*tāvatī*); this should be applied such that its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is likewise "only so much" action (*kriyā*).

Even in the absence of distinct objects and the like, because acceptance (*abhyupagama*), manifestation (*prakāśa*), and impetus (*saṃrambha*) never waver from being composed of light (*prakāśamayatva*), it is said to be "extremely subtle" (*susūkṣma*), meaning it possesses the very fitness for the conventional usage of "will" and so forth.
Extreme subtlety is to be sought because, through non-differentiation from the primordial [reality], no conceptualization of differentiation occurs; for this very reason,

it is said that there is an equilibrium of powers (*śakti-sāmarasya*) due to its nature as the manifestation of pure, full consciousness alone, and that its ultimate state is the bliss of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa-āhlāda*).

The manifestation of the object and the subject—consisting of the jar and Devadatta, differentiated by the variety of what is called the non-recognition of the identity with Consciousness—is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the meaning is that it is an action whose constituent parts occur in a temporal sequence.
[This is followed by] the absorption into that experience which consists solely of the bliss of Consciousness.
To that extent is His will, to that extent is His knowledge, and to that extent indeed is His action.
It exists through the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the three extremely subtle powers;
it is the supreme reality, eternally undivided, consisting of the bliss of the nature of consciousness.
Thus, even at the time of perceiving a jar or other objects, one knows "I know the jar. Here,
in this very act of knowing, there is no impairment of the experience for one who is free from desire.

Due to the absence of such orientation (*aunmukhya*), there is no cessation of that [desire] without bliss; for the establishment of objects depends upon consciousness. One does not engage with what is hateful at all, nor can one know anything without consciousness.
Thus, as it is said on page 180:
"Whatever one desires to know or to do, that action proceeds from desire."
For its former and latter portions must be conceived as they were in the past.

The attainment of the manifestation of that action is its unfolding; and by way of this unfolding, [Śiva’s nature] has been established as being oriented toward manifestation (*aunmukhya*) through an illustrative example for the sake of clarification here in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*. As it is said:
For when one observes the initial state of water that is moving yet free from waves,
its subsequent state of being highly agitated is understood through that very observation of the beginning.
As the hand moves toward the state of a fist, its initial trembling is observed;
this is the delight of consciousness, established in itself, regarding the act of creation.
The expansion of that conviction is what they call its orientation toward the object;
some great masters maintain that this very state is a slight swelling [of consciousness].
His will has become an effect through which he becomes possessed of will;
that gross expansion of his orientation is established as will (*icchā*).
"Thus, Śiva sometimes assumes grossness," and so forth. This has been made heart-felt precisely because it is endowed with reason and constitutes the very life-force of the essence of all the Āgamas.
"He is this one"—as it has been stated—that he, joined with the emission of power (*śakti-visarga*), emanates the universe.
That supreme Kaulikī power, which is said to exist within this [consciousness] as the desire to emit,
certainly attains the nature of emission (visarga) through the force of agitation (kṣobha).
Thus,
the seventeenth digit (kalā) is therefore of the nature of the form of nectar;
it has spread forth through the movement of the bindu, which is the essential nature of both the transcendent (parā) and the immanent (apara).
She is the illumination of all things, yet she is devoid of emission (*visarga*);
she is both Śaktikuṇḍalikā and Prāṇakuṇḍalikā,
and at the limit of emission, she is known as Parā Kuṇḍalinī.

Thus, the Supreme Lord emits the universe, and that [universe], beginning with the earth and ending with the power (śakti), consists of the forms of the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*; such is its extent.

The power of emission (visarga-śakti) is sung of as the sixteenth digit (kalā); they call that the immortal digit within the Puruṣa who possesses sixteen digits. [This is because it causes the nourishment of even those sixteen digits, and because it is called "immortal" due to its being eternally risen and its immeasurability. This is the digit.

Thus, this is neither the Sāṃkhya view nor the Vedāntic view, but rather the Śaiva view alone—[as it is said: "The innate state is the emission of one's own self into one's own self within one's own self"]. And the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*) itself, which belongs to the Supreme Lord, is the seed of the ground of supreme bliss. As it has been said:
In the Siddhayogīśvarīmata,
Kuṇḍalinī is the seed-syllable, the life-force consisting of consciousness; from her arises the triad known as Dhruva, Icchā, and Unmeṣa, and from those, in turn, the phonemes.
Thus, in this way, the form of the letter *a* and so forth,
having assumed the nature of the *yoni* through the attainment of density, remains without falling away from its own essential nature; that very thing is its own true nature.
Thus, when it migrates into the form of the *yoni*, it is called the "state of emission" (*visargapada*). As it has been said:
"O Great Goddess, that place where this emission finds its rest is called the mouth of the Guru; it is called the Wheel of Power (*śakticakra*)."
And so forth; the *ka*-group is the density (*ghanatā*) of the vowel *a* itself, because it is produced in the throat. As it has been said:
"There are eight places of articulation for the phonemes: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head;
the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate."

Thus: for example, the vowels *a*, *u*, and *ṛ* (in their unvoiced release) are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*); *i*, *e*, *y*, and *ś* are palatals (*tālavya*); *ṛ*, *ṭ*, *u*, and *r* are retroflexes (*mūrdhanya*); *ḷ*, *t*, *u*, *l*, and *s* are dentals (*dantya*); *u*, *ū*, and the *upadhmānīya* are labials (*oṣṭhya*);
*ñ*, *ma*, *ṇ*, *na*, and *ṅ* are nasals (*nāsikya*); *e* and *ai* are gutturo-palatals; *o* and *au* are gutturo-labials.
The *jihvāmūlīya* is indeed [the sound] produced at the root of the tongue. The *anusvāra* is nasal (*nāsikya*). The *c*-group belongs to the vowel *i* because it is palatal;
the *p*-group belongs to the vowel *u* because it is labial; the *ṭ*-group belongs to the vowel *ṛ* because it is retroflex;
the *t*-group belongs to the vowel *ḷ* because it is dental. *Ya* and *śa* are within the *c*-group; *ra* and *ṣa* are within the *ṭ*-group; *la* and *sa* are within the *t*-group.

The letter *va* also belongs to the *tavarga*; it is the density (*ghanatā*) of the *ta* and *pa* groups. Even though the insentient (*abodha*) is formless (*amūrta*), its state of being insentient is due to its lack of autonomy (*svātantrya-rāhitya*), as has been stated.

Māyoparimā and Mahāmāyā; therein resides the state of those who are "consciousness-alone" (vijñānakevalins). According to their etymology, "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to a form that consists of pure awareness (bodha), yet is "alone" (kevala) in being devoid of autonomy (svātantrya), as described in the Pratyabhijñā.
Even though they consist of pure consciousness, those who do not possess supreme agency have been created by the Lord as distinct from Himself due to the absence of that agency.

Thus, even for pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), that very power of action arises precisely through the sequence of the sixfold group of powers according to the method already described. Therefore, the five [elements], when multiplied by six, become thirty;
together with the six [powers], they become thirty-six. In this way, it is the seed of Śiva itself, by virtue of its sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
When it has become solidified within a certain body in the form of Śakti, it exists as a flower and is designated as the *yoni*.

Indeed, that very flower—by the principle previously stated—consists of the three corners of the grasped (*grāhya*), the grasping (*grahaṇa*), and the grasper (*grāhaka*); in reality, it becomes the locus of procreation precisely through its union with the seed, for at that very moment it possesses the nature of a flower.

But at other times—[the word "anyadā" refers to the first instance]—such a designation occurs solely by virtue of its suitability [the word "tathā" means "as a womb"]. And thus, that very flower, by virtue of its triangularity, takes the form of a womb.

That which consists of the manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal of the moon, sun, and fire—the forms of the distinct objects of perception and so forth—and which comprises the triad of corners consisting of *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*, as well as merit, demerit, and the variegated [unmanifested], is the Mudrā of the Supreme Lordess, the venerable Bhairavī.
Because she is the support for the womb (*yoni*) that has that very form, she is designated as the "Womb" (*yoni*); and thus it is said:
In the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, within the investigation of the *khaṇḍacakra*, this very point has been taught as the primary subject: "Above Māyā is Mahāmāyā, whose nature is the bliss of the triangle."

For this very reason, it is taught in the *Śrītrikatantrasāra* that the union of Śiva and Śakti— which is the single, dense state of the seed and the flower— is to be worshipped by oneself through one's own self:
"By means of the complete absorption of Śiva and Śakti, [the worshipper] consists of the dense essence of Śiva and Śakti."
One should worship the supreme triad, which is the attainment of Śiva and Śakti.

Thus, although this condensation (*ghanībhāva*) becomes manifest in the form of *vaikharī*, it nevertheless resides primarily within the body of *parā-vāk*, which is the self of all things. In that regard, the specific distinction is that even the vocal organs (*sthāna-karaṇa*), such as the throat and lips, are themselves the self of all things. For indeed, even internally—

"One would speak" and "one would see"—this is indeed a clear experience; for there is no such thing as an impossibility regarding what is actually perceived. Furthermore, the distinction [between them] is produced solely by their location and so forth.

Because the phonemes have the Veda as their sole life-breath, what need is there for much more? Even a child, while being instructed, internally reflects upon the multitude of objects in that same form—that is, in the form of internal discourse (*saṃjalpa*). This "error" (*viparyaya*)—where error is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), defined as the apprehension of contradictory, manifold forms within a single substratum—is thus present.

Doubt: Even through doubt, one reflects; for as long as there is a discernment, it is indeed experienced, and that is produced solely by the reflection of speech. For this very reason, there are the distinctions of *saṃvāra* (closure), *vivāra* (opening), *alpapraṇa* (slight breath), and *mahāpraṇa* (great breath). That very breath, which is the wind (*vāyu*), ascending upwards, being struck at the head, turns back and strikes the internal cavity (*koṣṭha*).
When the chest is slightly struck, because the opening of the throat is constricted, the phonetic quality of *saṃvāra* (constriction) arises;

because it is open, *vivāra* (opening) arises. When the throat-opening is constricted, there is *nāda* (voicing), and when it is open, there is indistinct *nāda*. These two—breath (*śvāsa*) and *nāda*—which reside above, are called the *anupradāna* (external articulation).

*Anupradāna* is that which is given (*pradīyate*) after (*anu*) the completion of the articulation (*varṇa*). Others, however, say that *anupradāna* is the resonance (*anusvāna*), like the ringing of a bell;
just as the ringing of a bell follows upon the sound, so too does it follow upon the sound produced by the impact against the vocal organs (*sthāna*).
When *nāda* (the internal resonance) is imparted, then, through the conjunction with the sound of *nāda*, a voiced (*ghoṣa*) sound is produced;

when *śvāsa* (the breath) is imparted, then, through the conjunction with the sound of *śvāsa*, an unvoiced (*aghoṣa*) sound is produced. When the air is great, it is a "great breath" (*mahāprāṇa*); when the air is slight, it is a "slight breath" (*alpaprāṇa*). [This is stated] in the *Siddhāntakaumudī* regarding the phonemes (*varṇa*).
The externality [of certain phonetic properties] has been established as follows: "There are eight external efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*)," according to the *Mahābhāṣya*. They are as follows:
