opening (*vivāra*), closure (*saṃvāra*), breath (*śvāsa*), resonance (*nāda*), voiced (*ghoṣa*), unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), weak aspiration (*alpaprāṇa*), and strong aspiration (*mahāprāṇa*).
Regarding their classification: *kha*, *pha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *tha*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *ka*, *pa*, *śa*, *pa*, and *sa* are openings and involve breath.

And [the following] are voiceless (aghoṣa): ha, ya, va, ra, la, ña, ma, ṅa, ṇa, na, jha, bha, gha, da, dha, ja, ba, ga, ḍa, and ḍha. Those that are characterized by complete closure (saṃvāra), resonance (nāda), and voice (ghoṣa) are as follows: the first, third, and fifth letters of each varga, along with ya, ra, la, and va, are "weak-breathed" (alpaprāṇa); whereas the second and fourth letters of each varga, along with śa, ṣa, sa, and ha, are "strong-breathed" (mahāprāṇa)—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, the conjunction of nasalization (*ṇatā*), aspiration (*śvāsa*), and emission (*anupradāna*) would likewise possess an internal nature appropriate to its own kind;
otherwise, there could be no differentiation among the points of articulation (*saṃsthāna*). Moreover, the powers of the internal organs (*antarhitakaraṇaśaktayaḥ*) must certainly exist as well.

Because it would be impossible for the variety of mental constructs—such as "I hear," "I have heard," "I see," "I have seen," "I intend," or "I intended"—to exist otherwise, one should, by this reasoning, enter ever more deeply into consciousness and investigate it, having scrutinized it through the logic that follows from direct experience. [Logic is reasoning that conforms to experience. Thus, for those who investigate by penetrating further and further within:
In that abode of the throat, lips, and so forth— which is a single, dense mass of consciousness wherein everything is the self of all—

there resides the Lord of Phonemes (*varṇabhaṭṭāraka*), whose nature consists of the great mantra, the essence of which is sovereignty (*svātantrya*) characterized by a single, dense awareness of such consciousness. As it is said in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
This consciousness, whose nature is reflective awareness, is the supreme speech (parāvāk) flowing by its own inherent force;
it is the true I-consciousness in which the entire multitude of phonemes has been withdrawn from beginning to end.

Thus [it is said]. Likewise, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, it is stated: "That reflective awareness of 'I', which, though consisting of light, has speech as its body, is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). * * * * * * * * * * * ||

Thus it has been said. Herein, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the ground of the singular density of consciousness, consisting of the absence of places of articulation (*sthāna*), producing organs (*karaṇa*), and phonemes (*varṇa*), because its nature is solely that of consciousness, like the state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpāvasthā*). For that which consists of places of articulation, producing organs, and phonemes is not a singular density of consciousness, as is the case with the plane of conceptualization (*vikalpabhū*); yet this [ground] is indeed a singular density of consciousness; therefore, [the pervasion holds].
It is not composed of places of articulation (*sthāna*), means of production (*karaṇa*), or phonemes (*varṇa*); thus, five members are accepted in logic:
*vyāpti* is the rule of concomitance; *pratijñā* is the statement of the subject (*pakṣa*) as possessing the property to be proven (*sādhya*);
*hetu* is the state of being a reason that makes known the mark (*liṅga*); and *udāharaṇa* is the citation of an example for the sake of clear comprehension.

The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the probans (*sādhana*) with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*), while the application (*upanaya*) is the restatement of the probandum (*sādhya*) with respect to the subject;
[this occurs] when there is non-differentiation consisting of the singular mass of pure consciousness.
If it is asked, "How is there a distinction such as 'this is the locus,' 'this is the instrument,' and 'this is the color'?"—

it is because that very sovereignty manifests within its own self of such a nature as "this is a jar," "this is pleasure," "this is knowledge," and "I am the knower. (In this regard, this must be discerned by one with subtle intelligence.)
The state of being. Regarding this, the question and answer are as follows:
"Now, since Anuttara and Ānanda are by their very nature devoid of differentiation, how is it that they have taken to themselves within their own essence such a vast variety?"

Listen, first of all: this Lord of Consciousness is of immeasurable nature, the master of the creative power that brings about the emergence and dissolution of the manifold variety of infinite energies.
If Maheśvara were to abide with a body of a single, unchanging form,
he would have forfeited his status as Maheśvara and his nature as pure consciousness, just like a jar or other such objects.
It is said that the defining characteristic of the insentient is its limited luminosity;
for consciousness, being distinct from the insentient, is not so delimited.
Thus:

"The state of consciousness as the knower— 'I am the Knower'— is established by the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures, independent of the collection of means such as the object of knowledge and so forth."
Thus, what effort, or how much effort, could there be for such a manifestation of his most variegated forms? For this very reason, all... [p. 188]
The stone, trees, animals, humans, gods, Rudras, Kevalins, Mantras, their Lords, Maheśas, and so forth—
all these exist as the single ground of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) alone, in the form of the Supreme Lord who is the self of all through His being the Self of everything.

Thus, [the word] refers to that which consists of various states and locations, and whose forms— whether distinguished or not, manifest or unmanifest— are characterized by the state of being the universal self.

That vital breath, having risen from the navel and being sustained by the chest, throat, and head,
attains the state of resonance and sound through soft, medium, and intense [efforts], beginning with the *mandra* pitch.
For in the scriptures, it is taught that the *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *jagatī* meters are respectively recited during the three libations by means of low, middle, and high pitches.

Thus, even though there is identity with the stable tone (*sthāyisvara*), just as the tone remains one and the same in its stable form despite the distinctions of high, middle, and low pitch, for this very reason it must be stated that it is indeed that same phoneme (*varṇa*), because everything has everything as its essence.

In some living beings, even when a sound manifests in another location, it occurs as follows: in the case of crows, when the letters *ka*, *kaṭa*, and *ra* are uttered, they are all perceived as being produced by the belly, anus, throat, and palate;
even though they are indistinct, [is it not true that those letters, such as *ka* and the rest, because of their indistinctness...]

Because they are similar to the phonemes beginning with *ka* that are articulated from locations such as the throat, he says: "even though they are unmanifest (*avyaktatve’pi*). Those [sounds] are indeed just as many, because they are sound (*śabdatvāt*), and because there is no sound that exceeds the *mātṛkā*. Furthermore, the claim that even a sound exceeding the *mātṛkā* is not included because it is unmanifest and useless is also incorrect; for if it were useful, then everything [would be included].

By stating that "the mother-phonemes (mātṛkā) are useful in every respect when [the word] is well-established," he implies that although letters such as *ka* and so forth exist in words like *dhvāṅkṣa*, they are not mentioned because they are heterogeneous (*vijātīya*) and thus useless; therefore, one must necessarily admit a word that transcends the mother-phonemes. To the question, "How then can it be said that 'they alone [constitute it]'? he says:

[This too is incorrect. Even for that which has the form of unmanifest phonemes—[the maxim of the staff and the rice-cake (daṇḍāpūpanyāya) should be understood here]—there certainly exists the capacity to produce pleasure and pain in sounds such as thunderclaps and ocean waves;
what other intended utility could there be for the unmanifest sound even in the case of the Supreme Lord? It is precisely through its primary nature as unmanifest sound.
The nature of mantra has been established for the most part— since it is precisely the half-moon and so forth that are designated as the essence of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of mantra— and therein,

It is established that sound is essentially composed of phonemes (*varṇātmaka*); just as a jar, even when situated at a great distance, remains a jar, so too it is established that this sound, consisting of phonemes, remains the very same even as it follows to another location through various distinctions such as breath-force (*prāṇabala*) and so forth. For this very reason, there exists now the knowledge of the cries of all beings, which was taught by the Sage Śeṣa.

And that which is attained through the mastery of meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and absorption (*samādhi*)— [the definition of *saṃyama* being the unification of these three in one object]— and which reaches its limit in the discernment of their distinctions, how could it culminate in the knowledge of the warbling of birds and the like, which exceeds the nature of indistinct phonemes, unless when...?
Thus, in the ultimate sense, the capacity to denote (vācakatva) is characterized by the identity of meaning with the phonemes themselves;

I take refuge in Vaikharī speech, which is articulated clearly through the mouth by means of the vocal organs.

Thus, this has been described in detail within the *Mātṛkā-jñānabheda*:

Thus, "immortal" (*amṛta*) means consisting of the state of expansion. Here, however, there is no insistence on that specific methodology, because its sole essence is fullness; and so it is.

The Mahāsiddha first resorts to that foundation where all disputants proclaim the state of non-conceptuality; and beyond that,

it is the power known as Kuṇḍalinī, ever intent on the activity of generating the universe.
Knowing this, men do not again experience childhood within the womb of a mother.

The *mātrā* (vowel), which is the most subtle and unsurpassed form, flows forth through union with the *kaulikī* power as that which is called the letter *ha*;
or rather, we consider that the *kuṇḍalinī* power, presiding over it, is intent upon the activity of generating the universe.
This consists of the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the nature of the *bindu*, whose essence is non-different from one's own true nature, within the state of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).

Through this transition, it comes to rest in its own essential nature as the single-syllabled consciousness (*ekākṣara-saṃvit*—that which is both "one" and "imperishable," hence *ekākṣara-saṃvit*, a *karmadhāraya* compound; the masculine form is used according to grammatical rule). The particle *kila* indicates a lack of dispute. According to the principle that "when an individual instance is negated, the universal persists," even the calculation of space and time is of the same nature; thus, it is "one."

The meaning is "all-pervasive. Indeed, by its very nature, and independently of spatial and temporal limitations, as well as material causes and so forth, according to the previously mentioned principle of the fullness of reality—as it has been said that "fullness of reality" is precisely this: the state of being conjoined with space, time, and the rest.
As it has been said:
"Those wise ones who consider that supreme state— which is devoid of limitations such as space and time— do not know its true nature."
Thus it is said; and likewise by Hari:
"Salutation to the Peaceful Radiance, whose form is infinite pure consciousness unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and for whom self-experience alone is the sole means of knowledge."
Thus: "In the ground of emission" means in the Śāmbhava emission. [p. 197] It rushes instantly to the ground of emission;
it is indeed the very union with the ground of emission.

The persistence of forms and so forth—which consist of bliss, will, lordship, unfolding, their emission, and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) in their manifoldness—is that very emission (*visarga*). The visarga, when thus elevated and having reached a state of solidification,
is designated as the *haṃsa*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the consonant (*vyañjana*), and the contact (*sparśa*).

Thus, the actual attainment of the state consisting of *ha* and *la* is, in reality, the abiding of the entire web of principles (*tattva*) beginning with *ka* and ending with *na*; and furthermore, *ha* and *la* themselves re-enter the *bindu* and culminate in the state of the Absolute (*anuttara*). Thus, it is one alone, whose form is non-dual and perfectly full.
This supreme Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, is the venerable mistress of the very existence of consciousness; herein, there is no application of sequence or the like.
As it is said in the *Tantrāloka*:
"But action such as cooking is subject to sequence because it is delimited by time."
"Even that which is considered barren at its final moment does not attain the state of being cooked.
Thus, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, it is stated:
"And the sequential nature of worldly action arises from the power of time (*kālaśakti*)."
But it does not apply to that which is eternal; for it would follow that [the eternal] is subject to another master, just as a master is subject to a superior.
Thus it is said: [p.

I spontaneously bow down to that Goddess, the abiding state of one's own Self, whose nature is the manifestation of "I" as a full and pervasive activity— the wondrous realization of the ultimate truth which is devoid of interruption.

They are so called because they "cause to resonate" (*svarayanti*)—derived from the verbal root *svṛ*, meaning "to sound" or "to cause pain"—and thus they "make sound."
They indicate their own mind— the word *sva* (own) signifying the self and what belongs to the self—

and they bestow (*rānti*) their very nature (*svarūpa*) upon the other subject by thus transmitting it; and they give (*dadati*) their own, which is their personal form consisting of the letters *ka*, *ca*, and so forth, manifesting it externally (*rānti-bahis*), [this being a form of the root *rā* meaning "to give"].

They give [their names], for these very vowels are sounds that indicate mental states (*cittavṛtti*), consisting of resonance (*nādātmaka*) such as compassion, eroticism, tranquility, and so forth, in [instances of] lamentation, flattery, praise, and the like.

Whether they are isolated or situated within the phonemes of a *yoni*, falling forth at the very outset even in the case of animals or those born on that particular day, they manifest— without depending on convention, obstacles, or the like— as having the nature of accents, intonations, and so forth, because they reside in close proximity to consciousness; thus, the acute (*udātta*) and other such qualities are properties of meaning (*artha-dharma*).

[Regarding the terms *udātta*, *anudātta*, and *svarita*: therein, when the effort (*prayatna*) follows throughout all the limbs and becomes intense, then there occurs a constriction of the body, a narrowing of the vocal aperture (*kaṇṭhavivara*), and a harshness of the tone due to the rapid movement of the breath; that they call *udātta*. But when the effort is mild...]
Then there occurs the relaxation of the body, the enlargement of the throat cavity, and a smoothness of the voice due to the slow movement of the breath; this they call *anudātta* (low tone).
Because of the proximity of the *udātta*, *anudātta*, and *svarita*, that which is characterized as "tone" (*svara*) is thus defined as an external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*).

"Sraṃsana" means laxity, lubricity, and softness. Precisely because the cavity of the throat is large, the air exiting quickly does not carry away the water-particles; therefore, the voice becomes lubricated.
Conversely, precisely because the cavity of the throat is narrow, the air exiting slowly [carries away] the water-particles.

It causes drying, thus it is "roughness" (*rūkṣatā*), which is a lack of oiliness (*asnigdhatā*). In the *Mahābhāṣya*, it is said: "Exertion, harshness, and minuteness belong to itself"; [these] are the instruments of sound. Exertion belongs to the limbs, harshness is the roughness of the voice, and [minuteness] belongs to itself.
The constriction of the throat-cavity; furthermore, the low-pitched qualities of sound consist of relaxation, softness, and expansion of one's own [body],
where "relaxation" refers to the loosening of the limbs, "softness" to the tone, and "expansion" to the throat-cavity.
This particular quality of tone is to be acquired through practice, like the notes *ṣaḍja* and so forth; thus says Śrī Kathyaṭa.
Pāṇini, however, states: "The high-pitched is the *udātta*, the low-pitched is the *anudātta*, and their combination is the *svarita*.
These [tones] have been taught because they consist of the nature of the *ṣaḍja* and other notes that manifest the fluctuations of the mind.

Thus, in every act of perception, all these powers— beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, skilled in the performance of various diverse activities— descend with a competitive urge (*ahamahamikayā*), as it has been said:
But *ahamahamikā* is that mutual sense of "I" which arises between one another.

Thus, in the *Kośa*: appearing only without succession, it is precisely through their nature as mental constructs (*kalanāmaya*) that they bring forth the spatial dimension indicated by the transition of the sequence of cognitions; otherwise, according to the maxim that "there would be no distinction between Mount Meru and a minute atom."
The nature of succession consists of the diversity of actions which internalizes the diversity of spatial entities; as they say:

"Time is the delimitation of entities through succession and non-succession. Nor should it be thought that only those entities adhering to consciousness appear, so how could the multitude of entities connected to that [consciousness] [appear]?
"Connection with time" (*kālayoga*) means that even succession and non-succession are included within the Supreme Lord himself.

[Objection: If this is so, then would there not be a connection with time for the Supreme Lord? [Response: We say no. Why? Because that "non-seating" (*tannāsana*) of the Lord is his power named Kālī; as it has been said, consciousness itself assumes a form differentiated from the objects of knowledge.

Through association with limitation, [the power of action] attains the state of being an object of knowledge; then, from the sky [of pure consciousness], the power of action (kriyā-śakti) descends with a longing to appropriate the object of measurement through its own sovereignty. Therein, in the eastern portion, is the path of time (kāla-adhvan), while in the northern portion is the path of space (deśa-adhvan). As it is said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
Through the diversity of forms, this Lord manifests the succession of space;
and through the manifestation of the diversity of actions, He manifests the succession of time as well.

Thus: manifesting time externally through the act of emanation (*yogana*), and swallowing it by means of its union within one's own self (*yuñjānatva*), even at the moment of its intense manifestation (*prollāsasamaye*)—[for at the very beginning, at the moment of intense manifestation... (p. 205).

In the supreme emission (*visarga*), which is like a waveless ocean, the unsurpassed Self, a mass of pure light, there first flashes forth the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), which is intent on the reflective awareness of its own nature alone; because there is no object of reflection distinct from it, this consciousness is devoted solely to self-reflection. That itself is the moment of the great outpouring (*prollāsasamaya*).
Thus it is said, so that his sovereignty may arise everywhere. This is the meaning:

by the very majesty of his own sovereignty, the Supreme Lord, whose essence is the light of the Absolute (*anuttara*), conceals his own true nature and abides in the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the rest.

It may manifest the entire range of differentiated existence; for example, that very Supreme Light, preceded by the manifestation of the stage of the contracted subject, brings forth the fourfold group of powers beginning with *udyoga*.
For instance, *udyoga* is the desire to manifest objects, which is always present in one who is attached to it.

By means of the sun— which is of the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whose essential form is attained through its identity with the *kalās* beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the visarga (excluding the twelve neuter vowels)—
and which is slightly contracted in each individual object, it should illuminate, project outward, and fulfill every state in the form of blue, pleasure, and so forth.

The meaning is that one should establish [the object] for some time in its very suchness (*tathātva*), reflect upon it, and then withdraw it by assimilating it into one's own self. For any cognizer who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) must first perceive the collection of objects as they have ascended into the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and subsequently [determine] "this is thus."

Thereafter, one should reflect: "This object has been known by me. Through this pride of satisfaction and the dissolution of its external form, one should cause it to rest within one's own self; this matter is witnessed by direct experience.
Thus, after the ascent of the Light of the multitude of objects that have attained the state of manifestation and so forth—

When the moon of the object of knowledge— consisting of the body and so forth— is sluggish within the limited subject, due to its own nature being obscured by the swallowing of emission (*visarga-grāsa*), which consists in the concealment of that [true] nature through the attainment of a swollen state; this state having been reached by means of the sixteen digits (*kalā*) beginning with the intellect and the senses, which manifest as its own form.

This is what is meant: the manifestation in a gross form—consisting of various subjects, objects of knowledge, and so forth—arises from the emission of the digit of nectar (*amṛtakalā*) into the *saṃjīvinī* [power]. Whatever collection of entities there may be, having first attained its respective limited identity (*īyattā*), it reaches the state of being an object of knowledge by ascending through the gateway of the senses.

By performing those respective purposeful actions and by generating a state of resting solely within its own self, it brings about the fullness of consciousness. As it was said by the venerable master Utpaladeva:
"The mandala of existence consisting of all things..."
Who else is equal to me, who offers oblations upon the sacrificial grass of my own power— which consists of the power of the universe—
while performing the sacrifice that is the cosmic oblation?
Thus, by means of their empty nature—in the form of emergence, manifestation, transition, and dissolution—they assume a twelvefold attenuated state. (p. 206)
Furthermore, through the perfection of the four arts— beginning with effort— pertaining to the women and others embraced therein, they emerge as sprouts; then,

becoming languid and entering into a state of fullness consisting of sixteen aspects, they release within and without that quartet of arts which is the essence of the reality of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), characterized by repose in the bliss of that nectar.

Thus experiencing this very play of the swing consisting of fullness and emaciation, they are adept at swallowing and vomiting the multitude of digits of the Moon and Sun— as it is said in the *Mahārthamañjarī*:
"Seventeen [digits] are in the eye of the forehead, twelve and sixteen in the other two eyes."

Thus it is said. In that context, the eye on the forehead is the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), the right eye is the power of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-śakti*), and the left eye is the power of the object of knowledge (*prameya-śakti*). Here, moreover, the meaning is as follows: the solar sequence of abodes (*dhāma-krama*) has the twelve rays as its domain; the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa-krama*) consists of the twelve vowels excluding the neuter vowels; these very [rays] are...

The rays fall here upon the twelve paths of emptiness, which are the first-arisen abodes free from obscuration; this is the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*), and thus is the pervasion of the wheel of light (*prakāśacakra*). In the wheel of bliss (*ānandacakra*), the sequence of abodes (*dhāmakrama*) occurs through the flow of the nectar of the *bindu* (the *baindhava-amṛta*), by means of the pervasion of the sixteen vowels together with the neuter sounds.

The sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) consists of the sixteen—the intellect, the organs of action, the senses, and the mind—and this is the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*), which is the pervasion of the Wheel of Bliss (*ānandacakra*). Likewise, in the Wheel of Forms (*mūrticakra*), there is the sequence of abodes (*dhāmakrama*) within the seventeen abodes that constitute the dense, unobscured domain of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*); this extends from the primordial phoneme (*ādivarṇa*) up to the final letter beginning with 'A' (*akārādyakṣara*).

The sequence of phonemes extends in seventeen ways. These very stages of the lunar [energies], which have turned away from the external, though they desire to reflect inwardly, are experienced together with Maya;
thus, the sequence of consciousness consists of exactly seventeen. [The letter A alone is at the beginning, and in the middle, that which is born from the womb of Ka and the others—]
And at the conclusion, bestowing the *bindu*, she is "I"—this very Blessed Lady is emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
Thus it was said by the venerable Somānandapāda in his own commentary: "Aṃ and aḥ—this very Mātṛkā consists of both modified and unmodified forms."

And so forth. They explain that "a" is the unsurpassed (*anuttara*), while the lunar days (*tithi*) begin with "ā"; alternatively, they explain that the dot (*bindu*) is the syllable "aṃ," and the lunar days begin with "a," ending in the visarga. They teach that this very reality of consciousness is *spanda* (vibration), and *spandana* is a slight movement from one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). If...

The penetration of another object is nothing other than its own movement; if it were not movement, it would be nothing at all. Therefore, within its very essence, that which is devoid of succession and the like—a state of wonder, an upward surging, a wave—is designated in the Āgamas by such terms as *matsyodarī* (the fish-belly) and so forth; this is *spanda* (vibration).

Thus it is said: because its nature consists of slight movement, that [power] has the form of Śiva and Śakti, being both universal and particular. This has been explained: the initial lunar days (*tithis*), ending with the *bindu*, are the Moon and Sun through their connection with time.

Within that very lineage, from the earth and so forth up to the pentad of Brahmā, how does the sequence of those vowels proceed? Furthermore, the "eating" of the sequence—that is, its consumption—is the "swallowing of time"; having done so, this serves as an adverbial qualification for [the states of] the auspicious vow, enjoyment, and emptiness.
And when enjoyment has ceased and fullness is attained, O observer of good vows, this very address (*āmantraṇa*) is to be explained in this way:

thus it is "rootless" (*amūlā*), meaning its root is the letter *A*, or that its root does not exist because it is beginningless. It is that sequence whose [nature]—through phonetic conjunction (*praśleṣa*)—is of a different form or otherwise, yet even so it is "rootless," belonging to that which is rootless.

That which is extended and stretched out, and that very same thing which is its sequential progression—this is to be known as the nature of the knower, and this alone is the object of knowledge, because nothing else exists.

That which is non-existent is the patient endurance (kṣānti), the silent abiding, incessantly taking the form of emanation and so forth; it is at the end, in the proximity of, these senses (akṣāṇām) belonging to the faculties.
That which is beginningless and endless is,
by way of metaphor, the emission (*sṛṣṭi*) ending with the *akṣa*-syllables; it is the bringing forth of what was previously non-existent.

Its essential nature consists of the entry into one's own self, which is the form of withdrawal; and it is this very [nature] that constitutes all mantras— those whose characteristics are reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*), which consist of the expansion of seeds whose essence is Śiva, and which exist in the form of the venerable phonemes (*varṇabhaṭṭāraka*) as the signified and the signifier.

This [knowledge] is equal— neither deficient nor excessive— in all respects, throughout all tantras and in all their expansions, in all ritual actions, and at all times; it bestows the entire collection of accomplishments upon all those vidyās that consist of the vibration of the womb whose nature is power (śakti), which have arisen from its seed, and which take the form of sensation.
Having pointed toward the nature of Māyā, which is the state of manifest nescience (*aprakaṭākhyāti*), the differentiation of the phonemes is thus explained:

those very phonemes, whose nature is pure mantra, first attain the state of the emission of existence (*bhāvasṛṣṭi*) consisting of cognitive determinations (*pratyaya*) such as the power of the fivefold misconceptions; for [they are] twofold...

Emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) consists of the emanation of dispositions (*bhāva-sṛṣṭi*) and the emanation of elements (*bhūta-sṛṣṭi*). Among these, the emanation of dispositions takes the form of cognitive determinations (*pratyaya*), while the emanation of elements takes the form of the subtle potentials (*tanmātra*). In this regard, the emanation of dispositions itself is the "re-emission" (*pratyavasarga*), which is termed error (*viparyaya*), incapacity (*aśakti*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and attainment (*siddhi*).
And from the suppression resulting from the inequality of the qualities, there are fifty variations of that [state].

Thus ends the creation of the mental realm (bhāva-sṛṣṭi). As for the creation of the elements (bhūta-sṛṣṭi): the divine [creation] is of eight kinds, that of the animal womb is fivefold, and the human is of one kind; thus, in brief, is the elemental creation.
In this regard, the classification of the qualities is as follows:
the creation at the top is predominantly characterized by *sattva*, while that at the root is predominantly characterized by *tamas*;
in the middle, it is predominantly characterized by *rajas*, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.

Thus, the divine creation (*daivasarga*) is eightfold: Brāhma, Prājāpatya, Aindra, Pitrya, Gāndharva, Yākṣa, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca. The animal womb (*tiryagyoni*) is fivefold: beasts, wild animals, birds, reptiles, and stationary beings.
Since there is no distinction in form among the four [other classes], the human state (*mānuṣya*) is considered one alone. [These states] conceal their true nature.

(210) The five [afflictions]— ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life— which are designated as darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), great delusion (*mahāmoha*), gloom (*tāmisra*), and utter gloom (*andhatāmisra*)— make five; thus, there are eleven obstructions of the organs and seventeen obstructions of the intellect.

Thus, there are twenty-eight [factors]: the nine contentments (tuṣṭi)—consisting of four internal and five external—and the eight accomplishments (siddhi), which are reasoning, oral instruction, study, the removal of the three kinds of suffering, the acquisition of a friend, and generosity.
Among these, the incapacities (aśakti) are as follows:
Deafness, leprosy, blindness, numbness, as well as loss of smell,
muteness, lameness, crippledness, impotence, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and intoxication.

Thus, these eleven constitute the incapacity of the intellect (*buddhi*) caused by these factors. Regarding the incapacity of the intellect in its own nature, it has been stated that this results from the inversion of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and attainment (*siddhi*). As for contentment, there are five internal types—namely, those relating to nature (*prakṛti*), means (*upādāna*), time (*kāla*), and fortune (*bhāgya*)—and there are also five [types] relating to the objects of sense, such as sound and so forth; furthermore, there are five forms of renunciation (*uparama*). And what is renunciation?
For considering that service and other such means of acquiring wealth cause suffering to the servant and others,
there is a turning away from actions that bring about suffering. The varieties of misconception arise, as does incapacity due to the impairment of the instruments [of action].
Contentment has twenty-eight varieties, while attainment is ninefold and eightfold.
Thus, these very cognitions, which take the form of the emission of bound souls (paśu-sṛṣṭi), are primarily the fetters (pāśas). As it has been said:
"And his powers, ever-arisen, serve to veil his true nature;
for the emergence of cognition does not occur without being permeated by sound (śabda)."
Thus: "In that way,
the loss of the essence of supreme nectar for him arises from [the arising of] a conceptual cognition."

Thus, by means of internalizing the creation of the phonemes (*pratyaya-sṛṣṭi*), the creation of the phonemes belonging to *māyā*— which appear as a sequence consisting of clearly audible sounds— is described as being embraced by the primordial, ultimate, pure form, thereby bestowing the fruit of their respective effects.
In the Śrīpūrvaśāstra,
which contains the essence of the meaning of all scriptures, by means of such [a teaching]...
Having fully awakened by means of this [knowledge] and having agitated the womb (yoni) through his power,
the Lord created the phonemes (varṇas) which possess an equal number of syllables as that [source].
Thus embraced by various [beings], they bestow the fruits of all desires;
in this manner, these [powers] are described as always being unmanifest to those blinded by *māyā*, yet manifest to those who know them.

"O you whose nature consists of pure sensation (*śuddhavedanā*), in whom there is everywhere the manifestation of the power of your own intrinsic nature, and in whom there is no obstruction to the flow [of that power]—thus is the address: 'O you of auspicious vows' (*śobhanavrate*). This, then, is the summary of the meaning here.
The Supreme Goddess Bhairavī herself shines eternally, characterized solely by the wonder of immersion in the single essence of absolute freedom.
The essential nature of that [consciousness] is unceasing and eternally manifest,
through Sadāśiva, the earth, animals, blue, yellow, pleasure, and so forth.
Through its own manifesting natures, which possess self-luminosity,
consciousness— which has self-awareness as its essence— manifests in the form of those very appearances.

Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—meaning the manifestation of manifestation itself, which is the very existence of such a light—is described as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The sense is that there is no requirement for any other means of valid cognition here;
for there is no need for a means of valid cognition regarding an object that is protected by one's own self-awareness.
That which shines forth through its very equality with the ignorant, the animals, and the omniscient—[the "ignorant" being one who knows only a little; the "animal" being one who is deluded].
The sense-faculties, the three-fold logical mark, the sequence of another's words,
similarity, the impossibility otherwise, the non-arising of what is expected, and restraint.
That in which everything beginning with this [world] is perceived merely as a gateway,
and which consists of uninterrupted manifestation, is called self-awareness (svasaṃvedana).
Even for those animals who possess no specialized knowledge even regarding the mere names of the lunar mansions, forms, and so forth,
their consciousness nevertheless shines forth in the same way.
(213) Thus, speech by its very nature consists of the self-reflection of its own form;
and that which is the self-reflection of its own form is itself the body of supreme speech.
Because it possesses a manifold nature, this [consciousness] consists of a manifold manifestation;
for in its manifestation, it never at any time experiences dependence upon anything else.

How can there be dependence on others, such as the obstacles to convention and so forth? That Light is not dependent, for dependence consists precisely in being an object of manifestation (*prakāśyatā*), and being an object of manifestation is nothing other than the requirement of another Light; yet no other Light exists here. Thus, Light is one and independent, and therefore no reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) pertains to it.
Its nature is conceptualizable because it is non-conventional;

therefore, it is devoid of convention— that is, the convention (saṃketa) consisting of the agreement (samaya) established by an elder or similar authority that "this is the denotation of this"— it is the reflective awareness of its own essential nature.
Beyond space, time, parts, illusion, location, destruction, and action,
everything is complete in itself and distinct from all forms. Precisely because of its absolute freedom (*svātantrya*),
being devoid of the limitations of space and time, it is all-pervasive, eternal, and possesses a nature that is both with form and without form.
Thus it is stated elsewhere.

The essential nature of the Great Consciousness (*svābhāvikamahāsaṃvit*) is characterized solely by the latent impression of existence [as stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "the impression of an existing thing is the conferral of another quality"]. Its form consists of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), which is of a dual nature as "I" (*aham*), since the "this-ness" (*idantā*) is implied by that very "I-ness."
The state of being.
That very form of the Mātṛkā is the innate body of the elements beginning with earth;
it is their ultimate form by virtue of its nature as the undecaying essence of the Veda.
It is declared to consist of the seed-syllable (bīja) and the womb (yoni), having the nature of Śiva and Śakti.
But from the union of Śiva and Śakti, through their mutual surging forth, [the world arises].
The mutual union, which bestows bliss upon the world,
has as its ultimate reality a true form that encompasses everything from the internal to the limits of the universe.
That which is determined as *vīrya* (vital energy) is the conjunction and disjunction;
that is called *visarga* (emission), and it is said to be the *dhruvadhāma* (the abode of the eternal). As it was stated in the *Devībhāvanā* within the *Pañcastavī* hymn:
O Bhavānī, having emerged from the hollow of the root-basin and pierced through the six lotuses like a flash of lightning,
you surely enter once again that circle of the moon.
She is the form of the flowing water of supreme nectar.
Thus,
this very method is easily accomplished for the attainment of the unsurpassed state;
it has been described from this very collection of phonemes belonging to the realm of *māyā*.

In the *Śrīpūrva*, it is stated that by relying on *māyā*, the emission (*sṛṣṭi*) is indeed distinct and imperishable, consisting of the production of cognitions divided into fifty varieties. As it is said in the *Spanda*: "Just as there is the loss of the essence of supreme nectar when a cognition arises for one [who has realized it]..."
Therefore, it attains a state of non-independence, and that [consciousness] has only those [objects] as its domain.
Thus ends the evolution of the intellect (pratyayasarga).
By its very nature, it is of the form of a bond (*bandha*), consisting of the obscuration of its own essential form (*svarūpa*).

Within this very [mass of phonemes, which is free from *māyā*], those various *khecarīs* are included. Indeed, the powers such as *khecarī* are twofold; they take the forms of *khecarī*, *gocarī*, *dikcarī*, and *bhūcarī*. And their twofold nature is as follows:
For those purified by the descent of the supreme *śakti*, because these [powers] have the nature of emitting the expansion of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*),

they constitute the ultimate reality through the manifestation of one's own nature— characterized by non-duality, universal agency, fullness, and pervasiveness— due to being untainted by time; however, for those deluded by *māyā*, they do not bestow bliss.
Because they move within the plane of the empty subject— which consists of time, limited agency, impure knowledge,

attachment, and necessity— they are the binders; however, for those who have received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), their movements (*gocaryas*) proceed within the planes of intellect, ego, and mind, which are characterized by speech and consist of discursive thought.

They grow from pure resolve, pride, and intention; yet for others, they are contrary. Moving through the ten directions—that is, through the ten external senses—they are "those who move in the directions" (*dikcarya*).
For those who are graced, their essence is the manifestation of non-duality; yet for others, they fall into the perception of duality.

The fivefold [elements] beginning with earth (*bhū*) constitute the domain of the object of knowledge (*meyapada*). Those who move within that—namely, the *bhūcaryas*—have attained identity with it through a state of non-solidity consisting of its intense contemplation (*ābhoga*). They manifest as the body of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśaśarīra*) for the awakened, while for others they display total delimitation. Thus, there is a twofold state. In this regard:
Their state is indeed for the purpose of re-binding, since they are said to consist of objects (*viṣaya*), according to the root *viñ* meaning "to bind. Consisting of objects,
they extend the manifold cycle of transmigration (*saṃsṛti*) composed of karma, *māyā*, and the limited soul (*aṇu*).
Its identity with its own nature consists of the state of pure Bhairava.
The state of being a living soul and the state of liberation have already been declared as ultimately real;
and the supreme body is non-different from that [reality], even though the creation of castes appears to be distinct.
What has been described here as *vīrya* (vital potency) is that by which the secrecy of the mantra is maintained;
it is precisely this "I-ness" (*aham*), whose nature is the unsurpassed emission (*visarga*).
The wise one who, knowing the supreme nature of his own self, is liberated while living, is forever free;
whereas those desiring supernatural powers and the like are bound by the constraints fashioned by that [ignorance].
We yogins worship the space of the heart, which is the navel-ornament;
this has indeed been briefly determined according to the words of the Guru and the scriptures.
Relying upon this realization, let that which arises be questioned by your own inner wisdom;
it is not by this much alone that [the goal] is weighed, but rather a portion of the path has been shown.
Who indeed could delimit this Bhairavī consciousness as being "only this much"? Such is the extent of this descent of power (śaktipāta) that has unfolded within us.
By virtue of the authority granted by him, we have made this manifest today,
or at any other time, for ourselves and for our other mothers.
Therefore, reasoning (tarka), even in its most subtle form, comes into being after not having been, and will continue to exist;
it is like the sun among all illuminations of the constituent parts of yoga.
That by which the liberated one and the liberator are determined in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra must be accepted in every way and reflected upon by those who desire the supreme goal.
Wise men, having abandoned for a moment that envy so easily found among mortals,
should thereafter maintain within themselves that state which arises from the very instant of discernment.
Therefore, the fragments of clouds over the sun of consciousness are naturally extinguished by their own essence.

Enough with this appearance of supreme realization! O you of great splendor, enough with this delusion! Desist from this refuge; abandon this wandering, for the one who laughs at the world perceives both the subsequent and the prior as devoid of inherent nature. Thus, protect yourself.
The great power of dwelling [in the self] is the destroyer of the ocean of suffering; it is the non-attainment of worldly success, the ground of the earth, and the stainless abode.

This is the external wandering, the land of liberation, spoken of as the unconditioned. Having seen the pure essence within this, the wandering one becomes free from the defects of womanhood. This is the unsurpassed supreme state, which, if it were not so, would be merely a false appearance.
As the drops of ash scattered from her mouth,
she became attached to him; then, having purified the seven impurities, the swan-like sage vanished, and Tamālī spoke thus.
O noble one, speak truly! This world is like a mirage; it is transient, unstable, and devoid of essence.
It is a mere illusion that vanishes at the end. You are the very embodiment of splendor, yet you are devoted to the purpose of non-violence, truth, and self-restraint.
You are free from envy and malice, and your heart is not agitated by lamentation. O beautiful one, do not let your mind be filled with such unhappiness.
"O you who are thirsty for that nectar, you who are intoxicated by the separation from me, why is this not drunk? For this reason, there is a great longing for caressing.
Thus, regarding what was said—that "there is no answer even to an answer"—it is included here through the portion [of the verse] beginning with "he is absorbed in that answer."
The Kula-self, which is Śākta and the expansion of emanation, has been determined in detail; and that "beyond" (uttara) has also been described as being like the "unsurpassable" (anuttara).
Now, however, the unsurpassable itself must be examined in its essential nature in detail. In this way, the injunction and the restatement are fulfilled if that which is being restated...

Furthermore, the portion being enjoined would consist of both its own essential nature and its implied characteristic, just as in the case where it is said, "The very remembrance of Śiva’s name is itself the surging forth of all happiness"—here, both portions are implied characteristics.

In this context, however, although there is no other entity whatsoever called "the unsurpassed" (*anuttara*)— since if it were something else, it would necessarily be subject to being surpassed— it has been stated previously that this formal arrangement is intended according to the relationship between teacher and taught as established by [the Lord's] sovereignty. Therefore, for the purpose of defining the nature of the unsurpassed in detail:
The introduction to another treatise: He defines that [number], O auspicious lady, as being joined with fourteen and endowed with the end of the lords of the lunar days (tithīśa). || 9 ||
O lady of beautiful hips, the third Brahman is the heart of the Bhairava-self;
this is not born from the Yoginīs.
One who is not Rudra does not clearly attain it. || 10 ||
The heart-mantra of the God of gods immediately bestows the liberation of yoga;
when its recitation is properly performed—
The great assembly of mantras and mudrās. || 11 ||
Immediately, it attains the state of being his very mouth,
which is characterized by the penetration of his own body.
But he who, sealed by the Cumbaka, remembers [it] for even a moment; || 12 ||
Then that person binds the entire multitude of mantras and mudrās,
as well as all matters of the past and the future.
When questioned, he also speaks.
Uttering whichever form of the deity is intended at the beginning of the watch,
one beholds it directly and without doubt.
It was drawn forth by the powers of Rudra. || 14 ||
By recollecting [this] for merely two watches (prahara), one becomes situated in the sky;
by three [watches], all the Mothers [appear].
The mistresses of yoga, possessed of great power. || 15 ||
The heroes, the lords of heroes, the perfected ones, and the powerful host of Śākinīs.
Having arrived and given their pledge,
they were impelled by Bhairava.
They bestow supreme accomplishment or whatever fruit is desired; by this, those who have attained success will achieve it, and those yet to come shall do so as well.
And the practitioners of mantra accomplish [their goals]. || 17 ||
Whatever is found in the Bhairava Tantra,
all of that is accomplished through this;
even one who has not seen the mandala [attains success] in this way.

The Śākta [nature] is the essence of that Bhairava-form universe, which— by means of the logic and scriptural authority demonstrated— is of the nature of the Supreme Lady (Aparā-Bhaṭṭārikā) in her human form;
its heart, its core, is the form of Śiva, [revealed] by the Supreme Sovereign, the Illustrious Parā-Bhaṭṭārikā.

Embraced by the term *bhairava*, it is the form of the universal essence of all things (*viśvasya sarvasarvātmakatāvapuḥ*), whose nature is power (*śaktirūpa*); [this refers] to the single differentiation with respect to the Self that is conjoined with that [power]. (p. 221)

The heart of this one in human form consists of Śiva to such an extent that, through supreme non-duality, he is indeed the Self of all; for without that [non-duality], as well as by means of it, this very duality would be impossible, as was stated previously. The address “O fair-hipped one” (*suśroṇi*) is not devoid of its meaning even when [the body] consists of the impure *māyā*, for that which exists in the hips is composed of pure consciousness.
The Heart has been described as having the form of the Yoni; it is that [Heart] within which all— the Great Lords of Mantra (Maheśas) and the rest— are contained,

and which consists of the fullness of Bhairava for us, whose essential nature is "I," and who possess the appropriate designations such as "ourselves" and "this world," extending through the entire network of subjects down to the level of stationary beings.

Brahman is the single mass of power consisting of the bliss of the separation of the *visarga*—which is of the nature of the surging forth of the universal potency (*viśvavīrya*) contained within—and it is vast, pervasive, and expanded; yet this is not like the vision of Brahman accepted by the reciters of the Vedānta, which does not distance itself from the doctrine of absolute emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). And this...

The third [state] is of a single form, supreme as Śiva, in relation to humans and others; for this very reason, in these scriptures and here [in this work], that alone is taught as the primary heart (*hṛdaya*) to be worshipped,
even by those whose heart lacks the essence of pervasion by such potency (*vīrya*).

By the mere practice of external conduct to that extent, the bonds of the fetters of animal existence— which had become slackened, loosened, shattered, and split asunder through the gradual process— [were released].

If they themselves rest in the pervasion of this very Heart, then [notions such as] "this is the entry into this Heart," "I have entered into this Heart," or "this Goddess is Parā"—all of which are constructed by verbal conceptualization—are, on the contrary, due to their searching for another interior path within the Heart; this has been explained at length. However—
The snares of the scriptures do not contract the heart,
nor does this world defile consciousness;
for it is the form that is perfectly complete in the path of its own true nature.
That very state would be one filled with the weight of a surging repose.
As I have stated myself in my hymn:
"For those whose minds have become exceedingly clear through the intense immersion of devotion to you,
this state clearly dwells within their hearts in an instant."

Thus, for this very reason, the three [energies] are to be worshipped in the corners, while in the center is the Goddess, whose nature is the churning of Parānandabhairava; she exists through the very flow of the essence of eternal bliss (*nityānanda-rasa*) as the emission (*visarga*) characterized by agitation. This is the tradition of the deities regarding the union of couples (*yāmala-yoga*), and it applies to the heroes (*vīra*s) as well.
"Born from the union with the host of dūtīs whose nature is the agitation of eternal bliss through the organ of bliss"—
thus,
even in the state of a solitary hero (*ekavīra*), by virtue of resting in the bliss of one's own essential nature, this applies to the person as well.
Because the mind is established below the triangular *kanda*, which is the abode of the emergence of the organs of bliss,
it brings about the production of the agitation of bliss; this occurs when there is a dense friction between the base of those organs and their extremities,
as stated here.
"In the midst of fire and poison... and so forth; thus, the yoga of bliss (*ānandayoga*) itself is the worship of the heart (*hṛdayapūjā*). As it is stated in the *Trikatantrasāra*:
"Worship is the expansion of bliss; one should perform that within the triangle."
With the fragrances of flowers, incense, and so forth, she brings satisfaction to her own heart.

Thus, everything is indeed permeated by the two mudrās, because their essence consists of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*). Among the deities, the *jñānamudrā* alone is predominant internally, while the *kriyāmudrā* is predominant externally; among the heroes (*vīras*), the reverse is the case.
However, entry [into the state of identity] occurs through equality and through this very reversal; for this same reason, [the deity] consists of the power of knowledge.

The bestowal of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) upon the *liṅga* has thus been described. This [system] is joined with and integrated into the fourteen [tattvas], consisting of fifteen [units], and is endowed with the sixteenth, the emission (*visarga*), which concludes with the Lord of the Lunar Days (*tithīśa*).

Alternatively, the "Heart" (hṛdaya) is that which is endowed with the fourteenth— the pair consisting of the fifteenth lunar days (tithis)— and the end of that [fifteenth], namely the seventeenth digit, the Unsurpassed (anuttara-kalā). All things, such as jars, pleasure, and so forth, are that very essence of the seed-syllable.

It has been explained in detail that [the powers] advance in the form of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); for this very reason, that heart is sixteenfold. This heart is thus: therein, according to the *Anuttara*, is that state of identity with Brahman (*brahmasāmarasya*) consisting of the object of knowledge and the subject of knowledge, and of the four stages beginning with exertion (*udyoga*).

The aggregate is the undivided ground, the primordial; that which is joined with it is likewise undivided. These lords of the lunar days (tithi), ending in the vowel *ū*, arise from that, as it is said: "In this succession of phonemes, the group of six vowels alone shall be the root. Thus it is stated that the final letters of those lords of the lunar days are the syllables of nectar (*amṛta*).

The third [state] is that which is correctly endowed with those four; it is the supreme form of Śiva in relation to the human subject and so forth, shining forth through the four stages as the knower. Through those very [stages], by means of their nature as nourishment and curiosity, he makes them one within his own self by attaining the dissolution of the agitation between the object and the subject. These are the digits of nectar (*amṛtakalā*).
The unsurpassed heart of the universe, whose characteristic is oneness, is to be reached through higher discernment (prasaṃkhyāna) or through practice, in the form of Bhairava.
One should enter [the state] as it has been said:

"The Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self. Having withdrawn this [world] into the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti), which is the Self shining forth through the will (icchā), one should follow [it].

In relation to the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), that very same nature consisting of will (*icchātman*) is the third form; at its initial stage (*prākkoṭau*), it is untainted by the object of desire and so forth. [For if it were tainted by the object of desire and so forth at its initial stage, how could it be Brahman? Therefore, the intended meaning is that it is untainted in its prior portion. This is the fourth state of Brahman.

With respect to the forty divisions of Bhairava, the principles (*tattvas*) together with the three supreme Bhairavas and supreme Śaktis are thirty-six to be purified, as it has been said: "The supreme Bhairava is the purifier; [the principles] are thirty-six to be purified."
Furthermore, regarding the "successive triad" as it was established at the outset:
the Mother is the great new creation resting upon the pure digit (vimalakalā), her body full; and the Father is the one of five faces, whose splendor is concealed.
May my heart, which consists of the natural outpouring of the vibration of the union of those two, and which is the family of the unsurpassed nectar, shine forth intensely.
Thus, the instrument (karaṇa) is the means of purification; this initiation, however, is the ultimate instrument, which is the ultimate reality.
(226) and so forth;

that which is joined with these is indeed the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), which, being prior to and beyond all forms, is full. How [is it] endowed with the lords of the lunar days (*tithīśa*), the seed-syllables (*bīja*), and those ending with the one who bears the form of the womb (*yonirūpadhara*)?—this is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*); that very [state] is it.
The Heart is everywhere here; its form, which is primarily accessible through *prasaṃkhyāna* (discriminative discernment), shines forth once and for all.

However, for those who are fit—purified by the supreme descent of power (*para-śaktipāta*)—or even for those who are merely eager for the illusory displays of a magician, this should be understood as the practice of yoga.

By way of intention, the third is "desire" (*icchā*); and that [desire] is increased by the non-differentiated, full Brahman which is being desired. There are fourteen [units] plus forty-four, which possess no divisions; for "interval" (*antara*) exists because the word *yuta*—though it denotes "separated"—is used in such cases as "due to being separately established" (*yutasiddhatvāt*), [whereas here it refers to] "the relation between two things not separately established" (*ayutasiddhayoḥ saṃbandhaḥ samavāya*).
In this context, the meaning is "between those that are separately established (*yutasiddha*) and those that are not separately established (*ayutasiddha*).

Having internalized this very intention, it is stated in the *Siddhāntacūḍāmaṇi*: "The root *yu-* [is used] in the sense of mixing and non-mixing. Within the Lord of the lunar days (*tithīśvara*), who consists of the supreme (*anuttara*) *kalā* of the *Kula*,...
Ānanda follows after that; it is rightly called "this" (idam), consisting of awakening.
With respect to Īśāna, it is the third, having the nature of will (*icchā*).
By virtue of its expansion, it has become vast and attained the state of Īśāna, [consisting of] forty-four [units] of the fourteen.

(227) That which has been described as "joined" (*yuta*) is that wherein there is a mutual intermingling; it is endowed with the first vibration of the power of *Kula*, which is the internal withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) of the reckoning (*kalana*) of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*), the *Akula* state of the Lord of the lunar day (*tithīśvara*).
When, through union with the power of knowledge whose nature is opening (*unmeṣa*), the third [face] becomes Brahmā-Īśāna himself—

[the phrase "when" and so forth establishes that Īśāna indeed possesses the state of being the third Brahmā]— it becomes such that it is joined with the first division of those very forty-four principles (*tattvas*) among the fourteen.
Likewise, [the mantra] is properly endowed with the initial vibration of the Kula-power (kulaśakti), which ends with the Lord of the lunar days (tithīśa), by virtue of the desire to ascend;
here, the prefix *sam-* implies the necessity of support (*bharaṇa*).
It consists of the previously determined central point between the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
Through the ascent upon the form of the letter *Ū*, which is supported by the digit (*kalā*) of *Ū*, that which is this Brahman— whatever is moving or unmoving—

is, in relation to the impure, pure-impure, and pure creations, the third, consisting of the pure creation; for this very reason, it is endowed with the Lords of the Lunar Days (*tithīśvara*) as its heart, and with those ending in them, from *ka* to *kṣa*.
Now, by following the tetrad of voids (*śūnyacatuṣka*), there exists a state consisting of the destruction of the four [elements] beginning with earth; that wherein this occurs is space (*vyoma*).
The third [wheel] is called Brahmeccha; it is endowed with the external splendor of the Lord of the Tithis (the Sun) at its extremity.
According to the explained sequence, this third [wheel], Brahmeśana, is likewise exactly like this.
The third is called *brahmechākha*; it is the internal period (*antardaśā*) of the four beginning with space (*nabhas*), wherein it is joined as a common support.
It consists of the nature of space (*vyomātma*) accompanied by that form which follows the light of fire (*tejas*) ending with the Lord of the lunar days (*tithīśānta*).

In the same way, the third Brahma is endowed with fourteen and joined with the end of the Lord of the lunar days (the letter *ha*); through the leap (*pluti*) into the form of the full void, it is the nature of Bhairava.
Indeed, the Will (*icchā*), accompanied by the Lord who is one's own innate nature, [attains] the state of space (*vyomasattā*) from the ground of the knowable.
When it ascends, having rested for a moment on the ground of light, it suddenly enters the infinite,
motionless expanse of space— which consists mostly of wood and stone—
wherein yogins who have entered the great void of objectless deep sleep are addressed.
"Even the sound of kettledrums and cymbals is not conducive to arousal," and so forth.
Now, regarding this aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is the wonderful mutual intermingling of the forms of the powers (*śakti*):

with that as its objective, when the Will (*icchā*) becomes characterized by entry into the state of the Absolute (*anuttara-pada*), then, following the agitation of the powers such as the tongue and so forth, it is said therein: "of the slow, medium, and rapid [movements]..."

The fourth state, characterized by the four sounds, exists within the vibrations of specific consciousness that possess the qualities of *sattva* and so forth; it is of the nature of universal vibration and is that *Akula*. Joined with that *Anuttara* (the Unsurpassed), which is *Akula*, there is the third *Brahman*, whose essence is Will (*icchā*) and who is accompanied by Sovereignty (*īśana*), ending with the letter 'A' of the Lord of Lunar Days (*tithīśa*), which is the nature of the power of Bliss (*ānanda*).

Endowed with that [power], it likewise enters once again into supreme existence; when that occurs, it becomes the self of Bhairava—perfectly full and expanded for us (*naḥ*), as before. For this very reason, this alone...

The pair of seeds (*bījayugma*), through the entry into such a variety of seeds, is capable of both concealing and bringing forth; thus it is spoken of by means of the application of the principles of desire and speech (*kāma-vāk-tattva*):
"One should desire desires with desire; one should unite desire within desires."
And so forth (p.
"The seed-syllable situated in the letter *e* is solely for the purpose of the manifestation of speech."

Thus, by means of the fifth and sixth letters, that which was stated— namely, the third Brahman joined with the fourteenth and endowed with the end of the Lord of the Tithis— is indeed entered into the state of Anuttara, whose nature is Bhairava. This very Brahman,
joined with the fortieth according to the aforementioned method and endowed with the end of the Lord of the Tithis, exists as the form of the realization of the self of Bhairava.
This entire network of principles, whose essence is the *bindu*, shines forth as the nature of Bhairava;
therefore, even when projected externally, it is the expanded Brahman consisting of emission (*visarga*).
And that which stands outside becomes one with the nature of Bhairava by means of the removal of the poverty of differentiation through the exclusion of dualistic distinctions.
"Augmented by the attainment of the state that is the self of all things"—thus has this state of emission (*visarga*) been determined through careful attention.

In this way, the sixteenfold pervasion of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) has been explained; however, the pervasion of the womb-syllables (*yoni*) for each individual letter was already explained previously.
However, with the intention of categorizing [the states],

one should describe the five-fold elemental body as consisting of a collection of four stages— namely childhood, youth, old age, and the assumption of another body— by means of the entry and exit [of breath] ending with the *tithīśa* [the fifteenth digit].
The third [state] is endowed with the nature of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka*, and is Brahman because of its vastness (*bṛhattvāt*);

and that which is the Void (*śūnya*) here is the Heart whose essence is Power (*śakti*). All these, indeed, consist of the forms of the body, the vital breaths, the *puryaṣṭaka*, the Void, and the Fourth Power (*turya-śakti*).

The subjects—designated as the external self (*bāhyātman*), the embodied self (*ātmabhūtātman*), the trans-embodied self (*ativāhikātman*), the inner self (*antarātman*), and the supreme self (*paramātman*)—are those who have attained, through a gradual process, the state of being that very reality characterized by the increasingly intense density of the seed-syllable *Śiva*, which is of the nature of awakening.
This Heart, whose essence is Bhairava, is the means of entry here: all [of these].
Regarding what was stated as "the levels of the knower" (*pramātṛbhūmi*),
all powers— such as seeing, touching, and so forth—
are perfectly simultaneous with respect to their respective objects of knowledge.
Having cast [the universe] within, you stand as the single crystal pillar, the one support of all.
Thus: "O Caṇḍikā, by whichever of the fourteen paths— namely the external organs, intellect, ego, mind, and suṣumnā— one may travel,"
O Mother, that digit [of yours] is the abode of Śiva; such a state as hers is difficult to attain in this world, even by the gods—how wonderful!

Thus: one should traverse the levels of the subject without limitation—the thirteen [faculties] consisting of the ten external and three internal organs, together with *prakṛti* as the fourteenth; doubled, they become twenty-eight; added to forty, they become sixty-eight; the lunar days (*tithi*) are fifteen; and *Īśa*— [The text continues: ...[the total] is one hundred and thirty-four. By means of this, one should contemplate the entire extent of the universe within the body. This is the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), which is the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*). It is said to be "eightfold" because it consists of the five elements, the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṃkāra*). It is called "city" (*puri*) because it is the abode of the individual soul (*jīva*). It is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) because it is imperceptible to the senses. It is called "body" (*deha*) because it is the support for experience. It is said to be "transmigrating" (*saṃsārī*) because it wanders through various states of existence. It is said to be "bound" (*baddha*) because it is constrained by karma and *māyā*. It is said to be "liberated" (*mukta*) when it has realized its identity with Śiva. It is said to be "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*) because it is not limited by space or time. It is said to be "eternal" (*nitya*) because it is not subject to birth or death. It is said to be "consciousness" (*cit*) because it is self-luminous. It is said to be "bliss" (*ānanda*) because it is free from suffering. It is said to be "pure" (*śuddha*) because it is untainted by impurity. It is said to be "free" (*svatantra*) because it is independent of anything else. It is said to be "omnipotent" (*sarvaśakti*) because it possesses all powers. It is said to be "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*) because it knows everything. It is said to be "all-doing" (*sarvakartṛ*) because it performs all actions. It is said to be "all-enjoying" (*sarvabhoktṛ*) because it experiences all objects. It is said to be "all-witnessing" (*sarvasākṣin*) because it observes everything without being affected. It is said to be "all-inclusive" (*sarvātmaka*) because it contains everything within itself. It is said to be "non-dual" (*advaita*) because there is no other reality besides it. It is said to be "one" (*eka*) because it is without a second. It is said to be "without parts" (*niṣkala*) because it is indivisible. It is said to be "without qualities" (*nirguṇa*) because it is beyond the *guṇas*. It is said to be "without attributes" (*nirlakṣaṇa*) because it cannot be defined by characteristics. It is said to be "without form" (*nirākāra*) because it has no shape or color. It is said to be "without support" (*nirādhāra*) because it does not rest upon anything. It is said to be "without cause" (*nirhetuka*) because it is uncaused. It is said to be "without end" (*ananta*) because it is infinite. It is said to be "without beginning" (*anādi*) because it has no origin. It is said to be "without middle" (*amadhyama*) because it is neither small nor large. It is said to be "without limit" (*anavacchinna*) because it is boundless. It is said to be "without change" (*avikārin*) because it is immutable. It is said to be "without decay" (*ajarāmara*) because it is ageless and immortal. It is said to be "without death" (*amṛta*) because it is eternal. It is said to be "without fear" (*abhaya*) because it is fearless. It is said to be "without sorrow" (*aśoka*) because it is free from grief. It is said to be "without desire" (*aniṣkāma*) because it is free from longing. It is said to be "without attachment" (*asaṅga*) because it is unattached. It is said to be "without duality" (*advaita*) because it is non-dual. It is said to be "without distinction" (*aviśeṣa*) because it is uniform. It is said to be "without difference" (*abhinna*) because it is undivided. It is said to be "without separation" (*avyatirikta*) because it is inseparable. It is said to be "without division" (*avibhakta*) because it is whole. It is said to be "without fragmentation" (*akhaṇḍa*) because it is undivided. It is said to be "without break" (*acchidra*) because it is continuous. It is said to be "without gap" (*nirantara*) because it is seamless. It is said to be "without interval" (*nirviśeṣa*) because it is without distinction. It is said to be "without pause" (*nirvirāma*) because it is uninterrupted. It is said to be "without cessation" (*niruparama*) because it is perpetual. It is said to be "without end" (*ananta*) because it is infinite. It is said to be "without limit" (*anavacchinna*) because it is boundless. It is said to be "without boundary" (*nirmaryāda*) because it is limitless. It is said to be "without shore" (*nirapāra*) because it is shoreless. It is said to be "without bank" (*nirvelā*) because it is timeless. It is said to be "without tide" (*nirvīci*) because it is waveless. It is said to be "without fluctuation" (*nirvikalpa*) because it is changeless. It is said to be "without movement" (*nispanda*) because it is motionless. It is said to be "without vibration" (*nirghūrṇa*) because it is still. It is said to be "without agitation" (*nirāvega*) because it is calm. It is said to be "without turbulence" (*nirākulita*) because it is tranquil. It is said to be "without disturbance" (*nirākula*) because it is serene. It is said to be "without agitation" (*nirudvega*) because it is peaceful. It is said to be "without fear" (*nirbhaya*) because it is fearless. It is said to be "without trembling" (*nirtrāsa*) because it is steady. It is said to be "without shaking" (*nirkaṃpa*) because it is firm. It is said to be "without wavering" (*nirvalana*) because it is constant. It is said to be "without fluctuation" (*nirvikāra*) because it is unchanging. It is said to be "without modification" (*nirvikṛti*) because it is immutable. It is said to be "without transformation" (*nirvikāra*) because it is eternal. It is said to be "without alteration" (*niranyathābhāva*) because it is identical. It is said to be "without difference" (*nirviśeṣa*) because it is uniform. It is said to be "without distinction" (*nirbhedaka*) because it is undivided. It is said to be "without separation" (*nirviyoga*) because it is inseparable. It is said to be "without disjunction" (*nirviśleṣa*) because it is whole. It is said to be "without fracture" (*nirbhaṅga*) because it is unbroken. It is said to be "without split" (*nirvidāraṇa*) because it is seamless. It is said to be "without fissure" (*nirchidra*) because it is continuous. It is said to be "without gap" (*nirantara*) because it is seamless. It is said to be "without interval" (*nirviśeṣa*) because it is without distinction. It is said to be "without pause" (*nirvirāma*) because it is uninterrupted. It is said to be "without cessation" (*niruparama*) because it is perpetual. It is said to be "without end" (*ananta*) because it is infinite. It is said to be "without limit" (*anavacchinna*) because it is boundless. It is said to be "without boundary" (*nirmaryāda*) because it is limitless.
The eleven Rudras are joined with the three Kālas; thus,
there are one hundred and twelve mantras consisting of the gross, subtle, and supreme forms of the vibration of Śakti located within the vital points (*marmas*).

One should cultivate the very existence of the body as the form of Bhairava—consisting of the agitation (*kṣobha*) arising from the union and separation that flash forth through the expansion of *vīrya* (vital energy)—by means of the method of simultaneous immersion (*yugapanniveśa-saṃpradāya*). This applies to any intoxicant such as wine, liquor, or spirits, which possesses four states: sweet, astringent, bitter, and sour. As it has been said:
One should perform even prohibited acts through the goddesses residing in the intellect, the ritual action, and the senses;
yet that which is prohibited and loathed by the world [must be avoided].
Thus it is said:
"Even though this supreme power is eternally manifest, nevertheless,
the state of Kaula is difficult to attain for one who is devoid of external conduct."
Thus it is stated elsewhere:
"One should employ everything here, both worldly and transcendental;
if one is trembling while seeking steadiness, one should forcibly diminish that trembling."
And it should not be thought that this [consumption of meat] must necessarily be performed;

for where is there meat, and where is devotion to Śiva? Where is there liquor, and where is the worship of Śiva? Indeed, Śaṅkara is very difficult to attain for those intent on worship with liquor and such things.

Because of such contradictions as these, what then should be understood here? That for those whose true nature has been recognized through re-cognition, no stain of doubt should be entertained. Even one who is free from suspicion and knows the reality [should remain thus] regarding the method of the seeker of liberation.
"One should not abandon the boundaries of the scriptures"—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.

Thus, because of the clear prohibition of [worship by] gods and others, therefore, in this matter, the *Mahārthamañjarī* alone is the authority in every respect, according to the principle that "one should act according to where one has devotion," and so forth. That [mantra] ends with the Lord of the lunar days (*tithīśa*).

That third impurity (*mala*), which consists of the substance of both emissions (*visarga*) and resides within the two senses, is denoted by the word "flower" (*kusuma*); it is the ash remaining from the burning of the fuel of the universe, whose nature is Bhairava, whose form is full, and which is the nourishing water and the heart.
That which exists within all the senses as both the essence and the solidified form is this very substance; these substances, according to their availability, dissolve impurities and distinctions.
As it has been said: "By whatever means and in whatever manner—whether sequentially or simultaneously—"
Doubt dissolves within him who possesses that [wisdom] wherein he may abide.

Thus it is; for this very sequence is indeed observed: this very doubt, consisting of contraction, as it arises and takes root, reaches its culmination in fruit and becomes the first production of the sprout of the tree that is the seed of saṃsāra—as was stated previously in this very work.
The virtuous declare that the root of the impurity consisting of illusion and karma is indeed the impurity called *saṃkoca*, which is the *āṇava* [impurity]; so say the blessed ones.
"That alone is the root of the withered tree of existence...

Thus it is said. Herein is the summary: as has been stated by this very [author], one's own self is not [to be purified] here through the discrimination between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit, or between purity and impurity—[a discrimination] which is devoid of the true nature of reality.
Regarding the term "causing weariness": purity and impurity are not the inherent nature of an object from the perspective of ultimate reality, because they are observed to be mutually exclusive.
For the wise, that which is considered purity in one context is remembered as impurity by others.
Even though giving has been prescribed, it is as [forbidden] when one is initiated.
This is merely a mental construction; therefore, let it be accepted as such by the wise. There is no certainty that this construction is real, for it is indeed false.
Therefore, in this investigation of the injunction (*codanā*), the status of being an answer belongs here;
indeed, this is beyond doubt for both the proponent and the opponent.

Thus it is said.
