In this regard, the following investigation arises: if it is argued that [the world] cannot be impure because of the Mīmāṃsaka statement that "injunction (*codanā*) is indeed non-sublatable," we reply: no; for it is established by reasoning that the injunction regarding Śiva alone is sublatable, just as it has been stated that the knowledge of the bound (*pāśava-jñāna*) varies according to its degree of contraction.
However, thorough knowledge [of the object] through the varying degrees of its manifestation acts as a sublater.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Śivopaniṣad:

"That purification which is prescribed by those of limited knowledge is not considered true purification in the vision of Śambhu. [The verse continues: "Purification is attained through the realization of the Self, through the cessation of all mental fluctuations, and through the constant remembrance of Śiva; there is no other purification."
Thus it is said:
"The conviction of the bound soul is: 'I am inert; I am fettered by karma; I am defiled; I am impelled by others.'"
Thus, by the accomplishment of attaining this other firm certainty,
the conscious self, whose body is the universe, immediately becomes the Lord.
Thus, that state exists for those who are unawakened;
it is imagined by the awakened and, although being imagined for the sake of the ignorant, it is firmly established for them.
It bears fruit precisely through its diversity; for this very reason, by virtue of being conceived as diverse,
it is designated by various terms such as "dharmas" and so forth, appearing in different forms in each scripture and in each region,
as it has been said:
"Debility is a plunderer; just as debility is a plunderer in the body during its throbbing, so too is its course born of ignorance.
If that [throbbing] is destroyed by its own unfolding, how could that [debility] exist without a cause?"
Thus [ends the section on] the body.

Thus, when this [identification with the body] suddenly dissolves, one becomes free from the stain of the fetters of the animal state (pāśava) and enters the heart of Bhairava; therefore, one should strive in every way to practice this.
This is the intended meaning in the *Śrītilakaśāstra*. It is also stated in the *Śrībhargaśikhā*: "One should rejoice in the Vīravow and practice it accordingly," and so forth.
It is likewise stated in the *Śrīsarvācāra*.
Out of ignorance, the deluded one fears; from that [ignorance] arise both creation and dissolution.
All mantras consist of phonemes, and all phonemes are of the nature of Śiva.
Water is traditionally known as that which may or may not be drunk; solid food is that which may or may not be eaten. That which is beautiful and that which is ugly—all that is called fire (tejas).
The touchable and the untouchable are known as air; the cavity is called space.
The offering and the offerer, and that which is received as the offering—[all these are one].
O Goddess, everything consists of the five elements; nothing anywhere is devoid of them.
Since the Self produces desire, how can doubt be entertained?
Thus it is said. This very intention is also stated in the *Śrīvīrāvaliśāstra*, and in the *Kramastotra* it is said:
"For the sake of the restraint of the world, for the Yama who is the restrainer, [and] for the withdrawal of all objects through self-restraint."
I bow to Kālī, who draws in [all beings] while being intent on the playful enjoyment of the great devouring of their bodies.
Thus it is said. And this has been explained by me at length in my commentary on the *Kramakeli*.
For this very reason, in the Trika scriptures (*ṣaḍardhaśāstra*), this very ritual act is generally worship (*pūjā*) because it is free from restrictive constraints;
and for the sake of fulfilling that [worship], even when all the ritual substances are unavailable, it may be performed four times, three times, twice, or once within the course of a year.
The procedure for the *pavitraka* has been declared. For the sake of completing the ritual and fulfilling the command of the sacrifice,
he who performs it neither four times nor once makes the *pavitraka* fruitless.
(Thus, p.

237) the sequence of consciousness has been explained in detail. Furthermore, there is no fixed status for castes such as the Brāhmaṇas and so forth, because they are merely conceptual constructs; however, the Blessed One stated that [the system of castes] is revealed through instruction in order to lead those of dull intellect who are like beasts to understanding.

This has been determined in detail in the *Mukuṭasaṃhitā*, but here it is established with ease. The fourteen qualities, beginning with Will (*icchā*), have been determined from the vowels; the Visarga situated between the letters *o* and *au*, ending with the Lord of the lunar days (*tithīśa*);
and the third Brahman situated between the letters *ṣa* and *ha*—this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the universe in reality. For instance, whatever there may be...

The sixfold form—consisting of the earthly, the elemental, and the illusory (māyīya)—shines forth; although it falls within will, knowledge, or action, because it is the self of all, it is threefold in nature. All of this is emitted into the supreme state of Śiva, and everything is emitted from the state of Śiva. Thus, this very uninterrupted flow is non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka), even though it is a conceptualization (vikalpa).

The enemy that is woman and so forth is thus an object of action; for this very reason, one becomes an agent of such actions, thinking "I have done it," "I am doing it," and "I will do it. Thus, the emission (*visarga*) is connected to the three times of the present, and its ultimate reality consists precisely in differentiation.
Thus, on the contrary, for those cursed by fate, the very ground of liberation— which is auspicious by nature— has always become a great desert forest of the fear of saṃsāra;
it is like a mass of the submarine fire, dense with flickering flames, emerging from the water.
From the moon, the abode of nectar, which is full from the tenth day until the full moon— [according to the scriptures, after its fullness, the emergence of a thunderbolt occurs]— there arises,
through the conceptualization of the path of the expansion of sovereignty, the destruction of transmigratory existence.
How wondrous, how truly marvelous, does this unfold from the expansion of the thwarted course of destiny!
It is also stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:

"For one who fully recognizes, 'All this is my own manifestation,' there is the state of the Great Lord even amidst the proliferation of mental constructs of the universal self; for that which is called the inner self..."
Any other being is a mere animal, whereas I am that very one who is the dense mass of light consisting of the grasped and the grasper as they are fully embraced;

I am that Being, and not anyone else. Therefore, even the creation of conceptual constructs is my own sovereign power, characterized by absolute freedom—when such a reflective awareness has become firmly established.

Even one whose conceptual constructions have been utterly destroyed by the truth is liberated while still living; as it has been said: "Even doubt should not be suspected; this state of being free from doubt is manifest."
Thus [it is said].

Thus; and just as within the very midst of forms there are forms such as four-armed, three-eyed, full-bodied, or emaciated, and within the very midst of substances there are substances such as wine, spirits, and so forth (p.

As if forcibly causing that very existence to rest within them, like written syllables, they are the ground of all letters (*avarṇabhūmi*). Thus, these [referring to the four-armed forms and so forth, as well as the written syllables] possess excellence. Likewise, even among all letters, this letter [the word *varṇa* implies that "this possesses excellence," which is the remainder of the sense].
To explain: the letter *sa* is, first of all, of the nature of the nectar of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). As it has been said:
"The reality of the fullness of desire (*kāma*) is clearly manifested in the union (*saṃghaṭṭa*);
the reality of the nectar of the object (*viṣaya*) occurs when the atom (*aṇu*) is emitted during its state of being concealed."
Thus, while shining forth, it seizes the entire collection of phonemes and shines as that very ultimate essence of truth, bliss, plenitude, and existence—
which is characterized by the sibilant *sītkāra*, the thrill of joy, trembling, and the contraction and expansion of the supreme organ. Indeed, that alone is [the reality].

The non-illusory, ultimate nature of truth and the other [categories] is as follows: for instance, those who are skilled in grasping the hearts of others through gestures can achieve their desired goal from the mere letter *ga* alone— even when that *ga* occurs at the beginning, middle, or end of an infinite series of words such as "gagana" (sky), "gavaya" (wild ox), and "go" (cow)— provided it is sufficient for that purpose.
p.
240) Because of the entry into the locus of truth (*satyapada*), the capacity to signify (*vācakatva*) belongs truly to each individual phoneme (*varṇa*) alone,
as has been stated.
Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition, there is a confusion;
through *saṃyama* upon their distinction, there arises knowledge of the cries of all beings.
[That is to say, regarding the distinction between those words, objects, and cognitions, by performing *saṃyama* upon that—performing *saṃyama* on these three as one.]
Thus is the technical definition of *saṃyama*. (Yogasūtra 3.17).

For this very reason, these particles (*nipāta*) such as *a*, *ca*, and others—which consist of single phonemes and include case-endings and so forth—are called "particles" (*nipāta*) because they "fall down" (*nipatanti*) upon meanings that are established by others.
Regarding the statement in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* that [consciousness] is non-substantial (*asattva*) because it lacks distinctions produced by gender, number, and grammatical case:
"The Self does not become something other than itself due to differences in reflective awareness such as 'I' (*aham*) and so forth."
I am the very object of this creation, just as the object is denoted by the verbal suffix.

Thus [it is said]. Here, for the sake of application to the subject at hand, a reversal between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) must be conceived; namely, that no distinct meaning—whether being negated or being combined—is denoted by the powers of the non-substantial particles (*nipāta*), which consist of the forms of suffixes (*pratyaya*), option (*vikalpa*), and aggregation (*samuccaya*), etc., just as [in the following example]:
The object that is distinct from the creation is designated precisely as that which is perceived by the "I," such as the "I-am-ness" (ahantā), the Lord (īśvara), or the Self (ātman);

it is not [designated] as "the Lord" or "the Self" and so forth. Even in the state of Māyā, there exists that which is as if ultimate, merged within the state of the subject, turned away from "this-ness" (idantā), and characterized by non-existence.

That this very is the intention of the venerable Bhartṛhari is what he stated on page 241, [namely] that words express such meanings as a negation, a conjunction, or a negation-conjunction, which are non-different in form from the respective things being negated or conjoined.

"Every word is distinct from the first word, and every word is expectant [expectant because of mutual superimposition]," thus it is said in the investigation of sentences (*vākyavicāra*). And so it is in the *Pārameśvara* treatises on Vedic grammar.
In words such as *mantra* and *dīkṣā*, etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is appropriate due to the similarity of their phonemes and letters; however, [an objection may be raised]:

"If this is so, then since everything is rooted in phonemes and letters, it would follow that everywhere an etymological derivation could be established merely through the similarity of phonemes and letters, because everything is rooted in them."

For there would be great harm for one who grasps the branches while abandoning the root of words and sentences; therefore, he says "But that... and so forth. He states the reason for this with the words "by the power of necessity" (*niyativaśāt*). Indeed, everything has been established by the Supreme Lord through the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*); consequently, by the combination of these syllables, this word has precisely this meaning.

The meaning is "restriction" (*niyama*). It is not conventional—meaning, by virtue of necessity—it does not extend to the worldly level. Thus, the letter *sa* is of such a nature; the diphthong *au* and the *visarga* have also been explained. As it is said in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
"The triad is pervaded by the letter *s*, and the fourth by the trident."

The supreme pervasion (*parā vyāpti*) is declared to be that which transcends everything by means of the emission (*visarga*). This number consists of three parts; thus it is a "triad" (*tritaya*), meaning it possesses the number three. That [triad] is designated as the earthly (*pārthiva*), the primordial (*prākṛta*), and the illusory (*māyīya*);
and that is pervaded by the phoneme *sa*. The meaning is that the pervasion of the letter *sa* extends up to that limit. [This is done] by means of the trident (*triśūla*).

"The fourth" means the fourth *śāktamaṇḍala*; and that, by means of the trident and the seed-syllable *au*, as previously stated in the thirty-six [verses], he describes as "transcending that" with the word "all"—this is clear. The sense is that this is the supreme initiation (*parā-dīkṣā*).
Thus,
as stated on page 242),
the disciple should likewise receive [the teaching] only when the guru has been satisfied.
[By means of] body, substance, consciousness, birth, action, qualities, and so forth, [and by training in other treatises].
But when she has been pierced by that Guru with a joyful mind,
then she should be known as the bestower of accomplishment, and not otherwise, O Goddess worshipped by heroes.
Thus it is said. Elsewhere also, there is one seed-syllable consisting of emanation, as it has been stated:
"One is the seed-syllable consisting of emanation, and one is the *khecarī* mudrā."
He in whom these two arise abides in the state of supreme peace.
Thus. * * * * * * * * * | Thus. For this very reason, there is a rule in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* that [the teaching] should not be written in a book:
"The living soul (jīva), endowed with the left shank, has come down through the lineage of succession."
Thus it is said; here too it will be stated:
"Just as [the tree] resides within the seed of the Nyagrodha...
This is the heart of the Bhairava-self—because of its nature as the letter *na* in relation to the *Mālinī*, though in reality...
And from the Yoginī whose form begins with the letter *a*—

that is, from the power of emission (*visargaśakti*)— Rudra is born; he is manifested as the state of the subject (*pramātṛbhāva*), being both the obstructer (*rodhaka*) and the dissolver (*drāvaka*).

Only that person who is a *nā*—a man—clearly attains this; neither one who is not Rudra nor one born from the womb of a non-yoginī does so. Immediate union (*sadyoyoga*), which is identity with Bhairava, is itself liberation. As it has been said: "And liberation is indeed nothing other than the manifestation of one's own true nature."
And the intrinsic nature of the self is consciousness... [text fragment] ...consciousness.

Thus it is determined: he who receives that [teaching] is one of such a kind and no other; and he who is of such a kind is a Rudra born of the Yoginīs—this is established by the sense of the text. He certainly receives it clearly; in this way, he receives the Heart itself—that which bestows immediate union and liberation—this is the universal rule regarding mantras.

The venerable deities (*bhaṭṭārakas*)—such as Laukika, Pārameśvara, and others—are of the nature of both *manana* (contemplation) and *trāṇa* (protection), derived from the verbal roots *man* (to understand) and *trai* (to protect). They consist of conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-saṃvit*). Furthermore, the *mudrās* consist of the activity of all the instruments, such as the hands and feet; they are of the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). The "group" (*gaṇa*) is formed by these.

Having a single form consisting of the supreme power (*paraśakti*) which is the essence of the totality, [he perceives] his own self, beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void (*śūnya*),
as in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
And this very principle of consciousness (cittattva), which consists of agency and is intensified by *kalā*,
exists as a limited attribute of insentient entities such as the void (*śūnya*).
The primacy of agency and of consciousness belonging to the conscious self [is established];
knowledge regarding the void and other qualities is characterized by absorption into that.

The meaning here is as follows: because the aspect of consciousness (*saṃvid-bhāga*) is submerged by impurity (*mala*), the reality of the nature of consciousness—which consists of agency and is called "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*)—is supported by the principle called *kalā*.

Being suppressed by impurity, it is nevertheless stirred up [to a degree] such that it becomes immersed in the objective portion (*prameya-bhāga*), ranging from the body and so forth, which have attained the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*), up to the void (*śūnya*).

When even the state beginning with "void" (śūnya) and ending with the body exists through the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) alone— which is permeated by the intermingling of attributes such as sovereignty, permanence, and the majesty of being thus— as that is the Fourth State (*turyatā*). The penetration (*āveśa*) of the body is instantaneous.

The emergence of the subject (pramātṛ) as permeated by independent agency occurs through the penetration of the supreme nature and the concealment of insentience, which consists in dependence; likewise, "svadā" refers to the act of giving one's own nature to an object,
namely the activity beginning with will and ending with action— immersion (*aveśa*) therein is the very definition [of this state].

Having acted thus, that which arises when this seed-syllable is uttered—that is, when its upward movement (*ūrdhvacaraṇa*) is established—is determined in many ways by this very [term] *sadyaḥ*. By this, the penetration of *sa* and *ti* is indicated; it attains the state of being their face and the predominance of their supreme form (*tatpararūpa*), but not that form belonging to bound souls (*paśu*).
On the contrary, it conceals itself (p.
for this very reason, "for a moment" (*muhūrta*) means that which, although not limited by time, is merely an unfolding (*unmeṣa*) in relation to the calculation of another [time].

He remembers—that is, he connects with—it; he binds that very collection of explained mantras and mudrās, unifying them within his own self through non-duality. How? By means of the "kisser" (cumbaka)—that is, by means of the Śākta form which touches all things, in accordance with the root *cuvi* meaning "union of the mouth. Everywhere.

Having performed the sealing that is sealed on all sides—the particle *tu* being used for emphasis—only he who is thus sealed by the vibration of Śakti (*śāktaspanda*) and who contemplates the nature of Śiva as consisting of such reality acts in this manner; not, however, one whose form is merely human, such as a stone or the like. That which is past, that which is yet to come, and that which is of the nature of misfortune [is likewise overcome].
Because there is no other [state] prior to this, he explains the other as well: how does he bring the discourse to its conclusion through non-conceptualization?
When questioned, there is a desire to know regarding the inquiry.
One who possesses that which was asked about is "one who has been questioned. Indeed, whatever one desires to know,
that very thing he brings forth from within.
As it has been said:

"Just as the Creator, when requested according to one's desire, brings about for embodied beings the attainment of objects situated in the heart by causing the rising of the moon and the sun while they are awake."
p.

246) and so forth. For this [consciousness] is indeed one; even in recollection, imagination, and the like, it remains exactly that much [in duration], and neither the past nor the future exist, as has been stated.

"Unconditioned by time and both [space and object]," and so forth. For that which was previously non-limited in form, this state of being "once-for-all manifest"—inexpressible as "it knows again" or "it acts again"—is precisely because it cannot tolerate such contraction; therefore, it is said with respect to past and future.

Since, in the absence of that [temporality], the present time is in fact not applicable, it has been stated more than once that the true nature of reality is precisely its being untouched by time; for that very [Self] manifests the variegated power of time.
Furthermore, even that which is considered a "ghatikā" (a unit of time) during some waking state—
In that very state, the subjects existing in the dream-world experience manifoldness;
they even construct the variety of days, watches, years, and so forth.
According to this principle, the supreme Hara is the withdrawal (saṃhāra) known as Akula; immediately following that is the intended Sadāśiva-tattva, which is denoted by the word "preta."

Having performed the devouring—that is, the consumption (*adana*)—and the continuous movement (*atana*), which is the constant progression (*sātatyagamana*), of the form of the deity through the manifestation of the power of knowledge that has become established, [there occurs] the fashioning of forms and the devouring of the form of the witness together with the senses;
[the roots *ad* and *at* are used here in the sense of "eating" and "continuous movement," respectively]. Having done this, [one attains the goal].

Drawn by the powers whose forms are obstruction and liquefaction, he sees without doubt; this is what is meant: that which is called "vision" belongs to one who has ascended to the reality of the Kula, known as the subsidence of all waves [of mental activity].

Due to its union with infinite majesty and sovereignty, that very will of the possessor of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)— being internal to itself— attains the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which consists in the manifestation of a slight, indistinct differentiation from the object to be willed.
This very [power] is the externalization of all the senses, whose form is the vibration of a particular aspect of that power of knowledge.

Constant movement is that very running away, and that itself is devouring; these two—vomiting and devouring—belong to perception because perception consists of nothing but manifestation (*prathā*), and because manifestation possesses such diverse forms.
Furthermore, even in cases such as a post or a person where both possibilities are uncertain, the state of having an indeterminate object is indeed beyond doubt. Thus...
The power of the Supreme Lord consists of the impressions of past actions; thus, he says that Bhairava is the possessor of the power of memory, which has both transcendent and immanent forms.
"Two watches," and so forth. Thus, by recollecting this, one becomes the void (*vyoma*) wherein the *puryaṣṭaka* exists;

and while assuming the nature of that subject within the void, when one repeatedly contemplates and even remembers—as before—the form called "vision" which is characterized by the watch [of time], [one attains that state].

The connection is: "He sees directly and without doubt, drawn by the powers of Rudra. For it has been stated that even that [vision] is indeed a form of seeing. Thus, he is said to be "endowed with the power of conceptualization (vikalpa) consisting of the lower [nature]" by means of this triad: when, while seeing and remembering, situated in the void, he sees once again—by this [it is meant].

By means of the three perceptions characterized by the watch (prahara), the Mothers—who consist of the internal subject—are the powers of the Supreme Lord; and because they are subjects, they are established as independent of the establishment of objects for other subjects. Through yoga, which is characterized by identity with that very nature, there is sovereignty; thus, they possess a portion of autonomy that has been so grasped, and are great.

Those rays of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), whose power consists in having an unimpeded range everywhere in relation to the functioning of the external senses, are also indeed perfected (*siddha*)— because their activity is characterized by impetuous movement, entirely independent of the constraints of the fetters (*pāśa*) and injunctions (*śāsana*) that govern the bound soul (*paśu*) throughout the universe.
The *vīras*— those known as the organs of cognition and action— are indeed perfected beings (*siddhas*), and their lords,
whose nature consists of the phonemes beginning with *ka*, are also perfected beings; this is what is taught in the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the phonemes beginning with *ka*.

The collection of powers (*śakti-samūha*), whose essence consists of deities such as Brāhmī and others, and which is characterized by various mental fluctuations such as aversion and attachment, is likewise established; for this very reason, it is powerful. All these, acting together by the command of the Supreme (*parājñayā*)—that is, by the command of the Supreme who is the "Other" consisting of the conceit "I am [the other]" (*mānamayīm asau para iti vikalpātmikām*)—or rather, by the desired fruit itself.

I give and bestow [this] both when the purposeful action is unknown and when the purposeful action is known; this is the sequential application of the conceptualization. What need is there for much? Even those mantra-practitioners who have attained mastery over the mantras of other lineages—even they shall attain success through this Heart-mantra and become liberated while living; without this, [they cannot].

The sense is that ultimate accomplishment (*pāramārthikī siddhi*) does not occur [through other means]. As for the passage beginning with "whatever [is accomplished] by Bhairava," those who have attained accomplishments, those who are accomplishing them, and those who will attain them through the yoga of *aṇimā* and so forth—even they [attain their goals] by this very yoga; indeed, there is no entry into this Heart [of the teaching] otherwise.

Even worldly accomplishment (*vyāvahārikī siddhi*) is not possible without this, because whatever collection of accomplishments exists within the *Bhairava* Tantra— the system whose self is the universe— arises from that very source; thus, it is this Supreme Lord alone who is the essence of the Heart.

Thus conceived as possessing a unity with infinite consciousness— which, by its very nature, is perpetually arising and withdrawing while nourished by the three powers— this unseen manifestation, which consists of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), is the impurity of *māyā*.

And it destroys the "egg" (*aṇḍa*) of entities—that is, their essence known as differentiation. In this way, even though this Heart-Maṇḍala is unseen, it is the destruction and contraction of the four eggs; that which is joined with this [Heart] is thus the Supreme Lord himself, who consists of both *vidyā* and *māyā*, the one alone who is a mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*), as it has been said:
Vision is the supreme Goddess; remembrance is the intermediate Goddess;
and conceptual thought is the lower Goddess—the Lord consists of these three powers.
Both Māyā and Vidyā belong to Him; however, Māyā consists of the four eggs (aṇḍas), while Vidyā is the consciousness of one's own true nature, auspicious and consisting of grace.

Thus [it is said]. However, if yoga is the primary factor, then one must first perform the vows and so forth as prescribed in the scriptures such as the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara); then, when this [mantra] is uttered, the rest should be clearly explained as follows:

In matters where the effect is already perceived, the collection of actions necessarily projects a fixed result, for even in the case of yogins, there is indeed a restriction due to the logic of experiencing the cultivation of the instruments of the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*). 17.
Now, regarding this threefold meaning, he explains the state of being supreme among all and unsurpassed— that which was stated as "the triad that is higher than the Kula"— with the words:
"even one who has not seen the maṇḍala [attains it] in this way."
Whoever knows this in its true essence shall eternally possess accomplishment; he is a yogi and he is truly initiated.
The *maṇḍala*—the circle of deities—even for one who does not perceive it and has not attained union with it, [herein this is the intended meaning]:

each individual goddess of the channels effortlessly and spontaneously brings about a meeting (*melāpa*) within her respective domain through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Primordial Goddess; such is the case for the sense-deities.

Regarding the phrase "the meeting of the twelve": even while not directly perceiving the mandalas— which consist of the body's channels (*nāḍī*), wheels (*cakra*), and sub-wheels— through the practice of yoga by means of conduct (*caryā*), night-faring (*niśāṭana*), forceful methods (*haṭha*), and so forth,
and even without seeing the mandala of the trident, lotus, and the rest—
p.

252) There is no need here for initiation through mandalas and the like; for someone who is thus favored by the descent of supreme power (para-śaktipāta) knows this very knowledge to be initiation itself—what other initiation could there be? Therefore, knowing it thus, [one is initiated] by the All-pervading Lord.
He was initiated by the venerable Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka; for this very reason, it has been said:
"Those of small intellect who take up mantras on their own suffer;
a mantra that remains merely as written text is considered here to be devoid of power."
"By the power of convention, his greatness does not spread from a book. Likewise:
"Those who have studied the sciences from books, yet are devoid of initiation and the observances (*samaya*)."
"Ascetics who are devoted to harming others wander about here excessively;

yet they do not know the reality, and for that reason they clearly partake in fault. [And regarding the phrase] "one who has received the mantra"—this refers to a mantra other than this very heart-mantra (hṛdaya), for this [heart-]mantra is not [of that kind].

Because it consists of the Heart (*hṛdayamayatva*) and because it transcends the forms of the Mantra-Maheśvaras and their Maheśvaras, this Heart is indeed not to be written in books; it has been determined that its attainment occurs in reality only through the grace of the supreme descent of power (*para-śaktipāta*). Likewise, "whoever [it may be]"—and so forth.
In this context, independence from caste, vows, ritual conduct, and so forth, is intended;
for here, realization alone is primary. That yogin attains perfection—since they maintain that "yoga is unity. (p. 253)
And its initiation (dīkṣā) is characterized by the bestowing of knowledge and the destruction of illusion; as it has been said: "It bestows the true essence of knowledge and destroys all impurity.
Because its nature consists of bestowing and destroying, it is indeed proclaimed as 'initiation' (dīkṣā)."
Thus [it is said]. The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis, and therefore it should be understood as applying to everything. Thus he says: "He alone is the yogi destined for success;
he alone is the initiated one, eternally. (18)
By the mere knowledge of this, he is known by all powers,
by all deities, and by all the omniscient ones through all their powers; indeed, it is while knowing this very thing that he is known.
Whatever is known by them as well is known by this [consciousness] through mere awareness, as before;
"by all the powers" (sarvābhiḥ śaktibhiḥ) is the instrumental case used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
Likewise,
[he is] common to the family of the Śākinīs.
For it may indeed exist even without yoga. || 19 ||

By the mere knowledge of this, even without the yoga of practice— which consists of the attainment of identity [with the deity] upon the fall of the illusory body— one becomes the Lord of the Wheel of Power (śakticakreśvara), whose nature is the universal vibration (sāmānyaspanda) and the form of Akula, belonging to the Śākini-kula, which is characterized by specific vibration (viśeṣaspanda). || 19 ||
Moreover,
one who was ignorant of the rules becomes a knower of the rules with respect to the sacrifice. (20)
The rule is as follows: action and knowledge—whosoever lacks this dyad is a bound soul (*paśu*). As it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*:
"The bound soul is eternal, indeed formless, ignorant, inactive, devoid of qualities, yet [potentially] sovereign;
he is all-pervasive, situated within the belly of Māyā, and intent upon seeking the means for experience."

Thus, even that animal, by the mere knowledge of this, becomes one who knows the procedure—that is, he is both the agent and the knower—and [attains] the instrument for the connection with the object. (p. 255)
The sacrifice is born again for him, and even that which was incomplete becomes complete—because the heart consists of everything. || 20 ||
For thus,
beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Māyā, [the sequence] resides within the body of Brahmā.
Śiva, who extends from Viśva to Ananta, is considered the supreme triad of powers. || 21 ||
From the world-spheres beginning with the principle of Earth (dharātattva) up to the principle of Māyā belonging to Kālāgni, [is the domain] of Brahmā, who is the letter *sa*.

From the world-sphere of Viśva within the body of the letter *kṣa*, starting from the principle of Vidyā and so forth, up to Śiva in the form of the power of Anāśrita—ananta being the letter *a*—there is the end (*anta*), which is the supreme triad of powers consisting of the Visarga; and that supreme [state] has been described.
And [the word] "with the vowel *ṛ*" (sārṇena), and so forth. || 21 ||
Whatever exists within that,
established upon the pure path—
The subtle one attains pure, divine knowledge before long.

Whatever object is established— meaning that which has come into various states (the suffix *-ita* is applied here according to the *tārakādi* class)— that which exists in its manifold state is pure when it resides within the seed-syllable of the Heart; and that very thing is the Lord’s knowledge, the *aṇu*, because it is "breathed" (*aṇyate*), "animated" (*prāṇiti*), and "sounds" (*aṇati*) due to its limited articulation.
The "foremost" (mūrdhanya), by the power of the Lord, very soon attains [the state of] being foremost through the form of sounding;
becoming foremost, he very soon attains divine knowledge.
However, this is not the case for those who, despite possessing the nature of pure awakening, do not have supreme agency.
These emanations, distinct from his own self, were created by the Lord through the cessation of his agency.
According to this principle, [the self] consists precisely of pure awakening; as it is stated in the *Śrī Spandakārikās*:
"Then, when the moon and sun have dissolved into that great void, the deluded one becomes awakened and unobscured, like the state of deep sleep."
Thus, this indeed is the mutual distinction between the knowledge of Brahman and the knowledge of Śiva. To explain:
when one has transcended *māyā*, the attainment of Brahman occurs in one case, while in the other, there is the state of *vijñānākala*;
such a sequence must be discerned here by those possessing subtle discernment. Furthermore, even if one lacks such higher awakening (*aparā-bodha*), there is no fault whatsoever.
p.
257) How is he the impeller of that? [The intention here is as follows: Śiva alone, the Guru, is to be known as the impeller of that sovereignty.]

Once the state of pure essential nature has been attained, although sovereignty characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) is indeed established without effort, there are nevertheless two possible courses therein: that which arises from necessity (*niyati*), as it has been said: "All those such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others are colored by attachment to limited knowledge (*vidyā-rāga*)."
They do not know the supreme reality... [omitted] ... ||
Thus, for that very purpose it was said, "and that which impels it" (*taccodaka*); likewise it was stated:
"It attains the status of mantra through the awakening brought about by Ananteśa.
For that same reason, it is said here "that which impels it"; therefore, it is not merely knowledge alone.

Because it is stated that "the reason consisting of one's own nature is characterized by self-reflection," the primacy of contemplative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is taught in the Śaiva scriptures; for this very reason, it is said that "perfect knowledge arises from oneself, from the scripture, and from the guru.
Thus, Śiva is to be known.
The Supreme Lord is omniscient; he is all-pervading, stainless, pure, satisfied, self-abiding, and holy. || 23 ||

He who is the teacher who impels one toward that [Śiva] is to be known as Śiva himself; Śiva alone is that impeller. And he is to be known as the Knower himself, the abode of his own self, for he extends (tanoti) his own movements (ayān)—that is, the states of being whose nature is consciousness. All of this has indeed been determined in detail. || 23 ||

Having thus explained in detail, he concludes with the essential meaning: "He concludes"— the five members, namely the proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*), constitute the parts of reasoning (*tarka*) for the sake of convincing another.

Thus, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the probandum by way of incorporating the meaning established by the four members [of the syllogism]; the sense is that it "concludes" (*nigamayati*) by establishing the proven object.
For example: [as contained within] the seed of a banyan tree...
The great tree is of the nature of power (śakti);
likewise, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings resides within the seed-syllable of the heart.
Thus, for one who knows this according to reality,
initiation leading to nirvāṇa becomes certain.
It is devoid of oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter. || 25 ||

In this context, that which is non-existent [is illustrated] as follows: "In the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, it is stated that the All-pervasive Lord is connected even with such things as the horn of a hare. Likewise...
If non-existence does not manifest, then existence alone remains;
if existence manifests, then because it has the nature of existence, existence alone remains.
Likewise,
what specific excellence of existence does a sky-flower possess over a [real] flower,
such that the world is animated by its manifestation, and yet manifestation is common to all?
Thus,
whatever extent of expansion belongs to the Lord of Teachers during the state of the unfolding of the universe,
that same extent occurs during the closing of the universe in the state of cosmic density (*kalila*).
Thus, it should be understood that the analogy of the liquid inside a peacock's egg is clearly established here. [Until then, nothing—thus the universe has been described.

And because it is the soul of the universe, just as within a banyan seed the sprout, branches, leaves, and fruits exist in their appropriate forms, so too does this entire universe exist within the heart; such thorough knowledge is itself the indubitable initiation into liberation, as it has been said:
This alone is the attainment of the nectar of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into Nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva.

Thus, although other initiations (*dīkṣā*) might also bestow enjoyments (*bhoga*), this very thorough knowledge is initiation in the true sense; for that reason alone it possesses supremacy here, due to its superiority even over the Kula scriptures. For instance, among the marks on a scale, even though the measurement increases higher and higher, there is an infinite difference in the degree of rise and fall.
Thus, in the higher and higher levels of reality (tattva), there is indeed an infinite interval between the perceptions of space, time, and experience.

In this very way, it may even exceed thirty-six; for since initiation is nothing other than pure consciousness (*saṃvedana*), it has been said that the hero or the yoginī who has entered into this consciousness possesses their own and the supreme state, which is eternally arisen.

"By one who has been initiated and so forth, and is sustained by the nature of the 'I' (ahaṃrūpa) whose reality has been determined as consisting of the Lord Parabhairava— the sovereign of the wheel of twelve deities who are the rays of the internal and external organs of the illusory [nature]"—
in this way, the unsurpassed state (anuttarapada) occurs precisely through the non-abandonment of its own transcendent form.
Having been determined at length through both detailed and concise explanations, this which is now to be spoken is stated:
in all the scriptures,
it is taught that those Supreme Lords abide, concealed, having assumed human bodies.
Those who worship the threefold purpose within the heart, even if it is devoid of vigor;
Thus, how can there be worship of this [deity]? Nevertheless, one must contemplate her here as well with unsurpassed reality, precisely because she is unsurpassed.
Desiring to resolve this inquiry, he introduces another passage:
"In the head, in the mouth, and in the heart..."
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the secret parts and likewise on the physical form, and having tied the topknot, (p. 261).
[She who has been] consecrated with twenty-seven mantras. || 26 ||
Having first given three claps of the hands, one should apply the binding of each of the ten directions individually.
With sound, for the pacification of obstacles. || 27 ||
Then, one should sprinkle all the flowers and other offerings in sequence with water consecrated by reciting the *śikhā-mantra* the prescribed number of times.
Either upon a linga or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 28 ||
The preparation of the seat is performed with a flower consecrated fourteen times;
there, the hero should worship the emanation.
Then, once again, [one should perform] the seating. || 29 ||
Having encapsulated the emanation,
one should thereafter commence the worship.
Perfectly complete with all the principles (tattvas) and adorned with all ornaments.
One should worship the Goddess Maheśānī,
consecrated with twenty-seven mantras; thereafter, with fragrant flowers...
One should worship according to one's ability. || 31 ||
One should worship with supreme devotion and offer oneself as well;
thus is sacrifice described.
This same rule applies even in the case of a fire-related rite. || 32 ||

The crown of the head and the other [limbs], though appearing externally as appropriate forms, are in reality nothing other than the manifestations of consciousness, will, knowledge, and action— the essence of Īśāna and the others— which constitute the true nature of the elements from space to earth, described as being of fivefold nature and identical with the Supreme Brahman; this is known from the indicative mark of the mantra, just as it is with the mantras themselves.
1. To the head of Īśāna; 2. To the face of Tatpuruṣa; 3. To the heart of Aghora.
4. To the secret Vāmadeva; 5. To the form of Sadyojāta. (p. 263)
Thus, in this context, that which consists of the non-differentiation of the pentad is the form at the beginning and the conclusion;

in the middle, however, when differentiation shines forth, each one of the five possesses a fivefold nature—thus there are twenty-five. It is precisely here that the *mālinī* and other mantras enter, as do the three goddesses.
Each of these, through association with the triad beginning with desire (*icchā*), attains a ninefold nature;

furthermore, by virtue of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), they again fall into a threefold state—thus they are remembered as twenty-seven. This is by means of the heart-seed-syllable (*hṛdbīja*) [HRĪM], which consists of the sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) that conceives of everything from the form of the Earth (*dharaṇī*) up to the End (the Absolute).

The bondage of that [power] which is metaphorically designated by the forms of the supreme consciousness (*paracit*), intellect (*buddhi*), touch (*sparśa*), breath (*prāṇa*), the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and the exit (*vāha*)— consisting of identity whose essence is the non-differentiation of all— is present even in each of the individual locations such as the head and so forth,
wherein all [faces] beginning with the eastern one are mutually qualifiers; and this has indeed been determined.
The directions themselves are nothing other than pots and so forth, as they are indicated precisely by the determination that everything is of the nature of everything.

And these [directions], in relation to themselves, are only ten. Even there, this very thing is the bond—the realization of the Self—and this occurs through three *tālas*, wherein a *tāla* is the resting in *pratiṣṭhā*. In that regard:
That which begins with the letter *sa* is the heart itself;
and that [heart] is the sound *sa*, ending in the *madhyamā* state, for sound is indeed the act of sounding, and that is precisely the *madhyamā* [speech], as opposed to *vaikharī*.

This has been stated many times: because they consist of that as their remainder. And this is the pacification of the stains of the waves of differentiation—the essence of which is contraction consisting of fragmentation—within the undivided Supreme Self whose nature is non-duality;
it is indeed identity with the ocean of the non-dual Bhairava, as the venerable Somānanda-pāda has said.
May Śiva, who has entered our very form, perform the warding off of obstacles by himself through his own self by means of the supreme power; salutations to that pervasive Self.

Thus it is said. In this very way, water consecrated twenty-seven times constitutes the ritual for the *argha* vessel. Here, all the water is of the nature of the fluid of the Heart; because it is unrestricted and because it bestows freedom from limitation, it is explained as being the flower and the *liṅga*.

This point has also been definitively established: within the reality that is the Self of the universe, during the act of sitting, both the locus and the agent—the seat and the sitter—are conceived as possessing independence, being conceived through their own autonomy.

By the fourteenth vowel, *au*, it has already been stated that this very [Heart] is of the nature of a trident. "Emanation" (*sṛṣṭi*) refers to the Heart consisting of identity with the entire alphabet from *A* to *Kṣa*; it is Power (*śakti*), the Secret (*guhya*), and thus Heroism (*vīratva*). For this very reason, the entire seat (*āsana*) is also located therein, because the support and the supported are mutually one in form, as it has been said:
"Seeing the Self abiding in all beings...

and so forth—because each letter from *a* to *kṣa* of this "encapsulating" (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*) emanation, as well as the whole, arises and is withdrawn into the Supreme Reality itself by means of the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdayabīja*), there is no infinite regress; this has already been stated.
And the unification of creation consists in the form of bliss arising from the agitation of the union of both;

there is also the consumption of the substance produced from that. Here, regarding the mere sequence of the cognition of words, when there is fullness through all the *tattvas* being perfectly non-different and inseparable everywhere—even down to a single atom—then [this occurs].

"Universal sustenance" (*samantād bharaṇam*) means making everything one's own; or rather, by all the subjects (*pramātṛ*)—whether they be jars, pleasure, animals, humans, *viriñci*, *viṣṇu*, *rudra*, mantras, or *sadāśiva*—who are the measures of its parts, the fact that it possesses parts while having "I" as its single essence (*ekarasa*) is indeed established. For this very reason...

The meditation on specific forms, weapons, and so forth is not mentioned here, because that is to be accomplished later; for one who desires to ascend [the path] and seeks only these much-needed goals, (p.

If it is asked, "How should he ascend?"—to whom does this state of being a seeker belong? Let him, then, not ascend; rather, let him rely upon the very prescriptions of the *Siddhātantra* and other such texts, which are delineated with that specific intention and which involve a limitation such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth. For one is not authorized in the uncontracted, unsurpassed state (*anuttara-pada*).

Thus, this very yoga is eternally arisen; as for the determination regarding perfumes, flowers, and so forth, the word "with" (*saha*) has the sense of accompaniment, and the instrumental case ending is stated in that very context.
One should worship with the Supreme [Consciousness] itself, whose form is the Heart. How?
With devotion—that is, with a self surrendered through the penetration of identity—with devotion fashioned by oneself.
Through the distinction between the object of worship and the worshipper, it is indeed the Object of Worship itself that creates [the worshipper];
for it is the supreme ultimate reality consisting of autonomous consciousness—not insentient like a jar or other objects—by virtue of the power of unsurpassed sovereignty.
This is the specific distinction here, as stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
The Lord, having fashioned his own self— which is by nature free from duality— through the volitions of Īśvara and other [deities] by means of his sovereignty, engages in worldly transaction.
Thus, through devotion (*bhakti*), secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and worship, the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattva*) is indicated;

for in all actions, the recognition of this very nature serves as the means (*upāya*). Just as in the mastery of the letters of *māyā*, the recognition of the form [of the supreme] is the means, one should offer oneself just as even that [recognition] enters into the potency of the phonemes (*varṇavīrya*).
Since there is no other offering (*nivedya*) [to be presented], one should thus cause oneself alone to be experienced in its entirety as the unsurpassed state (*niruttarapada*),
in accordance with the reality of the Unsurpassed (*anuttarasattā*). Here, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).

For it has been stated that [the Self] exists eternally as being of this very nature; however, according to the perspective of contemplative worship (*upāsā*), this applies even to ritual injunctions (*niyoga*) and so forth.
Thus, "worship" (*yajana*) is precisely that manifestation which consists in the unfolding of the ultimate, pure Śiva-nature—that which is everywhere, always, and entirely manifest.
Through the worship of the deity who is the consciousness of Supreme Bhairava,
and by effecting a state of perfect identity with Her, there occurs everywhere the cessation of the sense of ownership consisting of the limited nature of one's own self.

And because this very fire-rite consists of giving— which is the act of transferring one's own nature, which is essentially the power of Śiva consisting of the fullness of consciousness, to another— it blazes with a voracious appetite for swallowing the fuel of all objects and the seeds of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

In the great splendor of Supreme Bhairava, which is constantly kindled from the fire-drill of the Supreme Power (paraśakti) stirred by the agitation of the union of Śiva, there is the intense heat of abundant clarified butter in the form of total attachment;

through the oblation—that is, internal combustion—this very procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), extending even to initiation (*dīkṣā*), is the only one, and no other whatsoever exists separately. Thus.
The intended meaning is as follows: (p. 268) This mantra, which is the thorough knowledge of one's own true nature, is the ultimate reality.
This initiation and this yoga are unsurpassed even in the context of ritual action.
For this very reason, it was stated previously [in the commentary on the phrase "the unsurpassed even of the unsurpassed," which was already mentioned earlier]:
"It is not as elsewhere that one crosses over by means of the subsequent section on knowledge (*jñānagrantha*) following the practice of mantra-worship and so forth; it is not so here.
That which was stated in the aphorism "the unsurpassed even of the unsurpassed" has been fully established by this concluding section of the text.

Since the heart itself constitutes the nature of the sacrificial initiation (*yāga-dīkṣā-kriyā*), the word "nature" (*rūpatva*)—which is heard at the end of a *dvandva* compound—is connected to each individual term [according to the rule that "a word heard at the end of a *dvandva* is connected with each member"].

And because that [heart] is the Absolute (*anuttara*). However, according to the venerable Somānandapāda, the purification of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and so forth [are performed], for they are indeed of the nature of Śiva and Śakti.
The *sruva* and *sruc* ladles should be placed facing each other; such is the sequence even in the external ritual.
Furthermore, by demonstrating all-endurance (*sarvasahatva*), it is described with the intention of its indivisibility (*akhaṇḍitatva*).

Thus, at the beginning, there are also the divisions of the limbs, the heart, and the dust-particles (*dhūli-bheda*), as well as the division of the powder (*cūrṇikā*) and so forth, which consists of the form of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). That is its nature.

Nothing here is tenable, nor is it logically consistent; neither does it exist, nor can its status as dependent upon lower treatises be established, for this has already been almost entirely determined.
What occurs through such worship? Thus, having properly performed the ritual of worship, he enters [the practice].
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) becomes perfected through recollection.
Thus, even amidst constant worldly activities, by remembering the seed-syllable alone and having performed the ritual of worship through that very remembrance,
one proceeds with excellence— transcending all other scriptures from the *Kula* texts down to the *Śaiva* and *Vaiṣṇava* traditions.
One who is possessed by the form of the Lord Bhairava-bhaṭṭāraka,

whose grand display of creative play (*bhāvakrīḍā*) is fashioned through the power of the wonder of the consciousness of both self and other, becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) according to the principle stated previously; thus, this is merely a recurring experience and nothing else whatsoever.
Recollection has been explained. In the Śrīmata scriptures,
it is stated that even a practitioner whose heart has not yet entered the essence of the reality of *vīrya*, by virtue of the majesty of the sequential worship (*kramapūjā*),
becomes fully perfected through the intense recollection of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), having attained the power of the *mantra* known as the *hṛdaya*.
Precisely through the greatness of the Krama worship, by virtue of its supreme excellence, or spontaneously from the mouth of the venerable Guru who is himself pleased—

From the lotus, one attains the potency of the mantra which consists of the heart, and thus becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta); this is the meaning. Here, the worship of the door-attendants, the retinue, and the guru does not bring merit; in this context, the word "not" (na) should be applied according to the "lamp-on-the-threshold" maxim (dehalī-dīpa-nyāya), and thus it neither brings merit nor—
The meaning is that it brings about the destruction of [the opposing view]. Or, it does not carry [that consequence], for that very reason it was described by the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda.
Here, however, the *kulaparvas* [are defined]: "A *parvan* is so called because of the fulfillment (*pūraṇa*) of the injunction; and it is sixfold:
the general (*sāmānya*), the general-general (*sāmānyasāmānya*), the general-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), the particular-general (*viśeṣasāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), and..."
Regarding the term "particular-particular" (*viśeṣaviśeṣa*), this has been explained in detail elsewhere. Its procedure is as follows:

even one who has not seen the maṇḍala, by worshipping on the festival days, attains in just one year the fruit described for a *putraka*, even without the performance of the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth; likewise is the procedure for the sacred thread (*pavitraka*), which must be performed according to the prescribed rule.

And as it has been stated, one who fulfills the command of the Supreme Lord finds everything to be fruitless without the *pavitraka*; therefore, the determination of its timing should be sought elsewhere. Its procedure is as follows: one may make it from materials ranging from gold, pearls, and gems down to silk thread, cotton, or *kuśa* grass; and it should have knots equal in number to the *tattvas*.
If one possesses the means, one should perform the *pavitraka* rite every month, or at least once every four months;

if it is not performed, one should recite the prescribed expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Even a wise man, if he possesses wealth, incurs sin by failing to perform it, as well as the fault of disparaging sacred knowledge. Furthermore, the term *pavitra* refers to the perfection of the ritual procedure of worship.
O wise ones, that wherein all things appear internally and which shines everywhere— that alone is the one throbbing reality, the supreme heart.
p.

271) Whether it be a she-donkey or even a mare, having simultaneously expanded that which is the source of the birth of its own world, and then contracting it— having contracted it, turned it inward, and then expanded it—

Having turned [the senses] outward, one rejoices; one experiences an excess of bliss within oneself. In the same way, there is the great bliss (*mahānanda*) of both Bhairava and Bhairavī, which means the state of emission (*visargabhū*). For this indeed is the unique, non-common form of this supreme Light, which is always present.
"Because it performs creation and destruction; for otherwise, there would be no distinction between this [consciousness] and insentient things.
Thus he rejoices in his heart.
Likewise, one should worship within the heart of the Suṣumṇā, the center of both great joys,
the throbbing Heart characterized by emanation.
Whether one is meditating, remembering, reflecting, or acting anywhere at all, that in which one finds rest and from which the heart overflows with joy—that is it. As it has been said:
"When the great root-pain is unified within the innate heart..."
One finds rest in that which is beyond, through the yoga of filling all things.

Now, let it be seen that through the very fullness of that [consciousness], which consists of the immersion into the universe, there exists within the repose of the Self of Light the perception "I am."
In the supreme reflective awareness (*anuttara-vimarśa*), which is initially devoid of activity and the like,
the reflective awareness of consciousness— the supreme I-consciousness— should flash forth as it first unfolds.
Thus [it is said].
That alone is the one supreme conceptual knowledge wherein exist the principles (tattvas),
the expansion of the worlds, and the subjects beginning with Śiva and ending with the bound souls (paśus).
Discovering each their own diverse ultimate nature, they indeed manifest that very diversity and proceed toward that supreme, variegated consciousness.
Even regarding the knowledge of the ten substances, the ritual actions, and the sacred sites, and so forth,
his worship is constantly active, proceeding entirely without hesitation.
In the Trika teaching, it is declared that in this worship, the mere sequential worship along with the Kula festivals and the purificatory threads constitutes perfect correctness.
As it has been said:
"The bodily [nature] of fluids is characterized by vigor; the seed of creation for the castes;
the Trika scripture among all teachings; and Bhairavī is the state of all liberations."
The attainment of the state of a lay devotee, the observance of vows, and the conduct of a hero;
likewise, within the sacred festivals, there are the family festivals in the Teaching.
The *pavitraka* is for the fulfillment of all sacrifices;
those who do not perform the *pavitraka* rite four, three, two, or even once [are deficient].

They do not know the festival of the lineage (kulaparva), and thus their spiritual vigor does not flourish. They find no radiance in the throbbing vibration; they have abandoned the supreme purity of the Self. O Goddess, know that at all times one must remain free from doubt; worship the innate state (sahaja) with devotion—this is the path of liberation. *Phura-i phuraṇama alaha kā-avyaha para de-u sohi a-usa magāha savya kāla nīsaṃkasa-ū sahajā jāṇu pūjasa pajja i i u u ha.* [Note: This is a mystical verse from the Bhaktamālā of Nābhādās, composed in the Brajbhāṣā dialect of Hindi.]

Thus, the nature of the unsurpassed has been determined in detail—that state wherein there is no room for meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the like, and which consists solely of profound contemplation (*prasaṃkhyāna*), characterized by a firm sense of wonder.

Wherein [the scripture] maintains a succession of preeminent means, culminating in the firmness of practice characterized by the internalization of the essential nature of the characteristics, yoga must be taught to those desiring spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*). For even when the accomplishments of visible yoga are brought about through one's own autonomy, they remain subordinate to worldly convention and necessity.
Because it does not transgress the necessity of the form of the Supreme Lord’s established order, as stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*: "Nevertheless,
for the sake of the work of painting [the world], the means must be described with care," even there,
there is no fragmentation whatsoever of that which is of the nature of the Absolute (anuttara)— just as in the case of one who exerts effort out of a desire to achieve a visible result.

Since even the attainment of that [state], the repose in its fruit, and so forth, consist solely of the Supreme, this is nevertheless called a "weak descent of power" (manda-śaktipāta) from the perspective of one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), because it is characterized by a state of being largely incomplete.
To define that path of yoga, the remainder of the treatise begins: "The seed-syllable, devoid of beginning and end, expanding within the midst of the lunar days."
One should meditate on that which resides within the heart-lotus;
one should constantly practice the portion of the Moon.
p.

274) This very seed-syllable of the heart, because it is devoid of a lamp [of external light], because it is empty of coming and going, and because it is perpetually arisen, is without beginning or end; that very same [seed] has reached a state of blossoming fullness, situated in the midst of the lunar days (tithis).

Because it is the heart, one should meditate upon that very [lotus]—which, by metaphorical attribution, possesses the nature of contraction and expansion—as being in the state of a lotus, within the bulb (kanda) or the secret place, using the heart itself. Furthermore, he describes its meditation: one should "emit" or project the lunar portion consisting of sixteen digits, having the form of the moon, all around—that is, on every side—of this full moon, by means of the digit situated in the pericarp of the heart.

Having attained the touch of nectar drawn from the location of the arising of flowers and other [substances] within one’s own respective *dvādaśānta*, and being sealed by the *kākacañcupuṭa-mudrā* characterized by the kissing [of the breath] following the upward-rising *nāda*,
there arises again the *nāda* spreading from the heart-lunar [channel], which expands through the tasting of the cool nectar-fluid that has receded from that [previous state].
Having again drunk the nectar churned from the moon— which is now full—
and having come to rest solely upon the letter *sa* (sakāra) within the vowel-less (*anacka*) syllable that arises as the digit of the sun,
one whose body is graced by horripilation, trembling, rising tears, shaking, and paralysis should practice.

Bhaṭṭa Dhaneśvaraśarman: One should deposit within the heart the mere letter *sa*, which is devoid of beginning and end, together with the sixteen forms starting from the lunar days (*tithi*), according to the sequence of the consumption of the digits (*kalā*),
moving like the drawing up of water by a reed-pipe.
Simultaneously within the root foundation (mūlādhāra), the auspicious bulb (bhadra-kanda), the heart, and the facial mudrās, which are pervaded by the movement of consciousness.
When the solar and lunar digits (kalās) have been consumed through the process of attaining the streams of slow, medium, fast, and extremely fast [recitation],

one should render it devoid of beginning and end; that is, by means of the initial and final [letters]— in relation to the Mātṛkā, this means being free from the vowels *au* and the consonant *sa*— it becomes the fixed (*dhruva*) seed-syllable whose power is realized through the method of analytical separation.

One should meditate upon that very nectarine portion of the moon, consisting of sixteen parts, which is the emission (*visarga*), the center of the fifteen expanding lunar days (*tithi*); it is the sixteenth day, devoid of lunar days and swallowed by time, and beyond even that is what is called the seventeenth digit (*kalā*)— one should contemplate that very thing within the heart-lotus.

"One should practice this constantly," so say our teachers. For instance: the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka Soma exists as the friction resulting from the agitation of the union (*samāpatti*) with the Blessed Lady Umā—an agitation consisting in the churning of the *tattvas*. He is a portion of that whole, the possessor of parts, whose nature is the perfect "I-consciousness" (*ahamātman*).
Blue, pleasure, and so forth— he thus practices this by means of the rosary of the axle of the revolving wheel of emanation and withdrawal that turns back upon its own nature;
that which is contemplated as the truth is indeed this ever-arisen heart-recitation (*hṛdayajapa*).
The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
Others, however, [state that] the movement from the heart-center to the *dvādaśānta*, which measures thirty-six finger-breadths, occurs there.

Having shone forth in the form of the sun and rested for the duration of half a *tuṭi*, when the lunar digit (*somakalā*) known as the indestructible nectar— the nature of emission (*visarga*)— arises, filling each lunar digit one by one during every *tuṭi* measuring two and a quarter finger-breadths, until the fifteenth *tuṭi* is complete.

In the heart-lotus, [the breath] becomes full for the duration of half a *tuṭi*, and there too it comes to rest; thus, the movement (*cāra*) consisting of sixteen *tuṭis* amounts to thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
In this state, it is devoid of beginning and end because it does not set, and it is contained within the blossoming [moments] beginning with the second.

"Having joined the lunar portion, which is the nature of the visarga, with the [solar] portion in the center of the heart-lotus, one should practice the 'devouring of the digits' (kalāgrāsa) while meditating upon that which consists of seventeen principles through constant cultivation. All such instructions should be understood as entirely appropriate. And here, there is an infinite explanation through repetition.

Because it is a *sūtra*, this is entirely appropriate; for the teachers have stated that it is called a *sūtra* because it strings together (*sūtraṇāt*) infinite meanings, and that the *Triṃśikā* is an unsurpassed *sūtra*. This applies likewise to the preceding verses and *sūtras*. (33)
What occurs when there is such practice? To this he says:
"Whatever desires he may desire—"
One shall swiftly attain those various [goals];
from this, omniscience becomes manifest—of this there is no doubt. || 34 ||

Thus, through such practice, whatever one desires, that very thing is attained without delay; for one who possesses the vigor of a heart composed entirely of that [desire], there arises a specific force of support from the expansion of will,
and through the exertion and intensity of effort accompanied by enthusiasm, there occurs a repeated practice characterized by the firm establishment of that state.
"What need is there for much [explanation]? One attains omniscience—the state of being the very self of Supreme Bhairava—in this very body.

Having stated all this, it is concluded at the end: "For in the final withdrawal of the expansion, upon attaining the reality of Akula, which is the nature of repose, one becomes Bhairava"—as has been stated more than once. (34)
This is the concluding passage:
"In this way, the attainment of the fruit of the mantra is the Rudrayāmala."
Through the practice of this, perfection is attained, and omniscience is reached. || 35 ||

"The fruit of the mantras belonging to other scriptures and of their phonemes is obtained in this way and not otherwise"— thus [it is said] at the conclusion; for the *Yāmala* of Rudra and Rudrāṇī begins from the expansion of the reflective awareness of their own essential nature, which consists of questions and answers in an indivisible form.

"Up to the manifestation of hundreds of endless and incalculable cycles of creation and dissolution externally, that which is within is precisely withdrawn into Akula"—this is the conclusion regarding *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment).
"From the practice of this, omniscience [is attained]"—this is the conclusion regarding the fruit of yoga. For this is eternally manifest for everyone.
Auspiciousness.
Thus, he who acts as a bee at the lotus feet of the illustrious Maheśvara— who is intent on uplifting the people who have sought refuge—
has composed this commentary, which contains within it an investigation of the *Trikarahasya*.
Having received [his] birth from Cukhalaka of Kaśmīra. || 1 ||
Who could forcibly weigh this [reality], saying "it is only this much," when the words of the venerable Śambhu have transcended all limitations?
This indeed appears within the Self of all; since it has appeared to me, the wise should not turn their backs on this. || 2 ||
It produces perfectly firm knowledge for the ignorant person, or for one who possesses doubt or error;
and it establishes in the heart that certainty which has already taken root.
Such is this composition that it brings about agreement.
With a heart ascended by a continuous stream of contemplation upon this synthesis of meaning and aesthetic flavor, one should reflect even further than this:
that even if there were a subsequent [reality], it could not possibly endure; this is not so.
This is the stainless staircase for one desiring to ascend to the supreme state.

In Kaśmīra, King Yaśaskara had a preeminent minister named the illustrious Vallabha, who was a twice-born man of noble birth and whose form was celebrated for its excellence. His own son, who was a worthy recipient of the path of universal renown due to his complete virtues, [was Abhinanda].
The illustrious Śauri, the sole ocean of jewels consisting of meditation upon the feet of the one who bears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. || 5 ||
She is the abode of virtue, the source of the expansion of another’s fame, the ground for playfulness, the birthplace and sustenance of compassion for the entire world,
and his very own companion named Śrīmad-Vatsalikā, radiant with devotion.
Her inner disposition is intensely stirred, and her mind expands in the praise of Śaṅkara.

His very self was the twice-born man named Karṇa, who had mastered the creation and maintenance of the world, and whose sole delight lay in the meditation upon, the worship of, and reflection on Śaṅkara.
He who, having abandoned attachment to sense objects even in childhood and youth, takes refuge in this steadfast path of inquiry which uproots the cycle of worldly existence; || 7 ||
My own brother, whose mind is firmly established in the teaching of Śiva, is named Manorathagupta; desiring to attain the Supreme Self,
he wishes to discern the entirety of the scriptures and tantras.
In order to attain the supreme state of Śiva and for the sake of shattering worldly existence. || 8 ||

He was one whose sole delight was in the Śiva scriptures, a knower of words, sentences, and means of valid cognition— [where "word" refers to grammar, "sentence" to Mīmāṃsā, and "means of valid cognition" to logic]—
and he was named Rāmadeva, his noble birth being fully adorned.
This exposition of the path, which I have composed with a heart deeply rooted in performing what is dear and beneficial [to others], [is now complete].
May it lead to the attainment of auspiciousness for all. || 10 ||

Having attained birth within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi) under the name Atrigupta, that foremost of beings entered the illustrious land of Kashmir, which is an incarnation of the Moon-crested Lord.
Whose peripheral regions were purified by innumerable [beings]. || 11 ||
Born from a great lineage, having obtained his birth through the protection of a boar,
he was one who turned his back upon the course of worldly existence.
With his mind fixed solely on Śiva, he was named Cukṣala. || 12 ||
Therefore, having obtained a state of embodiment purified by the Supreme Lord from among all categories of objects that have been clearly distinguished, [one attains liberation].
Having attained fearlessness, he who is named Abhinavagupta caused this secret reality of the Trika to enter [into his understanding]. || 13 ||
Salutation is better for those whose hearts are barren of solitude;

yet others, though they strive for solitude, have not reached its further shore—fie on those dull-witted ones! But as for another who stands firm in the conviction that the path has discernment as its essence:
Perhaps even one person in a hundred thousand might bring my efforts to fruition.
For those who display even indolence toward discerning their own true self, no fruit whatsoever shall be harvested from their petitions other than self-inflicted torment;
whereas for those of steady intellect who exert themselves for the sake of discerning this entire universe, [the fruit is different].
I myself have performed this respectful prostration with my head in order to entreat them. || 15 ||

Wandering about themselves, those of dull intellect cause the circle of deluded beings to wander; having made it their own by means of the power of naming the qualities, they bind it firmly with bonds.
Thus seeing the cattle following one after another for the sake of carrying heavy burdens, [the wise feel compassion].
I have fashioned this trident of knowledge for the purpose of severing those bonds.
Though I have been led astray by many who consider themselves teachers of reality,
even the two syllables "tat-tvam" (That-Thou) [have not been understood].
Whose tongues did not touch [it]? || 17 ||
The Supreme Lord, whose heart is moved by compassion to uplift those who have sought refuge [in Him].
The glorious Lord Śambhu has directed me toward this reality.
The doctrine of the venerable Somānanda has, as it were, entered of its own accord into the heart that discerns the stainless state of ultimate reality.
This has been composed by me after due reflection. || 19 ||
O Goddesses, who are filled with the intense bliss produced by the movement within the wheel of the heart, whose upward-pointing shafts of gnosis are expert at shattering the millions of our bonds,
may this mind, speech, and body— freed from the arising of the fear of worldly existence— be perfectly established in you.
That which was woven by him, as it were, forcibly enters my heart immediately and brings about grace. || 20 ||
Having entered into the state of a teacher, you have appointed me to the sequence of duties such as exposition;
therefore, O Goddesses, this fickleness of my speech and mind—
O you who stand with beautiful grace, poised and detached from the wheel [of worldly existence], please forgive us. || 21 ||
This *Tattvavivaraṇa* on the *Parātriṃśikā* is completed.
This *Triṃśikā* has been expounded in one hundred and nineteen [verses];
it shall shatter the knots within all the Trika scriptures.
Thus ends the venerable *Parātriṃśikā*,
and here [is] the commentary by His Honor, the most excellent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the venerable...
Composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta,
[this work] rests upon the true sciences (sadvidyā) of both the texts and the learned.
When the array [of the teaching] had undergone decline due to the operation of time, [the author],
endowed with the vigor of true discernment and solely intent upon upholding the various aspects of the True Dharma, acted for the sake of its practical application.
Having deliberated with his chief ministers who were devoted to righteousness, the illustrious sovereign of Kaśmīra established [this work],
which is the essence of spiritual knowledge and worldly science.
That which is the principal office for the extraction of texts. || 2 ||

May this work, which has been refined through completion, purification, and exposition by virtuous men who have entered upon the right livelihood and rely on Mukunda and Rāma as their presiding lords, be successful.
This completed work is for the welfare of virtuous people. || 3 ||
(Tilaka) May this [offering] become an auspicious dedication to one's own self as Śiva.
